lens: Anabaptist / Mennonite (Schleitheim Confession, Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective 1995)

simulation.headline: Firmly synergist, memorialist, covenantal
simulation.comment: Answers as a typical informed Mennonite (CFMP 1995 / Schleitheim): S1 -2, S2 +2, S3 -1 (faith is a gift of grace, but not tied to unconditional election); S4 -1 (Christ present in the gathered body, not the elements), S5 +2, S6 -2; S7 +1, S8 -1, S9 +1 (prophecy weighed by the congregation, 1 Cor 14:29); S10 -1, S11 +1 (one people of God, uneasy with 'true Israel'), S12 -2; S13 -1 (creeds have derived authority only), S14 +2, S15 +1 (the congregation tests interpretation, CFMP Art. 4, but 'the church... final interpreter' reads as magisterium); S16 -1, S17 -1 (Mennonite worship is planned and plain, not 'free-form'), S18 -2 (communion twice a year to monthly). Raw: grace = (-1)(-2)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-1) = 5 -> round(11/12*100) = 92; table = (-1)(-1)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-2) = 5 -> 92; spirit = (-1)(1)+(1)(-1)+(-1)(1) = -3 -> round(3/12*100) = 25; kingdom = (1)(-1)+(-1)(1)+(1)(-2) = -4 -> round(2/12*100) = 17; tradition = (-1)(-1)+(1)(2)+(-1)(1) = 2 -> round(8/12*100) = 67; worship = (-1)(-1)+(1)(-1)+(-1)(-2) = 2 -> 67. Headline: |score-50| = 42, 42, 25, 33, 17, 17; top three by deviation with index tie-break = grace (92, 'firmly synergist'), table (92, 'memorialist'), kingdom (17, 'covenantal'). Distances: Anabaptist (75,85,55,30,70,60): 17^2+7^2+30^2+13^2+3^2+7^2 = 289+49+900+169+9+49 = 1465 -> 38.3 (84% match). Charismatic non-denom (70,80,5,60,85,90): 484+144+400+1849+324+529 = 3730 -> 61.1. Wesleyan (80,40,45,25,45,40): 144+2704+400+64+484+729 = 4525 -> 67.3. Pentecostal 69.4, SBC 88.9, Reformed Baptist 102.7, Anglican 105.7, Presbyterian 116.0, Dispensational 116.7, RC 125.2, EO 126.8, Lutheran 128.0. It lands, and it is robust: a moderate Mennonite (67,92,33,33,58,58) lands at 27.5, and a community-hermeneutic Mennonite who answers S15 = +2 and S13 = 0 (tradition 50) still lands at 43.1. Two things went wrong on the way there: (1) the second-nearest tradition shown on the card and in the share text is 'Charismatic non-denominational', which no Mennonite would accept as a neighbour; no peace church or free church is anywhere near because nothing on the six axes measures the believers'-church / nonresistance / church-and-state question that defines Anabaptism; (2) the headline names me with two other traditions' vocabulary ('synergist' is the Formula of Concord's heresy label, 'covenantal' is the Reformed federal system used to justify infant baptism against us). The largest divergence from the hand-set coordinate is Spirit: I score 25, the coordinate says 55; there is no cessationism in any Anabaptist confession, so 55 is too far right (propose 40).

findings.claim: No axis measures the things that make an Anabaptist an Anabaptist (believers' church under discipline, nonresistance, no oaths, separation from the state), so the 'Anabaptist / Mennonite' entry is defined by nothing Anabaptist and any non-Calvinist, non-dispensational, believers'-baptism evangelical is told they are a Mennonite.
findings.evidence: Schleitheim (1527) Art. II (the ban), IV (separation from the world), VI ('the sword is ordained of God outside the perfection of Christ'), VII (no oaths); CFMP 1995 Art. 14 (Discipline), 20 (Truth and the Avoidance of Oaths), 22 (Peace, Justice, and Nonresistance: 'we do not prepare for war, or participate in war or military service'), 23 (The Church's Relation to Government and Society). Arithmetic: a generic non-Calvinist evangelical with no peace theology at (75,85,50,30,80,70) is 15.0 from the Anabaptist coordinate = '94% match Anabaptist / Mennonite', next SBC at 56.1; a Free Will Baptist profile (85,90,60,50,85,70) is 29.6 from Anabaptist vs 47.4 from SBC. In my own simulation the second-nearest tradition printed in the share text is 'Charismatic non-denominational' (61.1) because no free-church neighbour exists in the space. The intro promises to 'name the traditions nearest to you'; for this family it cannot. The axis called 'Kingdom' compounds it: for Anabaptists 'kingdom' means the reign of God embodied now in a nonresistant community (Schleitheim's two kingdoms), and the axis measures Israel/church and the rapture instead.
findings.fix: Add a seventh axis, key 'sword', name 'Church & World', left pole 'Christendom' (0), right pole 'Nonresistant' (100). Statements: S19 'A Christian may serve in the military or police and use lethal force when the state lawfully requires it.' (direction -1); S20 'Jesus' command to love enemies rules out Christians taking part in war.' (direction +1); S21 'Christians should swear oaths in court and hold public office like anyone else.' (direction -1). Fair summary: 'The Christendom view holds that God ordains the state to bear the sword (Romans 13), so Christians may serve in it, fight in a just war, swear lawful oaths, and govern, and church and state can work together. The nonresistant view holds that the church is a voluntary community of disciples set apart from the state's coercion: Jesus' command to love enemies forbids Christians to kill or take part in war, and his word rules out oaths (Matthew 5:33-48).' Coordinates: Roman Catholic 20, Eastern Orthodox 20, Lutheran 15, Anglican 15, Presbyterian 15, Reformed Baptist 30, Southern Baptist 30, Dispensational 25, Wesleyan 35, Pentecostal 35, Charismatic 35, Anabaptist / Mennonite 95. Check: the generic evangelical at 30 on the new axis is then sqrt(225 + 4225) = 66.7 from Anabaptist and 56.1 from SBC, so lands on SBC; the simulated Mennonite (95) still lands at 38.3. Rename the existing 'Kingdom' axis 'Israel & Church' (or 'End times') so it does not claim to measure kingdom ethics.

findings.claim: The headline system names Mennonites with other traditions' vocabulary: at the quiz's own Anabaptist coordinate the headline reads 'Memorialist, Arminian-leaning, covenantal-leaning', and my simulation reads 'Firmly synergist, memorialist, covenantal'.
findings.evidence: Coordinate (75,85,55,30,70,60): deviations 25, 35, 5, 20, 20, 10; top three = table 85 -> 'memorialist', grace 75 -> band 3 'Arminian-leaning', kingdom 30 -> band 1 'covenantal-leaning' (tie with tradition 20 broken by index). Arminius was born in 1560, the year before Menno Simons died; Hubmaier's free-will treatises are 1527. 'Covenantal' is the Reformed federal system (Zwingli, Of Baptism 1525; Bullinger, De testamento 1534; Westminster 1646, which the quiz's own Kingdom history uses to define the pole) built to justify infant baptism against the Anabaptists. 'Synergist' is the term Formula of Concord Art. II rejects by name; CFMP 1995 never uses it, and the quiz's own cited author Olson (Arminian Theology, 2006) accepts it only as 'evangelical synergism'. The grace bands are inconsistent as a system: the outer bands are technical terms, the inner bands ('Reformed-leaning', 'Arminian-leaning') are denominational names, so anyone not in those denominations is filed under them.
findings.fix: Use position words, never denomination names, in the bands. Grace: 'firmly sovereign-grace', 'leaning sovereign grace', 'balanced on grace', 'leaning free response', 'firmly free-response'. Kingdom (with the pole renamed, see axis:kingdom:poles): 'one people of God', 'leaning one people of God', 'middle on Israel and the church', 'leaning Israel distinct', 'dispensational'. With these, the same Mennonite coordinate reads 'Memorialist, leaning free response, leaning one people of God', which a Mennonite would accept.

findings.claim: 'Covenantal' as the left pole files Anabaptists under Reformed covenant theology, the very system used to argue for infant baptism against them.
findings.evidence: The pole's own history line 1 ('1646 Westminster Confession sets out the covenant of works and the covenant of grace') and read-more (Horton, Introducing Covenant Theology) define the pole as Reformed federalism. Anabaptists hold one people of God and a present reign of God (CFMP Art. 9: 'the new community of disciples'; Art. 24 'The Reign of God') while rejecting the covenant-continuity argument (Schleitheim Art. I excludes infant baptism; the Anabaptist hermeneutic reads the Old Testament through the New). A Mennonite scoring 17 on this axis is told he is 'covenantal'.
findings.fix: Left pole: 'One people of God'. Keep 'Dispensational' as the right pole (its holders accept the name). Fair summary opening: 'The one-people view sees a single people of God across both testaments...'.

findings.claim: 'Synergist' is a condemnation label in Lutheran usage and a Reformed polemic term; no Anabaptist confession describes itself that way.
findings.evidence: Formula of Concord Art. II (Free Will) rejects 'the Synergists' by name. CFMP Art. 8 says only that 'through Jesus Christ, God offers salvation from sin and a new way of life to all people' and that we receive it when we 'repent of sin and accept Jesus Christ'. Hubmaier, On Free Will (1527): grace restores the will so it can accept or refuse. Reformed critics will happily share a card that says 'firmly synergist' as if the quiz had conceded their charge.
findings.fix: Left pole 'Sovereign grace', right pole 'Free response'. Keep the fair summary text but replace 'Monergists hold' / 'Synergists hold' with 'The sovereign-grace view holds' / 'The free-response view holds'.

findings.claim: 'The church, not the individual reader, is the final interpreter of Scripture' conflates a teaching office with the gathered congregation, so an Anabaptist who holds the community hermeneutic must either misanswer or be scored toward Rome.
findings.evidence: CFMP Art. 4: 'Insights and understandings which we bring to the interpretation of the Scripture are to be tested in the faith community'; 1 Corinthians 14:29 ('let the others weigh what is said') was the Swiss Brethren's rule; the pole's fair summary defines 'with tradition' as 'creeds, councils, and the church's teaching office'. Arithmetic: a Mennonite who answers S15 honestly at +2 with S13 = -1 and S14 = +2 gets raw = 1 -> 58 'balanced on authority'; with S13 = 0, raw = 0 -> 50, twenty points left of the hand-set coordinate 70. The statement measures 'who interprets' while the axis is labelled by 'is anything beside Scripture infallible', which are different questions (Catholics: magisterium; Anabaptists: congregation under Scripture; Baptists: soul competency).
findings.fix: 'The church's teaching office (bishops, councils, or a magisterium), not the individual reader, has the final say on what Scripture means.' Mennonites and congregational Baptists can then disagree cleanly; if adopted, move the Anabaptist tradition coordinate from 70 to 75.

findings.claim: 'Christ is truly present in a way that goes beyond a symbol' can be honestly affirmed by a Mennonite who believes the risen Christ is present in the gathered congregation, not the elements, and it would score him sacramental.
findings.evidence: CFMP Art. 12: 'the Lord's Supper is a sign by which the church thankfully remembers the new covenant... the members of the church renew their covenant with God and with each other', with the commentary locating the presence of the risen Christ in the gathered body (Matthew 18:20). Pilgram Marpeck's 'co-witness' view goes further still. The statement never says where Christ is present, so the Marpeck strand and many modern Mennonites would Agree while remaining memorialist on the elements.
findings.fix: 'In the Lord's Supper, Christ is truly present in the bread and wine themselves, not only in the gathered congregation.'

findings.claim: Double-barreled: Anabaptists (with Arminians and Catholics) affirm the first clause, that saving faith is God's gift, and deny only the election clause.
findings.evidence: CFMP Art. 8 speaks of salvation as God's gift received by repentance and faith; Hubmaier's two free-will treatises (1527) insist the will is dead until grace restores it. A Mennonite who answers 'Agree' for the gift clause is scored monergist; one who answers 'Unsure' is pulled to the centre. The direction is right only if the respondent reads the second clause as controlling.
findings.fix: 'God gives saving faith only to those he has already chosen; faith is the result of his election, not the reason for it.'

findings.claim: 'The church is the true Israel, heir to every promise God made to Abraham' is loaded supersessionist wording that under-scores the Anabaptist one-people position.
findings.evidence: The biblical phrase is 'the Israel of God' (Galatians 6:16) and 'Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise' (Galatians 3:29); 'every promise' drags in the land promise, which Anabaptists read as transformed in Christ (Hebrews 11:10, 16), not inherited by the church. Mennonite Church USA's 2017 resolution 'Seeking Peace in Israel and Palestine' and decades of Jewish-Mennonite dialogue make many informed Mennonites refuse 'true Israel' language while fully holding one people of God, so they answer 0 or +1 and the Kingdom score drifts toward the centre.
findings.fix: 'Jews and Gentiles who trust Christ are together the one people of God, and the promises to Abraham are fulfilled in them.'

findings.claim: 'Worship should be free-form and led by the Spirit in the moment' is Pentecostal vocabulary; Mennonites disagree with it and with S16, so their whole Worship score is decided by S18 (communion frequency).
findings.evidence: Mennonite worship is planned, plain, hymn-centred and congregational (four-part a cappella singing from Hymnal: A Worship Book 1992 / Voices Together 2020, sermon, sharing time, prayer); Old Order and Amish worship follows a fixed traditional order (Ausbund, Lob Lied) without a prayer book. Simulation: S16 = -1, S17 = -1, S18 = -2 -> raw = 1 - 1 + 2 = 2 -> 67 'informal in worship'; the first two statements cancel and one statement carries the axis. The same is true for most Baptists.
findings.fix: 'Spontaneous contributions from the congregation, such as a testimony, a prayer, or a song, belong in Sunday worship.' (direction +1). Mennonites answer +1 (sharing time), Pentecostals +2, Anglo-Catholics -2. If adopted, the Anabaptist worship coordinate should move from 60 to about 75 (raw 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 -> 83 for the simulated Mennonite).

findings.claim: The 'Free worship' description bundles spontaneity with whole-congregation participation, so Anabaptist plain worship, which has the second without the first, fits neither pole.
findings.evidence: Quoted text: 'Free worship keeps the form open so that the Spirit can lead in the moment, with an emphasis on spontaneity, sincerity, and the participation of the whole congregation.' Multivoiced participation (1 Corinthians 14:26; Eleanor Kreider's term) is Anabaptist and Quaker; 'the Spirit can lead in the moment' and 'spontaneity' are Pentecostal. A Mennonite scored 60-79 reads a description of a worship style he does not practise.
findings.fix: 'Free worship holds that no fixed rite is required: the congregation orders its own service, simply and sincerely, around Scripture, preaching, prayer, and song, with room for members to take part and for the Spirit to lead, whether the service is planned in plain forms or open to the moment.'

findings.claim: 'Informal in worship' (60-79) misdescribes plain-church worship, which is non-liturgical but highly formal.
findings.evidence: Old Order Mennonite and Amish services have a prescribed order, prescribed hymns (Ausbund) and a two-sermon structure; a conservative Mennonite at 65 would object to 'informal'.
findings.fix: Bands: 'liturgical', 'liturgy-leaning', 'flexible in worship', 'simple in worship', 'free in worship'.

findings.claim: The memorial pole's reading list is headed by Zwingli, under whose influence Zurich drowned the first Anabaptists, and contains no Anabaptist author for a pole on which Anabaptists sit at 85.
findings.evidence: Quoted: 'Zwingli, On the Lord's Supper' / 'Schreiner & Wright, Believer's Baptism'. Zurich made rebaptism a capital offence on 7 March 1526; Felix Manz was drowned in the Limmat on 5 January 1527; Zwingli's Elenchus (1527) is a polemic against Anabaptism, and he was a paedobaptist, so he represents only half the pole. The axis's own history credits '1525 First believer's baptisms in Zurich; the Anabaptist movement begins' and then hands the reader the man who suppressed them.
findings.fix: Right: 'Hubmaier, On the Christian Baptism of Believers (1525)' and 'Rempel, The Lord's Supper in Anabaptism' (or keep Schreiner & Wright as the second). If Zwingli is kept, move him to the history array, not read-more.

findings.claim: The passage list omits the texts believers'-baptism traditions actually cite and includes two that are specifically paedobaptist proof texts, so three of six lean to the sacramental side.
findings.evidence: Present: John 6:53-58 (real presence), Acts 2:38-39 (v. 39 'the promise is for you and for your children' is the Reformed infant-baptism text; Anabaptists cite v. 38 alone), Colossians 2:11-12 (the circumcision-baptism argument). Absent: Matthew 28:19-20 (teach, then baptize; the order was the Anabaptist argument in the 1525 Zurich disputations), 1 Peter 3:21 (baptism as 'the pledge of a good conscience toward God', central to Hubmaier and Menno; CFMP Art. 11 calls baptism 'a pledge before the church'), 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 (one bread, one body; Schleitheim Art. III's Supper text).
findings.fix: Key passages: John 6:53-58; 1 Corinthians 11:23-29; Acts 2:38-39; Colossians 2:11-12; Romans 6:3-4; Matthew 28:19-20; 1 Peter 3:21; 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 (drop Matthew 26:26-28 if the list must stay at six or seven; it duplicates 1 Corinthians 11).

findings.claim: The Spirit coordinate 55 places Mennonites in 'undecided on the gifts' and slightly toward cessationism; no Anabaptist confession is cessationist and the simulation lands at 25-33.
findings.evidence: Schleitheim, Dordrecht (1632), and CFMP 1995 contain no cessationist clause; CFMP Art. 3 describes the Spirit giving gifts to the church without restriction; anointing with oil for healing (James 5:14) is standard Mennonite practice in the Minister's Manual; congregational weighing of prophecy (1 Corinthians 14:29) is the Anabaptist hermeneutic; the 1970s Mennonite charismatic renewal was absorbed, not expelled. Simulation: S7 +1, S8 -1, S9 +1 -> raw -3 -> 25; a cautious Mennonite (0, -1, +1) -> 33. Moving spirit from 55 to 40 cuts the simulated distance from sqrt(1465) = 38.3 to sqrt(1465 - 900 + 225) = 28.1 and does not disturb any other tradition's nearest.
findings.fix: spirit: 40. Also, if statement 15 is reworded as proposed, tradition: 75; if statement 17 is reworded as proposed, worship: 75. Grace 75, table 85, kingdom 30 are acceptable for 'typical adherents' (Mennonite Church USA/Canada are mostly amillennial, Mennonite Brethren historically premillennial, so 30 is a fair average).

findings.claim: The midpoint band 'centered on the sacraments' reads as the left pole's doctrine (the sacraments as centre) rather than a middle position, and uses the word memorialists do not use.
findings.evidence: Bands run 'sacramental', 'sacramental-leaning', 'centered on the sacraments', 'memorial-leaning', 'memorialist': band 2 sounds more sacramental than band 1. Mennonites and Baptists say 'ordinances' (as the axis's own fair summary acknowledges: 'both are ordinances obeyed by believers'), so a Mennonite at 50 is labelled in the other side's vocabulary.
findings.fix: Band 2: 'between sign and sacrament'.

findings.claim: 'Centered on the kingdom' as the 41-59 band sounds like a doctrinal position (kingdom-centred theology), not a midpoint.
findings.evidence: Same defect as the Table midpoint; for Anabaptists 'kingdom-centred' is a description of their whole theology (Schleitheim's two kingdoms, CFMP Art. 24), and it would be given to people who are simply undecided about the rapture.
findings.fix: Band 2: 'middle on Israel and the church'.

findings.claim: The 1525 Zurich line is accurate but the pole's founding confessional statement, Schleitheim 1527, and the cost of the position are missing.
findings.evidence: Schleitheim Art. I ('Baptism shall be given to all those who have learned repentance... This excludes all infant baptism') and Art. III (the bread 'in remembrance of the broken body of Christ') are the first confessional statement of the believers'-baptism-plus-memorial-Supper pole; Felix Manz was drowned by Zurich on 5 January 1527, six weeks before Schleitheim was signed.
findings.fix: Add after the 1525 line: '1527 — Zurich drowns Felix Manz for rebaptism; the Schleitheim Confession sets out believers' baptism and the Supper as a memorial of the one body.'

findings.claim: The history jumps from Luther 1525 to the Remonstrance 1610, skipping the first Protestant free-will tradition.
findings.evidence: Balthasar Hubmaier, On Free Will and On the Freedom of the Will (both 1527), are the first Protestant replies to The Bondage of the Will, two years after it; Menno Simons taught the same (God 'wills not the death of the sinner'). The right pole's story is told as Erasmus, the Remonstrants and Wesley, which lets the Reformed reader think free response entered Protestantism only through Arminius.
findings.fix: Insert after the Luther line: '1527 — Balthasar Hubmaier, On Free Will: the first Anabaptist reply to Luther; grace restores the will so that it can accept or refuse.'

findings.claim: The memorial-side summary is written in Baptist/Zwinglian terms and omits what Anabaptists add: baptism as a covenant with the church under mutual accountability, and the Supper as the reconciled community's covenant renewal.
findings.evidence: Quoted: 'baptism a public confession of a faith already held, so both are ordinances obeyed by believers rather than channels of grace.' CFMP Art. 11: baptism is 'a pledge before the church of their covenant with God to walk in the way of Jesus Christ' and a commitment 'to give and receive counsel'; Art. 12: 'the members of the church renew their covenant with God and with each other', with admission conditioned on being 'at peace with God and with their brothers and sisters'; Schleitheim Art. III requires that communicants 'be united beforehand by baptism in one body'.
findings.fix: 'The memorial view holds that the Supper is a remembrance of Christ's death in which the reconciled congregation renews its covenant, and baptism a public pledge of a faith already held that binds the believer to Christ and to an accountable church, so both are ordinances kept by believers rather than channels of grace in themselves.'

findings.claim: 'A decision to follow Christ' is revivalist decisionism vocabulary; Anabaptists speak of a pledge or covenant made before the church.
findings.evidence: CFMP Art. 11 ('a pledge before the church of their covenant with God'); Schleitheim Art. I (baptism for those who 'have learned repentance and amendment of life... and desire to be baptized upon their own request'). Mennonites still answer +2, so no mis-scoring, but the wording tells them the pole belongs to someone else.
findings.fix: 'Baptism is the outward sign of a faith in Christ and a commitment to follow him that a person has already made.'

findings.claim: The Scripture-alone summary leaves no room for the Anabaptist way of reading Scripture: Christ-centred and tested in the congregation rather than by the individual reader.
findings.evidence: CFMP Art. 4: Scripture is interpreted 'in the light of Jesus Christ', and interpretations 'are to be tested in the faith community'; Stuart Murray, Biblical Interpretation in the Anabaptist Tradition (2000). The current text implies the only alternative to a teaching office is the lone reader.
findings.fix: Append to the right-pole sentence: '...says otherwise. Many in this camp read Scripture together, with Christ at the centre and each reader's interpretation tested in the congregation.'

findings.claim: Fairness to the other side: the history gives the tradition pole four entries (Vincent, Trent, Newman, Dei Verbum) and the Scripture-alone pole one (Westminster 1646).
findings.evidence: The obvious missing right-pole entry is Luther at Worms, 18 April 1521 ('unless I am convinced by Scripture and plain reason... my conscience is captive to the Word of God'), which is also where statement 14's 'bind the conscience' language comes from.
findings.fix: Insert before the Westminster line: '1521 — Luther at Worms: unless convinced by Scripture and plain reason, he will not recant; conscience is bound to the Word of God.'

findings.claim: The right pole's history opens with the Puritan regulative principle, which is a strict Reformed rule for ordering worship, while the free-church plain-worship stream has no entry at all.
findings.evidence: Quoted: '1600s — Puritans articulate the regulative principle: only what Scripture commands belongs in worship.' The Ausbund (first edition 1564), the Anabaptist martyr hymnal still sung in Amish services, is the oldest hymnal in continuous use and the clearest early witness to worship without prayer book, calendar, or priest; Quaker unprogrammed meeting (1650s) is the other missing witness.
findings.fix: Add before the Puritan line: '1564 — The Ausbund, the Anabaptist martyr hymnal still sung in Amish services: plain worship of song, Scripture, and preaching without prayer book or priest.'

findings.claim: Both 'Free' read-more titles are Reformed (Frame, Presbyterian; Kauflin, Sovereign Grace); nothing represents free-church or Anabaptist worship.
findings.evidence: Quoted: 'Frame, Worship in Spirit and Truth', 'Kauflin, Worship Matters'. Alan and Eleanor Kreider, Worship and Mission after Christendom (2011) is the standard Anabaptist treatment.
findings.fix: Right: 'Kreider & Kreider, Worship and Mission after Christendom' in place of Frame, or as a third entry.

findings.claim: Matthew 18:20 is missing; it is the Anabaptist worship and ecclesiology text.
findings.evidence: 'Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them' is the ground of the free-church claim that the gathered congregation, not a rite or a building, is where Christ is present; it sits behind statement 4 as well.
findings.fix: Add 'Matthew 18:20' to the Worship key passages.

findings.claim: A Mennonite scoring 17 on Kingdom is sent to two Reformed books, one of which argues for infant baptism from the covenant of grace.
findings.evidence: Quoted: 'Horton, Introducing Covenant Theology', 'Riddlebarger, A Case for Amillennialism'. Ladd, whom the history already credits ('1950s George Eldon Ladd's historic premillennialism'), wrote the standard non-Reformed one-people, present-kingdom book.
findings.fix: Left: 'Riddlebarger, A Case for Amillennialism' and 'Ladd, The Gospel of the Kingdom'.

findings.claim: The middle option is labelled 'Unsure', which forces respondents whose honest answer is 'neither / it depends' to describe themselves as uncertain.
findings.evidence: Statement 13 is the Mennonite case: the creeds are affirmed in content (Hubmaier's Twelve Articles expound the Apostles' Creed; CFMP Art. 1-3 are Nicene) but carry only derived authority (CFMP introduction: a confession 'is subject to the authority of the Bible'), so the honest answer is 'neither', not 'unsure'. HTML answers row: 'Strongly disagree / Disagree / Unsure / Agree / Strongly agree'.
findings.fix: Label the 0 option 'Neither / it depends'.

lens: Anglican (broad, Thirty-Nine Articles / Book of Common Prayer)

simulation.headline: Sacramental, liturgical, covenantal
simulation.comment: Answers as a typical Prayer-Book Anglican: S1 +1 (Art. XVII predestination to life, read pastorally with Art. XVI), S2 +1 (Art. XVI, Homily of Falling from God), S3 +1 (Art. X, XVII: chosen 'in Christ', faith a gift); S4 +2 (Art. XXVIII, Catechism 'verily and indeed taken and received'), S5 -2 (Art. XXVII: baptism 'as by an instrument' grafts into the Church; infants have made no decision), S6 +2 (Art. XXVII); S7 0 (three gifts bundled plus 'as in Acts'), S8 -1, S9 +1; S10 -1, S11 +1, S12 -2; S13 +2 (Art. VIII), S14 0 (forced: Art. VI says yes, Art. XXXIV says no), S15 0 (Art. XX yes, Art. XXI 'may err'); S16 +2, S17 -2, S18 +1 (post-Parish-Communion norm). Raw and scores: Grace (-1)(1)+(1)(1)+(-1)(1) = -1 -> round(5/12*100) = 42; Table (-1)(2)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(2) = -6 -> 0; Spirit 0+(1)(-1)+(-1)(1) = -2 -> 33; Kingdom (1)(-1)+(-1)(1)+(1)(-2) = -4 -> 17; Tradition (-1)(2)+0+0 = -2 -> 33; Worship (-1)(2)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(1) = -5 -> 8. Headline: |score-50| = 8, 50, 17, 33, 17, 42 -> Table (0, 'sacramental'), Worship (8, 'liturgical'), Kingdom (17, 'covenantal'). Distances: Roman Catholic sqrt(169+25+49+4+529+4) = sqrt(780) = 27.9; Anglican (broad) sqrt(4+625+144+9+9+144) = sqrt(935) = 30.6; Eastern Orthodox sqrt(1355) = 36.8; Lutheran sqrt(2230) = 47.2; Wesleyan sqrt(4420) = 66.5; Presbyterian sqrt(5530) = 74.4; Reformed Baptist 109.7; Anabaptist 114.2; Southern Baptist 135.5; Charismatic 138.7; Pentecostal 149.1; Dispensational 158.7. Nearest is Roman Catholic (89% match) with Anglican second (88%). What went wrong: 625 of the Anglican 935 comes from the Table axis, where the tradition is placed at 25 but the three Table statements can only give an Article XXVII/XXVIII Anglican 0-8 (even with S5 = -1, Table = 8 and the margin is Anglican 24.5 vs RC 27.6, a coin flip). Fix A: Anglican (broad) -> [40, 10, 35, 20, 30, 15]: d = sqrt(4+100+4+9+9+49) = sqrt(175) = 13.2, clearly nearest, RC second at 27.9. Fix B (preferred, keeps existing coordinates honest): replace S5 with a statement that splits the sacramental camp (see scoring finding); the same respondent then answers it -1, Table raw -3 -> 25, d(Anglican) = sqrt(310) = 17.6 vs d(RC) = sqrt(1155) = 34.0.

findings.claim: The coordinates [40, 25, 45, 20, 30, 20] make a typical Prayer-Book Anglican land on Roman Catholic first and Anglican second, which is exactly the screenshot this product cannot afford ('Theology Compass says Anglicans are really Catholics').
findings.evidence: Simulation scores [42, 0, 33, 17, 33, 8]: d(Roman Catholic) = sqrt(780) = 27.9, d(Anglican) = sqrt(935) = 30.6. 625 of the 935 is the Table axis alone. Any Anglican who believes Article XXVII ('a sign of Regeneration... whereby, as by an instrument, they that receive Baptism rightly are grafted into the Church'; 'The Baptism of young Children is in any wise to be retained'), Article XXVIII and the Catechism ('verily and indeed taken and received by the faithful') answers S4 +2, S6 +2 and S5 -1 or -2, so Table = 0-8, never 25. Spirit 45 also sits right of the tradition's centre: the Church of England has an authorised healing ministry (A Time to Heal, 2000; Common Worship Wholeness and Healing), a very large charismatic wing (HTB, New Wine), and a majority Global-South membership that is renewal-shaped; 'undecided' is not where the typical adherent is. Worship 20 is high for a church whose Sunday service is by canon a set liturgy: the simulation gives 8.
findings.fix: Set Anglican (broad) to [40, 10, 35, 20, 30, 15] (d = sqrt(175) = 13.2, RC second at 27.9). Or, better, adopt the S5 replacement in the scoring finding, which makes the current Table 25 correct (same respondent then scores Table 25, d = 17.6 vs RC 34.0).

findings.claim: The three Table statements only separate credobaptist-memorial from paedobaptist-real-presence, so every real-presence paedobaptist scores 0-8 and the graded coordinates RC 5 / EO 5 / Lutheran 15 / Anglican 25 / Presbyterian 35 encode a ranking (transubstantiation to memorial) that the quiz never asks about.
findings.evidence: Westminster Presbyterian: S4 +1 (WCF 29.7 'really, but spiritually, present'), S5 -2, S6 +2 -> raw -5 -> 8, not 35. Confessional Lutheran: -6 -> 0, not 15. Anglican: -5 or -6 -> 0-8, not 25. S5 and S6 are both baptism questions and both credo-versus-paedo, so one is redundant and the axis has no statement on the mode of presence, which is the only thing that distinguishes these five traditions.
findings.fix: Replace S5 with: 'After consecration the bread and wine are the body and blood of Christ in substance, and may rightly be reserved and adored.' (direction -1). Article XXVIII ('The Sacrament of the Lord's Supper was not by Christ's ordinance reserved, carried about, lifted up, or worshipped') gives Anglican -1, Lutheran 0 to -1, Roman Catholic and Orthodox +2, Reformed -2, Baptist -2, yielding Table roughly RC 0, Lutheran 17-25, Anglican 25, Presbyterian 42, Baptist 100, i.e. the coordinates already in the file. Memorialists still reach 100 through S4 and S6. If the statement is kept, compress the coordinates instead: RC 5, EO 5, Lutheran 8, Anglican 10, Presbyterian 20.

findings.claim: One point for 'Anglican (broad)' is a centroid that no actual Anglican wing occupies; the three honest wings each land on a different non-Anglican tradition, so the label promises a placement the math cannot deliver.
findings.evidence: Anglo-Catholic answers [0, 1, 0, 2, -2, 2, 1, -2, 1, -2, 1, -2, 2, -1, 1, 2, -2, 2] -> scores [58, 0, 17, 8, 17, 0]: Eastern Orthodox 24.8, Roman Catholic 27.6, Anglican 49.5. Reformed evangelical Anglican [2, -1, 2, 1, -1, 2, -1, 1, 0, -1, 2, -2, 1, 2, -1, 1, -2, -1] -> [8, 17, 67, 8, 67, 33]: Presbyterian 32.7, Lutheran 37.4, Anglican 57.0. Charismatic Anglican [0, 1, 0, 1, -1, 1, 2, -2, 2, -1, 0, -1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1] -> [58, 25, 0, 33, 42, 42]: Wesleyan 53.0, Anglican 56.1. The spread inside one tradition is 50 points on Grace, 67 on Spirit and 50 on Tradition. Reformed Baptist / Southern Baptist and Pentecostal / Charismatic already get split entries, so the precedent exists.
findings.fix: Keep the corrected broad entry and add 'Anglican (Anglo-Catholic)' at [55, 5, 20, 10, 15, 5] (the Anglo-Catholic simulation then lands there at d = 8.7 instead of being told it is Eastern Orthodox). An evangelical Anglican landing on 'Presbyterian / Reformed' and a charismatic one on 'Wesleyan / Methodist' are honest neighbours and can stand. Add to the 'Closest traditions' note: 'Broad churches (Anglican, Methodist) are placed at their centre; their wings sit nearer other entries.'

findings.claim: 'Every doctrine must be proven from Scripture alone; tradition can never bind the conscience' is two statements, and the Anglican formularies answer yes to the first and no to the second, so the tradition's actual position collapses to 'Unsure'.
findings.evidence: Article VI: 'whatsoever is not read therein, nor may be proved thereby, is not to be required of any man, that it should be believed as an article of the Faith' (Agree). Article XXXIV: 'Whosoever, through his private judgment, willingly and purposely, doth openly break the Traditions and Ceremonies of the Church, which be not repugnant to the Word of God... ought to be rebuked openly' (Disagree); Hooker, Laws III.viii, is a whole book on why the church may bind in things Scripture leaves open. Lutherans (FC X on adiaphora) split the same way. The statement is written in the Puritan/biblicist idiom, not in the idiom of the Reformation's own sola scriptura.
findings.fix: 'Nothing may be required of Christians as an article of faith unless it can be proved from Scripture.' (direction +1). Anglicans, Lutherans, Reformed and Baptists then agree; Rome (Dei Verbum 9: the Church 'does not draw her certainty about all revealed truths from the holy Scriptures alone') and Orthodoxy disagree. Note the coordinate consequence: Anglican and Lutheran Tradition scores rise to about 45-50; adjust those two coordinates to 45.

findings.claim: 'Communion should be celebrated every week as the center of the service' measures eucharistic frequency, which cuts across the liturgical/free axis in both directions, so it pushes classic Prayer-Book Anglicans toward 'Free' and free-church weekly-communion bodies toward 'Liturgical'.
findings.evidence: The 1662 rubric requires only that 'every Parishioner shall communicate at the least three times in the year'; the classic Anglican Sunday was Morning Prayer, Litany and Ante-Communion, the most fixed liturgy in English, with Communion monthly; weekly Communion became normal only with the Parish Communion movement (Hebert, 1937), and many evangelical Anglican parishes still keep a Service of the Word as the main service. Conversely Plymouth Brethren and Churches of Christ break bread every week as the centre of a wholly unscripted service and would answer +2, scoring as 'liturgical'.
findings.fix: 'The church year, with Advent, Lent, Easter and the rest, should shape what a congregation reads, sings and prays each Sunday.' (direction -1). Anglicans, Lutherans, Catholics, Orthodox +2; Presbyterians and Baptists -1; Pentecostals -2.

findings.claim: 'Liturgical worship follows a set order, the church calendar, and a weekly Eucharist' makes weekly Eucharist definitional, which excludes three centuries of Book of Common Prayer worship and most Lutheran and Reformed liturgical practice.
findings.evidence: The 1662 Prayer Book is the archetype of English-language liturgical worship and did not assume a weekly celebration (rubric: at least three times a year); Morning and Evening Prayer are its normal Sunday offices. Weekly Eucharist is a feature of Catholic, Orthodox and modern Anglican practice, not of liturgical worship as such.
findings.fix: 'Liturgical worship follows a set order and the church calendar, usually with the Eucharist at its centre, so that a congregation prays with the historic church in words tested over centuries.'

findings.claim: 'Tongues, prophecy, and healing continue in the church today, as they did in Acts' bundles three gifts and then adds 'as they did in Acts', so the large open-but-cautious middle (most Anglicans, the Catholic Church) is forced to 'Unsure' and scored as more cessationist than it is.
findings.evidence: The Church of England's A Time to Heal (2000) and Common Worship healing rites affirm continuing healing; the Catechism of the Catholic Church 799-801 affirms continuing charisms; neither claims Acts-level normativity or frequency. A respondent who believes God heals today but is unsure about tongues has no honest answer.
findings.fix: 'The Spirit still gives tongues, prophecy, and healing to the church today.' (direction -1).

findings.claim: 'The church is the true Israel, heir to every promise God made to Abraham' is the opponents' caricature ('replacement theology') rather than the covenantal side's own words, and it is harsher than the quiz's own fair summary.
findings.evidence: The fair summary says 'the church, Jew and Gentile together, inherits the promises to Abraham', which its holders accept. Official Anglican teaching explicitly disowns 'replacement' language (Church of England Faith and Order Commission, God's Unfailing Word, 2019; Lambeth 1988, The Way of Dialogue); Romans 11:28-29, 'the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable', is read by most amillennial Anglicans as leaving a future for Israel, so 'every promise' is a clause they would not sign.
findings.fix: 'God's promises to Abraham are fulfilled in Christ and belong to everyone who is in him, Jew and Gentile alike.' (direction -1).

findings.claim: The left pole is described in Roman vocabulary ('the church's teaching office') and the right pole in Puritan vocabulary ('where Scripture is silent'), so the magisterial Reformation position that Anglicans and Lutherans hold, and that sits at 30-45 on this axis, is described by neither side in words it would accept.
findings.evidence: Anglicans receive creeds and councils as real authority (Article VIII; Canon A5; the 1559 Act of Supremacy named the first four General Councils) but have no 'teaching office' and hold that councils 'may err, and sometimes have erred' (Article XXI). On the other side, Article XXXIV binds in matters where Scripture is silent, so 'no council or teacher can bind the conscience where Scripture is silent' describes the regulative-principle wing only, not 'Scripture alone' as Luther, Cranmer or Mathison (the right pole's own read-more author, who calls this 'Tradition I') understood it.
findings.fix: Left: 'the creeds, the councils, and the church's continuing teaching are God's appointed means of guarding and interpreting his Word, and so carry real authority.' Right: '...insist that only Scripture is infallible, that nothing may be required as an article of faith that cannot be proved from it, and that no council or teacher can bind the conscience against it.'

findings.claim: The middle band (41-59) is labelled 'centered on the sacraments', which describes the left pole, not the middle; a respondent at 50 is told in the headline that their theology is 'centered on the sacraments'.
findings.evidence: The other axes use 'balanced on grace' and 'balanced on authority' for the middle; 'centered on the sacraments' is the Anglo-Catholic and Roman self-description and reads as a pole label.
findings.fix: Middle band: 'balanced on the sacraments'.

findings.claim: The middle band 'centered on the kingdom' is not a position between covenantal and dispensational; both poles claim to be centred on the kingdom, so the label is meaningless in a headline.
findings.evidence: Same pattern as the Table axis; compare 'balanced on grace' / 'balanced on authority'.
findings.fix: Middle band: 'balanced on Israel and the church' (or, if length matters, 'balanced on the kingdom').

findings.claim: The middle band 'undecided on the gifts' calls a settled, official position (open but cautious) indecision; this is the band applied to the Anglican coordinate (45) and the Roman Catholic coordinate (40).
findings.evidence: The Church of England House of Bishops (A Time to Heal, 2000) and the Catholic Catechism 800-801 take a deliberate position: the gifts continue and are to be discerned by the church. The band list is also asymmetric: bands[1] 'open to the gifts' has no mirror in bands[3] 'cautious about the gifts', so the right side gets two cautious labels and the middle gets 'undecided'.
findings.fix: Bands: ['continuationist', 'open to the gifts', 'open but cautious on the gifts', 'cessationist-leaning', 'cessationist'].

findings.claim: 'The infants of believing parents should be baptized' is Reformed covenant-theology vocabulary; Anglican, Lutheran, Catholic and Orthodox practice baptizes infants brought by sponsors and grounds it differently.
findings.evidence: Article XXVII grounds infant baptism in its being 'most agreeable with the institution of Christ', and the 1662 service requires godparents, not believing parents; the parish system baptized any child presented. Everyone paedobaptist still agrees, so the direction is right, but the phrasing tells an Anglican the question was written by a Presbyterian.
findings.fix: 'Infants should be baptized, not only those old enough to profess faith.'

findings.claim: 'The miraculous sign gifts' is Warfield/MacArthur vocabulary; 'sign gifts' is not a category used outside cessationist writing, so non-cessationists are asked to answer inside their opponents' frame.
findings.evidence: The term derives from Warfield's Counterfeit Miracles (1918) and the Strange Fire literature; Anglican, Catholic and Pentecostal writing speaks of 'charisms' or 'gifts of the Spirit'.
findings.fix: 'The miraculous gifts, such as tongues, prophecy, and healing, ended with the apostles or the completion of the New Testament.'

findings.claim: 'Worship should be free-form and led by the Spirit in the moment' implies that set liturgy is not led by the Spirit, which no liturgical Christian concedes; disagreeing feels like denying the Spirit.
findings.evidence: Article XXXIV and the BCP preface ('Concerning the Service of the Church') claim the Spirit's guidance for the church's ordered worship; the fair summary itself is careful not to make this implication.
findings.fix: 'Worship is best when its shape is open and decided in the moment rather than fixed in advance.'

findings.claim: 'Covenantal' is Westminster vocabulary; Roman Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans, Anglicans and Methodists share the one-people-of-God position but none would call themselves covenantal, and the word is printed in their headline (the simulation headline reads 'Sacramental, liturgical, covenantal').
findings.evidence: The Thirty-Nine Articles contain no covenant of works or covenant of grace; Article VII simply says the Old Testament 'is not contrary to the New'. The history array itself dates 'covenant of works and covenant of grace' to Westminster 1646.
findings.fix: In the accordion sub-label and share line show 'Covenantal (one people of God) <-> Dispensational (Israel distinct)'; or rename the left pole 'One people of God' and the bands 'one people of God' / 'leaning one people of God'.

findings.claim: 'Wesley and Whitefield divide the evangelical revival over predestination' omits that both were Church of England clergy, which is the point for this axis: Article XVII was read both ways inside one church.
findings.evidence: Both were ordained in the Church of England and died in its communion; Wesley's Predestination Calmly Considered (1752) and Whitefield's Letter to Wesley (1740) are intra-Anglican documents.
findings.fix: 'Wesley and Whitefield, both Church of England clergy, divide the evangelical revival over predestination.'

findings.claim: The history jumps from Trent (1546) to Westminster (1646) and skips the settlement that defines the middle of this axis: Article VI (1571) and Hooker (1594).
findings.evidence: Article VI, 'Holy Scripture containeth all things necessary to salvation', is the classic statement of sufficiency-without-biblicism; Hooker's Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity (1594-97) is the standard defence of Scripture read with reason and the church's tradition, and is cited by both Catholics and Protestants as the via media text.
findings.fix: Insert before the Westminster entry: '1571-1594: The Thirty-Nine Articles make Scripture the test of what may be required as necessary to salvation; Hooker's Laws defends the church's authority in what Scripture leaves open.'

findings.claim: 'Puritans articulate the regulative principle' presents one side of an intra-Anglican debate without the reply that shaped the liturgical pole for the English-speaking world.
findings.evidence: The regulative principle was argued against the Prayer Book (Admonition to Parliament, 1572); Hooker's answer, that the church may order what Scripture does not forbid (the normative principle), is the stated rationale of every Anglican and Lutheran liturgy since.
findings.fix: '1570s-1600s: Puritans argue that only what Scripture commands belongs in worship (the regulative principle); Hooker replies that the church may order what Scripture does not forbid.'

findings.claim: The Table passages omit 1 Corinthians 10:16-17, the text Article XXVIII quotes verbatim for the Supper, and Mark 10:13-16, the Gospel read at every Prayer Book infant baptism.
findings.evidence: Article XXVIII: 'the Bread which we break is a partaking of the Body of Christ' (1 Cor 10:16); the 1662 Publick Baptism of Infants appoints Mark 10:13-16 as its Gospel and builds its exhortation on it.
findings.fix: Add '1 Corinthians 10:16-17' and 'Mark 10:13-16'.

findings.claim: Romans 8:28-30 is missing, though it is the passage Article XVII paraphrases and the 'golden chain' every party on this axis argues over.
findings.evidence: Article XVII: 'they be called according to God's purpose... they be justified freely... they attain to everlasting felicity' tracks Romans 8:28-30 clause by clause; Hebrews 6 and 2 Peter 3:9 are included while the primary text is not.
findings.fix: Add 'Romans 8:28-30'.

findings.claim: The liturgical read-more list (Schmemann, Webber) has no Prayer Book title, although the Book of Common Prayer is the most widely used Protestant liturgy and the history line already names Cranmer.
findings.evidence: Dix, The Shape of the Liturgy (1945) is the standard Anglican study; Alan Jacobs, The Book of Common Prayer: A Biography (2013) is the accessible one.
findings.fix: Add 'Dix, The Shape of the Liturgy' (or 'Jacobs, The Book of Common Prayer: A Biography') to the left list.

findings.claim: 'Unsure' is the only middle option, so a considered 'yes to one half, no to the other' answer (which Anglicans must give on S14, S15 and S7) is recorded as not knowing.
findings.evidence: Statements 7, 14 and 15 each contain two claims that the Anglican formularies answer differently; the middle button is the only honest choice and its label misdescribes it.
findings.fix: Label the middle option 'Unsure / mixed'.

findings.claim: The share text and result card carry 'Closest: Roman Catholic · Anglican (broad)' with no trace of the on-page caveat 'Approximate positions of typical adherents, not official teaching', so the screenshot that circulates loses the one line that would defend it.
findings.evidence: shareText() emits only the axis bars, the two names and the link; the card shows 'Closest traditions · name · name'.
findings.fix: Change the share line to 'Closest (typical adherents, approximate): name · name' and add the same qualifier under the card's closest-traditions line.

simulation.headline: Sacramental, rooted in tradition, liturgical
simulation.comment: Answers (typical informed Catholic; Thomist-leaning as the seminary default, Trent as the floor): S1 Agree (+1: single predestination, CCC 600; a Molinist would say 0), S2 Strongly agree (+2: Trent VI canon 4, the will 'can dissent'), S3 Agree (+1: faith is a gift, Trent VI ch. 8; Aquinas ST I q.23 a.5 on election before foreseen merit; a Molinist would say -1), S4 +2, S5 -2, S6 +2 (CCC 1250, 1376), S7 +1, S8 -2, S9 +2 (LG 12; CCC 67, 799-801, 2003), S10 -2, S11 +1 (reluctant, see finding), S12 -2 (CCC 676), S13 +2, S14 -2, S15 +2 (DV 10), S16 +2, S17 -2, S18 +2 (LG 11). Raw sums: Grace (-1)(1)+(1)(2)+(-1)(1)=0 -> round(6/12*100)=50. Table (-1)(2)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(2)=-6 -> 0. Spirit (-1)(1)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(2)=-5 -> round(1/12*100)=8. Kingdom (1)(-2)+(-1)(1)+(1)(-2)=-5 -> 8. Tradition -6 -> 0. Worship -6 -> 0. Headline: |s-50| = 0, 50, 42, 42, 50, 50; top three by distance then index = Table (band 0 'sacramental'), Tradition ('rooted in tradition'), Worship ('liturgical') -> 'Sacramental, rooted in tradition, liturgical'. Distances (squared sums): Eastern Orthodox [65,5,35,15,5,5]: 225+25+729+49+25+25=1078 -> 32.8 (87% match). Roman Catholic [55,5,40,15,10,10]: 25+25+1024+49+100+100=1323 -> 36.4 (85%). Anglican (broad): 3538 -> 59.5. Lutheran: 6643 -> 81.5. Wesleyan: 7783 -> 88.2. Presbyterian: 11413 -> 106.8. Anabaptist: 19043 -> 138.0. Reformed Baptist: 19418 -> 139.3. Charismatic non-denom: 24838 -> 157.6. SBC: 27708 -> 166.5. Pentecostal: 27948 -> 167.2. Dispensational: 36218 -> 190.3. A Catholic answering from the Catechism lands on Eastern Orthodox first. What went wrong: the RC Spirit coordinate of 40 contributes 1024 of the 1323 (the Church officially affirms the charisms and canonizes on verified miracles, so even a cautious Catholic scores 33, never 40+), and RC tradition/worship at 10 versus Orthodox 5 penalize a Catholic who answers those six statements exactly as an Orthodox would. Fix: RC = [55, 5, 20, 15, 5, 5]. Recheck: 25+25+144+49+25+25=293 -> 17.1 vs Orthodox 32.8, RC nearest. Cautious Catholic (spirit 33): RC 25+25+169+49+25+25=318 -> 17.8 vs EO 225+25+4+49+25+25=353 -> 18.8, still RC. Raising EO grace to 75 (Orthodox reject election before foreseen faith more uniformly than Catholics) widens the margin further: EO for the base case 100+25+729+49+25+25=953 -> 30.9.

findings.claim: The Roman Catholic coordinates [grace 55, table 5, spirit 40, kingdom 15, tradition 10, worship 10] send a Catholic who answers from the Catechism to Eastern Orthodox first. Spirit 40 is far too high for a church that officially affirms the charisms, and tradition/worship at 10 (Orthodox: 5) penalize an answer set identical to the Orthodox one on 15 of 18 statements.
findings.evidence: Simulation scores [50,0,8,8,0,0]. Distance to Eastern Orthodox [65,5,35,15,5,5] = sqrt(225+25+729+49+25+25) = sqrt(1078) = 32.8 (87% match); to Roman Catholic = sqrt(25+25+1024+49+100+100) = sqrt(1323) = 36.4 (85%). Spirit alone is 1024 of 1323. The Church is not agnostic on the gifts: Lumen Gentium 12 (charisms 'are to be received with thanksgiving and consolation'), CCC 799-801 and 2003, Paul VI's address to the Renewal (Pentecost 1975), Francis's CHARIS statutes (2019), Augustine City of God XXII.8, and canonization has required verified miracles since Urban VIII (1634). Even a cautious Catholic (S7 Unsure, S8 Disagree, S9 Agree) scores 33 on Spirit, never 40+.
findings.fix: Set Roman Catholic to [55, 5, 20, 15, 5, 5]. Recheck: simulation distance to RC = sqrt(25+25+144+49+25+25) = sqrt(293) = 17.1 vs Orthodox 32.8, RC nearest. Cautious Catholic (spirit 33): RC sqrt(318) = 17.8 vs Orthodox sqrt(353) = 18.8, still RC. Keep grace at 50-55; Thomist and Molinist Catholics already range 33-83 on the Grace axis as written.

findings.claim: bands[1] 'Reformed-leaning' and bands[3] 'Arminian-leaning' pin Protestant party names on everyone scoring 21-40 or 60-79, which is where most Catholics land. Every other axis uses the pole-name-leaning pattern; Grace alone names denominations.
findings.evidence: A Thomist Catholic answering S1 +2, S2 +2, S3 +2 gets raw -2+2-2 = -2, score round(4/12*100) = 33, headline adjective 'Reformed-leaning'. The Dominicans (Banez) defended exactly that position against the charge of Calvinism through the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1597-1607), and Trent Sess. VI canons 4 and 17 anathematize the Reformed positions. A Molinist (S1 +1, S2 +2, S3 -2) gets raw 3, score 75, 'Arminian-leaning'; Arminius borrowed from Molina, not the reverse. Both labels are factually false for their holders and would be screenshotted ('Catholic priest scores Reformed-leaning').
findings.fix: ["firmly monergist", "monergist-leaning", "balanced on grace", "synergist-leaning", "firmly synergist"]

findings.claim: Both pole descriptions are fair to Calvinists and Arminians, but the summary gives no words to the historic middle (Catholic, Orthodox, confessional Lutheran), which reaches 'balanced on grace' not by moderation but because a strong Yes to S1 and a strong Yes to S2 cancel. 'His saving grace cannot finally be refused' and 'election follows God's foreknowledge of faith' are each rejected by Thomist Catholics, who affirm election before foreseen merit AND resistible grace AND that the justified can fall.
findings.evidence: Trent Sess. VI ch. 5: man 'is able to reject' the inspiration of grace, 'yet is he not able, by his own free will, without the grace of God, to move himself unto justice'; canon 4; canons 16 and 23 (no certainty of perseverance without special revelation; the justified can lose grace). Aquinas ST I q.23 a.5-7: predestination is not caused by foreseen merit and its number is certain. CCC 600, 2001. Formula of Concord SD II and XI show the same middle for Lutherans (monergist conversion, resistible grace, no double predestination).
findings.fix: Append to fair_summary: "Catholic, Orthodox, and Lutheran teaching sits between these poles: grace comes first and enables every good act, and God's plan cannot fail, yet grace can be refused and the justified can fall away. People in those traditions usually score near the center, and that is a settled position, not indecision."

findings.claim: 'Synergist' is a label coined by opponents in the Lutheran synergistic controversy; no Catholic document uses it of Catholic teaching. Tolerable (the Orthodox use synergeia positively) but not the holders' own word.
findings.evidence: Formula of Concord SD II condemns 'the Synergists'. Trent Sess. VI ch. 5 speaks of 'freely assenting to and cooperating with' grace; CCC 2001: 'God's free initiative demands man's free response.'
findings.fix: Keep the pole names, but gloss the term once in the summary: "Synergists (those who hold that we cooperate with grace) hold that..."

findings.claim: "Saving faith is itself a gift God gives to those he has chosen, not the reason he chose them" is double-barreled: 'faith is a gift' is affirmed by everyone on the axis; only 'not the reason he chose them' discriminates. Molinist Catholics (and classical Arminians) must answer Yes to the first clause and No to the second.
findings.evidence: Trent Sess. VI ch. 8 (faith 'the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of all justification', given by grace), Orange canon 5 (the beginning of faith is a gift), and Arminius's Declaration of Sentiments all say faith is a gift. Molina's Concordia and most Catholic apologists today hold election post praevisa merita; Aquinas ST I q.23 a.5 holds ante praevisa merita. The Catholic Church deliberately left both open (Paul V, 1607).
findings.fix: "God chose who will be saved without regard to any faith or merit he foresaw in them."

findings.claim: After Orange (529) every entry is Protestant (Luther, Remonstrance/Dort, Wesley/Whitefield). The Catholic Church's own definitive statements on grace and free will are absent even though Catholics are placed on the axis, so the history reads as a Protestant family quarrel that Catholics wandered into.
findings.evidence: Trent Sess. VI, Decree on Justification (13 January 1547), the standing Catholic doctrine of prevenient grace and free cooperation; Paul V's 1607 ruling ending the Congregatio de Auxiliis and permitting Thomists and Molinists each to teach their view; Innocent X, Cum occasione (1653), condemning the Jansenist propositions that interior grace is irresistible and that Christ died only for the elect.
findings.fix: Insert after 'Luther, The Bondage of the Will': {"when":"1547","what":"Council of Trent, Decree on Justification: grace comes first and enables, yet the will freely cooperates and can refuse."} and {"when":"1607","what":"Paul V ends the Congregatio de Auxiliis, leaving Thomists (efficacious grace) and Molinists (middle knowledge) both free to teach."}

findings.claim: The cooperation text Catholics and Orthodox reach for first is missing; the list has three monergist and three synergist texts but none on grace-and-cooperation together.
findings.evidence: Philippians 2:12-13 is quoted in CCC 308; 1 Corinthians 15:10 is the other standard text; cf. Augustine, Sermo 169, quoted in CCC 1847 ('God created us without us: but he did not will to save us without us').
findings.fix: Add "Philippians 2:12-13" and "1 Corinthians 15:10".

findings.claim: "In the Lord's Supper, Christ is truly present in a way that goes beyond a symbol" is affirmed equally by a Catholic and a Calvinist, so the Table axis has no statement separating the Catholic/Orthodox/Lutheran pole from the Reformed spiritual-presence position. Presbyterians answering S4-S6 honestly score 0 on Table and sit on top of the Catholic pole, while their coordinate says 35. 'Lord's Supper' is also not the Catholic word.
findings.evidence: Calvin, Institutes IV.17.10-12 affirms a true presence by the Spirit while denying local presence; WCF 29.7: 'really, but spiritually, present'. Trent Sess. XIII canons 1-2 and CCC 1376 define substantial presence by transubstantiation. A Presbyterian answering S4 +2, S5 -2, S6 +2 gets raw -6, score 0, Table coordinate 35.
findings.fix: "In the Eucharist (the Lord's Supper), the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ." Catholic, Orthodox, and Lutheran adherents agree; Reformed answer Unsure or Disagree; memorialists Strongly disagree.

findings.claim: Naming the right pole 'Memorial' hands the Zwinglian sense of the word to one side, when the Catholic Church calls the Eucharist a memorial in precisely the sacramental sense. A Catholic reads 'Sacramental vs Memorial' as a false opposition; a Baptist would happily accept their own word, 'ordinance', which the fair summary already uses.
findings.evidence: CCC 1362-1366: 'The Eucharist is the memorial of Christ's Passover... In the sense of Sacred Scripture the memorial is not merely the recollection of past events but... they become in a certain way present and real.' Luke 22:19 'Do this in memory of me'; the Roman Canon's 'Unde et memores'; SC 47. The fair summary text: 'both are ordinances obeyed by believers'.
findings.fix: right_pole: "Ordinance"; bands: ["sacramental", "sacramental-leaning", "mixed on the sacraments", "ordinance-leaning", "ordinance only"]. Update the share caption ('a memorialist shows many on Table') to match.

findings.claim: "Fourth Lateran Council defines transubstantiation" overstates; Lateran IV used the word in its creed, and the dogmatic definition with canons is Trent (1551), which is also absent from the history.
findings.evidence: Lateran IV canon 1 (Firmiter, 1215): 'transubstantiatis pane in corpus, et vino in sanguinem'. Trent Sess. XIII (11 October 1551) ch. 4 and canon 2 define transubstantiation; CCC 1376 quotes Trent, not Lateran IV, as the definition.
findings.fix: "1215: Fourth Lateran Council adopts the word 'transubstantiation' in its creed." and add {"when":"1551","what":"Council of Trent defines the Real Presence and transubstantiation against the Reformers."}

findings.claim: The 'Sacramental' reading list has no Catholic author on an axis where Catholics sit at 5. Mathison's Given for You argues Calvin's spiritual presence, which is the 35 position, not the pole.
findings.evidence: read_more.left = ["Schmemann, For the Life of the World", "Mathison, Given for You"]. Mathison's subtitle is 'Reclaiming Calvin's Doctrine of the Lord's Supper'.
findings.fix: left: ["Schmemann, For the Life of the World", "Ratzinger, God Is Near Us"] (or "Pitre, Jesus and the Jewish Roots of the Eucharist"). Move Mathison to a middle slot if you add one.

findings.claim: The texts Catholics reach for first on presence and on baptism actually saving are absent.
findings.fix: Add "1 Corinthians 10:16-17", "Luke 22:19-20", "1 Peter 3:20-21".

findings.claim: "The miraculous sign gifts ended with the apostles or the completion of the New Testament" is written in Warfield-school vocabulary ('sign gifts') and its second disjunct presumes a canon that closed by itself rather than one recognized by the Church centuries later. Answerable, but a Catholic notices.
findings.evidence: Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles (1918) for the vocabulary; canon lists of Hippo (393), Carthage (397), Trent Sess. IV (1546); CCC 120.
findings.fix: "The miraculous gifts of the apostolic age ended with the death of the apostles."

findings.claim: Chrysostom (c. 390) followed straight by Azusa Street (1906) tells the reader the gifts were dead for fifteen centuries. The patristic counter-witness is missing, and Augustine's retraction is the single most-cited datum on the continuationist side; omitting it is unfair to both sides (cessationists lean on the early Augustine, continuationists on the late one).
findings.evidence: Irenaeus, Against Heresies II.32.4 (c. 180): prophecy, healing, exorcism, and raising the dead 'in the church'. Augustine, City of God XXII.8 (c. 426) catalogues some seventy recent miracles at Hippo; Retractations I.13.7 withdraws his earlier claim (De vera religione 25.47) that miracles had ceased. Urban VIII (1634) makes proven miracles a condition of canonization.
findings.fix: Insert before Chrysostom: {"when":"c. 180","what":"Irenaeus reports prophecy, healing, and even raising of the dead in the churches of his day."} and after Chrysostom: {"when":"c. 426","what":"Augustine, City of God XXII.8, records recent miracles at Hippo and withdraws his earlier view that they had ceased."}

findings.claim: "Charismatic renewal carries the gifts into mainline and Catholic churches" says the Catholic Church lacked the gifts until the 1960s. What entered in 1967 was Pentecostal-style practice; on Catholic teaching the gifts never left, and the Church had been verifying healings for canonization for three centuries.
findings.evidence: Duquesne weekend, February 1967, begins the Catholic Charismatic Renewal; Paul VI's address to the Renewal, 19 May 1975; Francis establishes CHARIS, 2019. LG 12 and CCC 799-801 treat charisms as a constant of the Church's life; Urban VIII (1634) on miracles for canonization.
findings.fix: "1967: Duquesne weekend begins the Catholic Charismatic Renewal, later welcomed by Paul VI (1975) and Francis (2019); a similar renewal spreads through mainline Protestant churches."

findings.claim: The Continuationist list is two Reformed charismatics; the largest continuationist body in the world has no entry.
findings.evidence: read_more.left = ["Grudem, The Gift of Prophecy", "Storms, Practicing the Power"].
findings.fix: Add "Cantalamessa, Sober Intoxication of the Spirit" (or "McDonnell & Montague, Christian Initiation and Baptism in the Holy Spirit" for the patristic evidence).

findings.claim: "The church is the true Israel, heir to every promise God made to Abraham" is hard supersessionism, which the Catholic magisterium has explicitly stepped back from; a Catholic who takes Nostra Aetate seriously answers Unsure or a reluctant Agree. It is loaded against the other side too: dispensationalists hear 'replacement theology', a description covenant theologians themselves reject. Placement survives only because S10 and S12 carry the axis.
findings.evidence: Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839-840 (the Jewish people remain God's people, Rom 11:29); Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews, 'The Gifts and the Calling of God are Irrevocable' (2015) §17: 'the Church does not replace the people of God of Israel'. Lumen Gentium 9 says 'new Israel', never 'true Israel'. Justin's 'true Israel' (Dial. Trypho 11, 123) is ancient but not current magisterial language.
findings.fix: "The church, Jew and Gentile together, is the one people of God and inherits the promises made to Abraham."

findings.claim: 'Covenantal' is the name of Reformed federal theology. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and Anglican adherents at the left pole are amillennial but not 'covenant theologians', and the headline adjective 'covenantal' will strike them as another tradition's vocabulary; the 1646 Westminster history entry reinforces that reading.
findings.evidence: Covenant theology means the covenant of works and covenant of grace (WCF ch. 7; Cocceius). The Catholic position is Augustine's reading of Revelation 20 (City of God XX.7-9) and the formal rejection of millenarianism (CCC 676; Holy Office 1944), stated with no federal framework. Scott Hahn's Catholic covenant theology is the exception that proves the rule.
findings.fix: Either rename the left pole "One people of God" (bands: "one people of God", "one-people-leaning", ...) or add to the fair summary: "This is the amillennial reading shared by Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, and Reformed churches, whether or not they use the word 'covenantal'."

findings.claim: The only Catholic marker on this axis is Augustine; the Church's formal rejection of millenarianism is absent, while Westminster's covenant of works (a Reformed-internal development that has nothing to do with Israel or the millennium) stands in as the left pole's landmark.
findings.evidence: Holy Office decree of 21 July 1944 (DS 3839): mitigated millenarianism 'cannot safely be taught'; CCC 676: the Church 'has rejected even modified forms of this falsification of the kingdom to come under the name of millenarianism'.
findings.fix: Add {"when":"1944","what":"Holy Office rules that even 'mitigated' millenarianism cannot safely be taught; CCC 676 (1992) repeats the rejection."}

findings.claim: "The church, not the individual reader, is the final interpreter of Scripture" is a false dichotomy that is unfair to the other side: magisterial Protestants deny both that the church is infallible and that the individual is the final interpreter, so a Presbyterian cannot answer honestly. The Catholic claim is about a teaching office, not 'church vs individual'.
findings.evidence: WCF 1.9-10 (Scripture interprets Scripture; the supreme judge is 'the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture'); WCF 31.3 (councils 'may err, and many have erred'); Mathison, The Shape of Sola Scriptura, distinguishes sola from 'solo' scriptura. Catholic side: DV 10, authentic interpretation 'has been entrusted exclusively to the living teaching office of the Church'.
findings.fix: "The church's teaching office can settle a disputed reading of Scripture with an authority that binds believers."

findings.claim: The Dei Verbum entry is accurate but omits the one sentence that answers the standing caricature of 'tradition over Scripture'.
findings.evidence: DV 10: 'This teaching office is not above the word of God, but serves it.' DV 21: the Church 'has always venerated the divine Scriptures as she venerates the Body of the Lord'.
findings.fix: "1965: Vatican II, Dei Verbum: Scripture and Tradition flow from the same divine wellspring, and the teaching office 'is not above the word of God, but serves it'."

findings.claim: The texts a Catholic actually opens first on church authority are missing; the current left-side texts (2 Thess 2:15, 1 Tim 3:15, John 16:13) are right but incomplete.
findings.evidence: Matthew 16:18-19 (CCC 553, 881); Acts 15:6-29 ('it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us'); 2 Peter 1:20-21 (no prophecy of Scripture is a matter of one's own interpretation); 2 Peter 3:15-16.

findings.claim: 'Scripture-first' (60-79) implies the tradition side does not put Scripture first.
findings.evidence: DV 21 (Scripture venerated as the Body of the Lord); DV 24 (Scripture 'the soul of sacred theology').
findings.fix: bands[3] = "leaning Scripture alone".

findings.claim: "Free worship keeps the form open so that the Spirit can lead in the moment, with an emphasis on spontaneity, sincerity, and the participation of the whole congregation" implicitly says liturgical worship is not led by the Spirit and is not participatory. The second claim is especially galling: 'active participation' is the watchword of Catholic liturgical reform.
findings.evidence: CCC 1091-1112, 'The Holy Spirit and the Church in the Liturgy'; SC 7 (Christ present in the liturgy); SC 14: 'full, conscious, and active participation' of all the faithful is 'the aim to be considered before all else'.
findings.fix: "Free worship keeps the form open, trusting the Spirit to shape each gathering as it happens, with an emphasis on spontaneity, sincerity, and every member's freedom to contribute."

findings.claim: "Worship should be free-form and led by the Spirit in the moment" pairs a form question with a loaded contrast; a liturgical Catholic must 'disagree' with being led by the Spirit.
findings.evidence: CCC 1091-1112 on the Spirit's work in the liturgy; SC 7.
findings.fix: "Worship should be shaped in the moment rather than follow a set order."

findings.claim: The liturgical side's history stops at Cranmer 1549; the most consequential liturgical event of the last four centuries for the largest church is absent, and it is the one that made 'participation' a liturgical rather than free-church watchword.
findings.evidence: Sacrosanctum Concilium, promulgated 4 December 1963; SC 14 'full, conscious, and active participation'. Pius V's Roman Missal (1570) standardized the Latin Mass for four centuries.
findings.fix: Insert after Finney: {"when":"1963","what":"Vatican II, Sacrosanctum Concilium: reform of the Mass and the call for 'full, conscious, and active participation' of the whole congregation."} Optionally add {"when":"1570","what":"Pius V's Roman Missal fixes the Latin Mass for four centuries."}

findings.fix: left: ["Schmemann, Introduction to Liturgical Theology", "Ratzinger, The Spirit of the Liturgy"]; move Webber to a middle slot if one exists.

findings.claim: The middle bands 'centered on the sacraments' (Table 41-59) and 'centered on the kingdom' (Kingdom 41-59) describe a score of 50 with words that mean a strong position; as headline adjectives they misrepresent the person and slight both poles.
findings.evidence: Table bands[2] = "centered on the sacraments"; Kingdom bands[2] = "centered on the kingdom". The person at Table 50 is not centered on the sacraments; the Catholic at 0 is (LG 11, the Eucharist as 'source and summit').

findings.claim: Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox answer 15 of 18 statements identically; the only separator is Grace, where Catholics themselves range 33-83. The top two for any Catholic will be RC and EO in an order set by noise, and nothing in the quiz tests a Catholic distinctive (papacy, purgatory, the sacrifice of the Mass, justification). The copy should say so, and the Orthodox grace coordinate should reflect that Orthodox reject election prior to foreseen faith more uniformly than Catholics do.
findings.evidence: John of Damascus, De fide orthodoxa II.30 ('God foreknows all things but does not predetermine all'); Ware, The Orthodox Church. An Orthodox answering S1 -1, S2 +2, S3 -1 gets raw 4, score 83, yet the coordinate is 65. With RC fixed to [55,5,20,15,5,5] and EO grace at 75, base simulation: RC 17.1 vs EO sqrt(100+25+729+49+25+25) = 30.9.
findings.fix: Set Eastern Orthodox grace to 75. Add under 'Closest traditions': "Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox answer these eighteen statements almost alike; the quiz does not measure what divides them." Do not try a papacy statement on the Tradition axis (it would push Orthodox toward 'Scripture alone').

findings.claim: 'Roman Catholic' excludes the 23 Eastern Catholic churches (roughly 18 million members) whose adherents answer these statements identically; the term is also of Anglican origin and not the Church's self-designation.
findings.evidence: Orientalium Ecclesiarum (1964); Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990); the Church names itself 'Catholic' in the creeds and 'Catholic Church' in the Catechism's title.
findings.fix: Rename the tradition entry "Catholic".

lens: charismatic non-denominational (Vineyard, Bethel, Hillsong, Third Wave)

simulation.headline: Continuationist, free in worship, Arminian-leaning
simulation.comment: Answers as a typical informed Third Wave member (Vineyard/Bethel-shaped, not AoG-shaped): Q1 Disagree, Q2 Agree, Q3 Disagree; Q4 Agree (reads 'truly present' as manifest presence), Q5 Strongly agree, Q6 Strongly disagree; Q7/Q9 Strongly agree, Q8 Strongly disagree; Q10 Unsure, Q11 Disagree (pro-Israel reflex), Q12 Disagree (Ladd/Bethel are not pre-trib); Q13 Unsure, Q14 Strongly agree, Q15 Disagree; Q16 Disagree, Q17 Strongly agree, Q18 Disagree. Raw = sum(direction*answer): grace (-1)(-1)+(1)(1)+(-1)(-1)=3 -> round(9/12*100)=75; table (-1)(1)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-2)=3 -> 75; spirit (-1)(2)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(2)=-6 -> 0; kingdom (1)(0)+(-1)(-1)+(1)(-1)=0 -> 50; tradition (-1)(0)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-1)=3 -> 75; worship (-1)(-1)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-1)=4 -> round(10/12*100)=83. Headline: |score-50| = spirit 50, worship 33, grace/table/tradition tied at 25; the HTML tie-break is axis index, so grace wins -> 'continuationist' + 'free in worship' + 'Arminian-leaning'. Distances (me = 75,75,0,50,75,83): Charismatic non-denom (70,80,5,60,85,90): sqrt(25+25+25+100+100+49)=sqrt(324)=18.0 (93% match); Pentecostal/AoG (80,85,5,75,85,90): sqrt(25+100+25+625+100+49)=sqrt(924)=30.4 (88%); Anabaptist 63.9; Wesleyan 81.5; Southern Baptist 85.4; Reformed Baptist 108.5; Dispensational Bible church 108.9; Anglican 112.4; Presbyterian/Reformed 122.6; Roman Catholic 133.0; Lutheran 135.3; Eastern Orthodox 135.8. Lands correctly, but only because Q10-Q12 pull kingdom to 50: the two charismatic entries sit 18.7 apart (sqrt(100+25+225)), less than a single Strongly-agree-to-Strongly-disagree swing on one statement (33 points on one axis), so the landing is fragile. Three secondary profiles: a Ladd-style Vineyard member (67,75,0,17,58,75) still lands Charismatic but at distance 53.5 (78%) because of the kingdom=60 coordinate; a younger AoG member unsure on Israel and the rapture (75,83,0,58,75,92) lands Charismatic (12.9) ahead of Pentecostal (21.1), i.e. wrong; a Sovereign Grace/Newfrontiers Reformed charismatic (8,83,0,42,75,75) has nothing nearer than 67.3. Fixes and their arithmetic are in the findings.

findings.claim: With these six axes 'Charismatic non-denominational' and 'Pentecostal / Assemblies of God' are not distinguishable, and real AoG members land on the charismatic entry.
findings.evidence: The two coordinates differ only by grace 10, table 5, kingdom 15: distance sqrt(100+25+225)=18.7, smaller than one answer swing on one statement (33 points on an axis). Simulated younger AoG member, Unsure on Q10 and Q12 (scores 75,83,0,58,75,92): Charismatic 12.9 vs Pentecostal 21.1 -> lands 'Charismatic non-denominational'. The real boundary between the two families is untested: AoG Statement of Fundamental Truths art. 7 (baptism in the Holy Spirit 'distinct from and subsequent to' the new birth) and art. 8 (speaking in tongues as 'the initial physical evidence'); Third Wave teaching denies both (Wimber; Grudem, Systematic Theology ch. 39; Storms, Practicing the Power; Vineyard USA Statement of Faith). No statement touches Spirit baptism or initial evidence.
findings.fix: Add a 19th statement that is NOT scored on the Spirit band (so a Third Wave respondent is not pushed toward 'cessationist') but is used as a seventh coordinate in the nearest-tradition distance: 'Speaking in tongues is the normal first sign that a person has been baptized in the Holy Spirit.' Map -2..2 to 0..100 and give traditions an initial_evidence coordinate: Pentecostal / AoG 95, Charismatic non-denominational 15, all others 0-5. Result: Charismatic<->Pentecostal separation rises from 18.7 to 86.6; the younger-AoG profile lands Pentecostal (29.1 vs 63.1); the Hillsong pre-trib profile lands Pentecostal (23.3 vs 69.7); the Third Wave and Bethel profiles stay Charismatic (21.2 and 34.2).

findings.claim: The middle-band adjectives 'centered on the sacraments' (table 41-59) and 'centered on the kingdom' (kingdom 41-59) assert a positive commitment that a score of 50 does not represent; they appear in the headline.
findings.evidence: The code gives 50 to anyone who answers Unsure to all three statements, or who splits (e.g. my Q10 Unsure / Q11 Disagree / Q12 Disagree = kingdom 50). A Baptist at table 50 would be headlined 'centered on the sacraments'; a respondent torn between Israel-has-a-future and no-pre-trib-rapture is headlined 'centered on the kingdom', which in Vineyard vocabulary is a doctrinal claim (Ladd's kingdom theology), not a midpoint. Every other axis uses a genuine midpoint word ('balanced on grace', 'undecided on the gifts', 'balanced on authority', 'flexible in worship').
findings.fix: table bands[2]: 'between sacrament and symbol'; kingdom bands[2]: 'undecided on Israel and the church'.

findings.claim: kingdom 60 puts the tradition in the 'dispensational-leaning' band, which Vineyard and Bethel explicitly reject; the coordinate should be near the center.
findings.evidence: Vineyard's whole framework is Ladd's inaugurated kingdom ('already and not yet'; Wimber, Power Evangelism, 1986; Vineyard USA Statement of Faith; Morphew, Breakthrough), and Ladd was post-tribulational (The Blessed Hope, 1956) with one people of God, which the quiz's own history[4] records. Bethel promotes Eberle & Trench, Victorious Eschatology (2006), an explicitly anti-rapture, partial-preterist view. Hillsong's belief statement fixes no rapture timing. Simulated: typical Third Wave kingdom 50, Ladd-style Vineyard 17, Bethel 50. At kingdom 60 the Ladd-style Vineyard member is 53.5 from the entry (78% match).
