Formula of Concord, Epitome, Summary (1577): the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures are 'the only rule and norm according to which all teachings, together with all teachers, should be evaluated and judged.' (Bainton, Here I Stand; Kolb-Wengert ed. of the Book of Concord.) A Protestant reader will screenshot a 'Scripture alone' history that has one Protestant line and three Roman Catholic ones.
findings.fix: Insert two lines so the array reads 434 / 1519–21 / 1546 / 1577 / 1646 / 1845 / 1965: {when: '1519–21', what: 'At Leipzig Luther concedes that councils have erred; at Worms he refuses to recant unless convinced "by Scripture and plain reason".'} and {when: '1577', what: 'Formula of Concord: Scripture is "the only rule and norm" by which teachers and doctrines are judged; the ancient creeds are received as witnesses to it.'} If length matters, drop the 1845 Newman line (it is already the first read-more title).

findings.claim: The Spirit history reads as the cessationist's story: the gifts are viewed warily (2nd c.), cease (c. 390), and reappear in Los Angeles in 1906. Count: Montanist-wariness, Chrysostom, Warfield, Strange Fire = 4 lines for cessation; Azusa, 1960s = 2 for continuation; nothing at all between 390 and 1906. The early-church witnesses to continuing gifts, which every Pentecostal historian cites first, are missing.
findings.evidence: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.32.4 (c. 180): believers 'drive out devils... have foreknowledge of things to come... heal the sick by laying their hands upon them... the dead even have been raised'; 5.6.1: 'many brethren in the Church who possess prophetic gifts and who through the Spirit speak all kinds of languages.' Augustine, De vera religione 25.47 (c. 390) says miracles were not allowed to continue; Retractationes 1.13.7 withdraws this, and City of God 22.8 (c. 426) catalogues some seventy recent miracles at Hippo. The 'Third Wave' (Wimber, Vineyard, Wagner's term, 1980s) is also absent although Grudem's 1988 book in read-more came out of it. (Kydd, Charismatic Gifts in the Early Church; Ruthven, On the Cessation of the Charismata.)
findings.fix: Add three lines: {when: 'c. 180', what: 'Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.32 and 5.6, reports prophecy, tongues, healings, and even the dead raised in the churches of his day.'}; {when: 'c. 426', what: 'Augustine, City of God 22.8, records recent healings at Hippo, withdrawing his earlier view that miracles had ceased.'}; {when: '1980s', what: 'The "Third Wave" (John Wimber, the Vineyard) brings the gifts into evangelical churches that had never been Pentecostal.'} With these the count is 4 : 5, and the array no longer jumps from 390 to 1906.

findings.claim: 'his saving grace cannot finally be refused' makes irresistible grace the definition of monergism. That is the Reformed doctrine, not monergism as such; confessional Lutherans are monergists who expressly deny it, and the position table itself places them at 20 ('firmly monergist').
findings.evidence: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration II (Free Will) and XI (Election): conversion is God's work alone, yet 'the Holy Spirit... can be resisted', grace is universal, and the regenerate can fall away (SD XI.42; SD IV.31). Quiz statement 2 ('A person can genuinely resist God's grace and refuse salvation to the very end') is therefore answered Agree by a Lutheran, and the summary tells him he is not a monergist. A Lutheran pastor will screenshot this.
findings.fix: Replace the first sentence with: 'Monergists hold that salvation is God's work from beginning to end: he chooses, calls, and keeps his people, and faith is his gift rather than the reason for his choice. (Whether that grace can be resisted divides Lutherans from the Reformed within this pole.)' Keep the synergist sentence as is.

findings.claim: 'Reformed-leaning' (21–40) and 'Arminian-leaning' (60–79) hang party names on a doctrinal axis, unlike every other axis ('sacramental-leaning', 'covenantal-leaning'). A confessional Lutheran, a Thomist Catholic, or a Jansenist who scores 25–40 is told he is 'Reformed-leaning'; a Molinist Catholic, an Eastern Orthodox (whose own word is 'synergy'), or a Wesleyan who scores 60–79 is told he is 'Arminian-leaning'. Those labels appear in the headline and share card.
findings.evidence: Aquinas, ST I q.23 a.5 (predestination not grounded in foreseen merit) and the Formula of Concord XI are monergist texts by people who were not Reformed; the Confession of Dositheus (1672) and the whole Greek patristic tradition of synergeia predate Arminius. The tradition table puts Lutheran at 20 and Orthodox at 65, i.e. right on these mislabeled bands.
findings.fix: bands: ['firmly monergist', 'monergist-leaning', 'balanced on grace', 'synergist-leaning', 'firmly synergist'].

findings.claim: The Grace history never gives the synergist pole a milestone of its own. Count: Augustine (0) and Luther (2) are monergist landmarks; Orange (1), Remonstrance/Dort (3), Wesley/Whitefield (4) are shared. The Eastern tradition, whose word 'synergy' names the right pole and which sits at 65 on the map, has no line on this axis (or on any axis).
findings.evidence: John Cassian, Conferences 13 (c. 426–29), the classic statement that grace and will cooperate, attacked by Prosper in Contra Collatorem c. 432 (Gonzalez, History of Christian Thought II; Pelikan, Christian Tradition I). Council of Trent, Session VI, Decree on Justification (13 Jan 1547), ch. 5 and canon 4: the will, moved by grace, 'is able to refuse' (potest dissentire, si velit).
findings.fix: Add {when: 'c. 426–29', what: 'John Cassian, Conferences 13: grace and the human will work together, the position the Christian East calls synergy.'} and {when: '1547', what: 'Council of Trent, Decree on Justification: the will, moved and awakened by grace, freely assents and can refuse.'} Sequence: 411–430 / 426–29 / 529 / 1525 / 1547 / 1610–19 / 1739–41.

findings.claim: '1740s' is the wrong decade for the Wesley–Whitefield breach; it opened in 1739 and was complete by 1741.
findings.evidence: Wesley preached Free Grace at Bristol on 29 April 1739 and printed it that summer; Whitefield's reply letter is dated Bethesda, 24 December 1740, and was printed in London in 1741, the year Whitefield's separate Tabernacle opened (Dallimore, George Whitefield, vol. 2; Rack, Reasonable Enthusiast).
findings.fix: {when: '1739–41', what: "Wesley's sermon Free Grace and Whitefield's printed reply divide the evangelical revival over predestination."}

findings.claim: 'Council of Orange' should be 'Second Council of Orange' (there was a first, in 441), and the line understates what the council said on the synergist side: it does not only reject predestination to evil, it also affirms that every baptized person can, with Christ's help, do what salvation requires.
findings.evidence: Orange II, canons 5–7 (the initium fidei is God's gift); Conclusion: 'we not only do not believe that any are foreordained to evil by the power of God, but... anathema'; and 'all baptized persons have the ability and responsibility, if they desire to labor faithfully, to perform with the aid and cooperation of Christ what is of essential importance in regard to the salvation of their soul' (Denzinger 370–397; Pelikan I, 329).
findings.fix: {when: '529', what: 'Second Council of Orange: even the first stirring of faith is God\'s gift (canon 5), yet the council anathematizes any predestination to evil and says all the baptized can, with Christ\'s help, do what salvation requires.'}

findings.claim: 'the Synod of Dort replies with five points' is a mild anachronism: the Canons are arranged under four heads (the Third and Fourth combined), and 'five points'/TULIP is a twentieth-century mnemonic.
findings.evidence: Canons of Dort (1619): First, Second, Third and Fourth, Fifth Heads of Doctrine. The TULIP acrostic is first attested in 1905 (McAfee) and popularized by Boettner (1932).
findings.fix: {when: '1610–19', what: 'The Remonstrance sets out five Arminian articles; the Synod of Dort answers them article by article in its Canons.'}

findings.claim: The Table history stops in 1559 and gives the memorial pole a single line. Count: Ignatius, Lateran IV, Calvin = 3 sacramental; Zurich 1525 = 1 memorial; Marburg = shared. Baptists, the pole's actual population (SBC 85, Bible church 90, Pentecostal 85), do not appear, and Zwingli's own argument, the read-more title for this pole, has no history line.
findings.evidence: Zwingli, Commentary on True and False Religion (1525) and On the Lord's Supper (1526), adopting Hoen's reading that est means significat. John Smyth's baptism of believers, Amsterdam, 1609; First London Baptist Confession (1644), art. 40, requires 'dipping or plunging' of professing believers (Lumpkin, Baptist Confessions of Faith).
findings.fix: Add {when: '1525–26', what: 'Zwingli, On the Lord\'s Supper: "this is my body" means "this signifies my body"; the Supper is a thanksgiving memorial.'} and {when: '1609–44', what: 'John Smyth baptizes professing believers in Amsterdam; the First London Baptist Confession (1644) requires their immersion.'} Sequence: c. 110 / 1215 / 1525 / 1525–26 / 1529 / 1559 / 1609–44.

findings.claim: The page promises 'the passages each side reaches for', but all six Table passages are the sacramental side's texts. John 6:53–58 (real presence), Acts 2:38–39 ('you and your children'), Colossians 2:11–12 (circumcision–baptism), Romans 6:3–4 and Matthew 26:26–28 (shared), 1 Corinthians 11 (shared). No distinctly memorialist or credobaptist text appears.
findings.evidence: Standard credobaptist proof texts: Acts 8:36–38 (belief precedes baptism), 1 Peter 3:21 ('an appeal to God for a good conscience'), Acts 16:31–33; the memorialist text is Luke 22:19 ('do this in remembrance of me'). See Schreiner & Wright, Believer's Baptism, which the quiz itself recommends.
findings.fix: key_passages: ['John 6:53–58', '1 Corinthians 11:23–29', 'Luke 22:19–20', 'Acts 2:38–39', 'Colossians 2:11–12', 'Acts 8:36–38', '1 Peter 3:21'].

findings.claim: Marburg produced fifteen articles, not fourteen; Luther and Zwingli signed fourteen and most of the fifteenth, differing only on whether Christ's body is bodily present in the bread.
findings.evidence: Marburg Articles, 1–4 October 1529: article 15 records agreement on both kinds, rejection of the mass as a sacrifice, and spiritual eating of the body and blood, and disagreement 'whether the true body and blood of Christ are bodily in the bread and wine' (Schaff, History VII, §108; LW 38:85–89).
findings.fix: {when: '1529', what: 'Marburg Colloquy: Luther and Zwingli sign fourteen of fifteen articles and most of the fifteenth, but not whether Christ\'s body is bodily present in the bread.'}

findings.claim: 'Fourth Lateran Council defines transubstantiation' overstates it. Lateran IV used the word in its creed; the dogmatic definition came at Trent. The line also makes a specifically Roman doctrine the sacramental pole's milestone, though the Lutherans and Orthodox placed at that pole reject transubstantiation.
findings.evidence: Lateran IV, canon 1 Firmiter (1215): 'transubstantiatis pane in corpus et vino in sanguinem'. Trent, Session XIII (11 Oct 1551), ch. 4 and canon 2, defines the doctrine (Denzinger 802; 1642, 1652). McGrath, Christian Theology, on the term's history.
findings.fix: {when: '1215', what: 'Fourth Lateran Council writes "transubstantiated" into its creed; Trent (1551) will define the doctrine.'}

findings.claim: Half the axis is about baptism, and the right pole gets a baptism title (Believer's Baptism) while the left gets none: Schmemann and Mathison are both about the Eucharist. A paedobaptist reader has nowhere to go.
findings.evidence: All four listed books exist as titled (Schmemann 1963; Mathison, Given for You, 2002; Zwingli 1526; Schreiner & Wright 2006). Geoffrey Bromiley, Children of Promise: The Case for Baptizing Infants (Eerdmans, 1979) is the standard short defense.
findings.fix: left: ['Schmemann, For the Life of the World', 'Bromiley, Children of Promise'] (or keep Mathison and add Bromiley as a third).

findings.claim: 'notes that the sign gifts had ceased' puts a twentieth-century category ('sign gifts') and a doctrine (cessation) into Chrysostom's mouth. What he says is an observation that the gifts Paul lists no longer occur in his day; he gives no teaching that they ended with the apostles or the canon, and he elsewhere celebrates healings and exorcisms at the martyrs' shrines.
findings.evidence: Chrysostom, Homilies on 1 Corinthians 29 (on 12:1–2), delivered at Antioch c. 390–92: 'This whole place is very obscure: but the obscurity is produced by our ignorance of the facts referred to and by their cessation, being such as then used to occur but now no longer take place' (NPNF1 12:168). Homily De sancta Pentecoste 1 argues signs were scaffolding for unbelievers. On St. Babylas and the homilies on the martyrs speak of demons driven out at the relics.
findings.fix: {when: 'c. 390', what: 'Chrysostom, Homily 29 on 1 Corinthians, remarks that the gifts Paul lists "used to occur but now no longer take place", an observation about his own day rather than a doctrine that they ended with the apostles.'}

findings.claim: 'MacArthur, Strange Fire' is the cessationist polemic whose subtitle is 'The Danger of Offending the Holy Spirit with Counterfeit Worship'; a charismatic will not accept a page that recommends a book calling his worship counterfeit as the fair account of the other side, and the quiz already lists the conference in the history. Both cessationist titles contain 'Counterfeit'. On the left, Grudem and Storms are both Reformed continuationists; the Pentecostal/Assemblies of God tradition, placed at 5 on this very axis, has no author.
findings.evidence: All four books exist as titled (Grudem 1988/2000, Storms 2017, MacArthur 2013, Warfield 1918). Measured cessationist statement: Richard Gaffin, Perspectives on Pentecost (P&R, 1979). Pentecostal scholarship: Gordon Fee (Assemblies of God), God's Empowering Presence (Hendrickson, 1994); Craig Keener, Gift and Giver (Baker, 2001).
findings.fix: left: ['Fee, God\'s Empowering Presence', 'Grudem, The Gift of Prophecy']; right: ['Gaffin, Perspectives on Pentecost', 'Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles'].

findings.claim: '1906: Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles launches modern Pentecostalism' skips the birth. Historians date the movement to Topeka, 1 January 1901; Azusa (April 1906) is where it spread from.
findings.evidence: Charles Parham's Bethel Bible School, Topeka; Agnes Ozman's tongues, 1 Jan 1901; William Seymour's Azusa Street mission from April 1906 (Synan, The Holiness-Pentecostal Tradition; Anderson, An Introduction to Pentecostalism).
findings.fix: {when: '1901–06', what: 'Topeka (Charles Parham) and the Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles (William Seymour) launch modern Pentecostalism.'}

findings.claim: The Kingdom history is shaped as a covenantal narrative: the ancient church is Augustine (amillennial), dispensationalism appears from nowhere in the 1830s, and the last two lines show it retreating (Ladd's 'one people of God', progressive dispensationalism 'softens'). Missing is the fact every dispensationalist and historic premillennialist states first: the second-century Fathers expected a literal earthly thousand-year reign.
findings.evidence: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 80–81: 'there will be a resurrection of the dead, and a thousand years in Jerusalem, which will then be built'; Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.32–36; Papias (in Eusebius HE 3.39); Tertullian, Adv. Marc. 3.24 (Pelikan I, 123–26; Gonzalez I). Augustine himself says in City of God 20.7 that he once held the chiliast view. 'Softens' is the covenantalist's verb; Blaising and Bock describe their work as revising the distinction, not softening it.
findings.fix: Add {when: 'c. 155–180', what: 'Justin Martyr and Irenaeus expect a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth in a rebuilt Jerusalem (chiliasm).'} before the Augustine line, and change history:5 to {when: '1990s', what: 'Progressive dispensationalism (Blaising, Bock, Saucy) revises the Israel–church distinction: one people of God, distinct roles.'}

findings.claim: 'J. N. Darby and the Plymouth Brethren teach a distinct Israel and a pretribulational rapture' attributes to the whole movement what divided it. The Israel/church distinction is Darby's from the Powerscourt conferences (1831–33); the pretribulational rapture is fully worked out by about 1839–40; and leading Brethren (B. W. Newton, S. P. Tregelles) rejected the secret rapture, which was one cause of the Darby–Newton rupture of 1845–48.
findings.evidence: Sandeen, The Roots of Fundamentalism, ch. 2–3; Ryrie, Dispensationalism, ch. 4 (Darby's system formed 1827–33 and developed thereafter); Darby, The Hopes of the Church of God (Lausanne lectures, 1840); Tregelles, The Hope of Christ's Second Coming (1864).
findings.fix: {when: '1830s', what: 'J. N. Darby, out of the Powerscourt conferences (1831–33), separates Israel\'s earthly hope from the church\'s heavenly one and develops the pretribulational rapture; some Brethren (B. W. Newton) dissent.'}

findings.claim: 'Westminster Confession sets out the covenant of works and the covenant of grace' is true but is not the point this axis measures. The covenantal claim tested by statement 11 (one people of God across both testaments) is Calvin's, and he states it exactly.
findings.evidence: Calvin, Institutes II.10.2 (1559): 'the covenant made with all the patriarchs is so much like ours in substance and reality that the two are actually one and the same'; II.11 on the differences in administration. Westminster ch. 7 (1646) builds on this but is about the works/grace distinction.
findings.fix: {when: '1559', what: 'Calvin, Institutes II.10–11: the covenant with the patriarchs and ours are one in substance, differing only in administration.'} Keep the 1646 line if space allows, but this one should come first.

findings.claim: 'Christ's kingdom is present now, with his return bringing the new creation' defines the covenantal pole as amillennial. Historic premillennialists (Ladd, whom history:4 cites for 'one people of God') and postmillennialists are covenantal on the Israel/church question but expect a millennium.
findings.evidence: Ladd, The Blessed Hope (1956) and A Theology of the New Testament: one people of God, future millennium. WCF and the Reformed confessions leave the millennium open; Riddlebarger's amillennial book in read-more is one option within the pole, not the pole.
findings.fix: '...inherits the promises to Abraham, and Christ's kingdom is already present, whatever they expect of a future millennium.'

findings.claim: The right pole and its top band are both called 'Scripture alone', but statements 14 and 15 ('proven from Scripture alone; tradition can never bind the conscience'; 'the church, not the individual reader, is the final interpreter') measure biblicism, not the Reformers' sola scriptura. The people who wrote the axis's own Protestant history line (Westminster) subscribe to binding creeds and confessions and so land at 35–45, labeled 'tradition-friendly' or 'balanced on authority'; the Reformation slogan is handed to the position Mathison's recommended book calls 'solo scriptura'.
findings.evidence: Luther subscribed to the three ecumenical creeds (Three Symbols, 1538); Formula of Concord receives them as binding summaries. WCF 31.3: decrees of councils 'if consonant to the Word of God, are to be received with reverence and submission'. Lutheran and Presbyterian ministers are bound by confessional subscription. Mathison, The Shape of Sola Scriptura (2001), argues precisely that the Reformers' view included the regula fidei. The tradition table itself puts Lutheran at 35 and Presbyterian at 45.
findings.fix: right_pole: 'Scripture over tradition'; bands: ['rooted in tradition', 'tradition-friendly', 'balanced on authority', 'Scripture-first', 'Bible-only']. Alternatively keep the pole name and reword statement 14 to 'No creed, council, or confession can bind the conscience; only Scripture can.'

findings.claim: 'the church's teaching office' is Roman magisterium language. The Eastern Orthodox, placed at 5 on this axis, have no teaching office; they appeal to the councils and the consensus of the Fathers.
findings.evidence: Florovsky, Bible, Church, Tradition (the quiz's own read-more title) explicitly contrasts the Orthodox view with a magisterium; Dei Verbum 10 is where 'magisterium' is the term of art.
findings.fix: '...hold that the creeds, councils, and the church's living teaching (the consensus of the Fathers; for Catholics, the magisterium) are God's appointed means...'

findings.claim: 'the participation of the whole congregation' is claimed as the free pole's distinctive. That phrase is the liturgical movement's own watchword, and a Catholic, Orthodox, or Anglican reader will object that responsive liturgy is congregational participation by design.
findings.evidence: Vatican II, Sacrosanctum Concilium 14 (4 Dec 1963): 'full, conscious, and active participation in liturgical celebrations... is the aim to be considered before all else'. Common prayer (Cranmer's title) means prayer said by the people. The free pole's real distinctive is that any member may contribute as prompted.
findings.fix: Free-pole sentence: 'Free worship keeps the form open so that the Spirit can lead in the moment, with an emphasis on spontaneity, sincerity, and room for any member to contribute as the Spirit prompts.' Also add to history: {when: '1963', what: 'Vatican II, Sacrosanctum Concilium: vernacular liturgy and the "full, conscious, and active participation" of the people.'}

findings.claim: Both right-pole authors are Reformed. Frame's Worship in Spirit and Truth is a Presbyterian defense of the regulative principle (he would answer statement 17 Disagree), and Kauflin is Sovereign Grace. The Pentecostal/Assemblies of God tradition, at 90 on this axis, has no voice for the position 'led by the Spirit in the moment'.
findings.evidence: All four books exist as titled (Schmemann 1966; Webber 2008; Frame, P&R 1996; Kauflin, Crossway 2008). Frame, ch. 3–4, argues for the regulative principle with broad application. Jack Hayford, Worship His Majesty (Word, 1987), by the Foursquare pastor who wrote 'Majesty', is the standard Pentecostal worship book.
findings.fix: right: ['Hayford, Worship His Majesty', 'Kauflin, Worship Matters'].

findings.claim: Justin's description is quoted only for its order; the same chapter says the presider prays 'according to his ability', the free-worship side's favorite second-century datum, and the line should carry both.
findings.evidence: Justin, First Apology 67 (also 65): the president 'offers prayers and thanksgivings, according to his ability' (ὅση δύναμις αὐτῷ); Bradshaw, The Search for the Origins of Christian Worship, on improvised presidential prayer.
findings.fix: {when: 'c. 155', what: 'Justin Martyr\'s First Apology 67: Sunday readings, a sermon, prayers, and the Eucharist, the presider giving thanks "according to his ability".'}

findings.claim: '1600s: Puritans articulate the regulative principle' is a century late for the articulation and vague on the landmark. The principle is sixteenth-century Reformed; the Puritan landmark is Westminster's Directory replacing the Prayer Book (1645) and WCF 21.1 (1646).
findings.evidence: Calvin, The Necessity of Reforming the Church (1543); Scots Confession (1560) ch. 20; the Vestiarian controversy (1566); Cartwright's Admonition controversy (1572). Directory for the Publique Worship of God, adopted by Parliament 3 January 1645; WCF 21.1: worship 'limited by his own revealed will'.
findings.fix: {when: '1645–46', what: 'Westminster\'s Directory for Public Worship replaces the Prayer Book; the Confession (21.1) states the regulative principle: only what Scripture prescribes belongs in worship.'}

findings.claim: 'Communion should be celebrated every week as the center of the service' pushes toward 'liturgical', but the two groups with the longest record of weekly communion without any liturgy, the Plymouth Brethren (weekly breaking of bread since the 1830s) and the Churches of Christ / Restorationists (weekly Supper since the 1800s), are among the most free-form congregations that exist. An honest Brethren answer is pulled toward the pole he rejects.
findings.evidence: Darby and the Brethren assemblies made the weekly, unled breaking of bread their defining practice; Alexander Campbell's Christian System (1835) makes weekly communion a mark of the restored church, with no liturgy.
findings.fix: Reword to test set form rather than frequency: 'Worship should follow the church year (Advent, Lent, Easter) and set forms for the sacraments.'

findings.claim: Three of the recommended authors (Grudem, Storms, Kauflin) belong to a Reformed-charismatic family (Sovereign Grace, the Piper circle) that has no node on the map. A Reformed continuationist answering honestly, roughly (10, 70, 10, 30, 55, 65), lands on 'Reformed Baptist' at about 71% only because the Spirit axis differs by 70 points.
findings.evidence: Distance to Reformed Baptist (10,70,80,30,55,65) = 70; to Charismatic non-denominational (70,80,5,60,85,90) = sqrt(3600+100+25+900+900+625) ≈ 78. Neither is a 'close' match.
findings.fix: Add {name: 'Reformed charismatic', position: {grace: 10, table: 70, spirit: 15, kingdom: 30, tradition: 55, worship: 70}}.

lens: confessional Lutheran (LCMS / WELS / Book of Concord)

simulation.headline: Sacramental, covenantal, liturgical
simulation.comment: Answers (FC SD XI election is certain and in Christ: S1 +2; grace resistible, FC SD II and XI.41: S2 +2; faith a gift and not the cause of election, LCMS Brief Statement 1932: S3 +2; real presence S4 +2; baptism regenerates, SC IV: S5 -2, S6 +2; gifts not the ordinary pattern, SA III.viii: S7 -1, S8 +1, S9 -2; AC XVII amillennial: S10 -2, S11 +1, S12 -2; creeds are norma normata but councils can err: S13 +1; FC Rule and Norm, AC XXVIII: S14 +2; Scripture interprets itself, neither church nor reader is 'final': S15 -1; AC XXIV liturgy kept, every-Sunday Mass: S16 +2, S17 -2, S18 +1). Raw: Grace (-1)(2)+(1)(2)+(-1)(2) = -2 -> round(4/12*100) = 33; Table (-1)(2)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(2) = -6 -> 0; Spirit (-1)(-1)+(1)(1)+(-1)(-2) = +4 -> round(83.3) = 83; Kingdom (1)(-2)+(-1)(1)+(1)(-2) = -5 -> round(8.3) = 8; Tradition (-1)(1)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-1) = +2 -> round(66.7) = 67; Worship (-1)(2)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(1) = -5 -> 8. Headline: |s-50| = Table 50, Kingdom 42, Worship 42, Spirit 33, Grace 17, Tradition 17; top three Table, Kingdom (index tie-break beats Worship), Worship -> bands 'sacramental', 'covenantal', 'liturgical'. Note the Grace band a Lutheran receives is 'Reformed-leaning' (33), which is the one word a confessional Lutheran will screenshot. Distances to Lutheran coords [20,15,70,15,35,20]: sqrt(13^2+15^2+13^2+7^2+32^2+12^2) = sqrt(1780) = 42.2 (83%); Presbyterian [10,35,75,15,45,45]: sqrt(529+1225+64+49+484+1369) = sqrt(3720) = 61.0 (75%); Anglican sqrt(3775) = 61.4; Roman Catholic 75.2; Wesleyan 84.0; Eastern Orthodox 85.2; Reformed Baptist 96.5; Anabaptist 113.9; Southern Baptist 124.3; Dispensational 144.2; Charismatic 153.6; Pentecostal 164.5. So it lands, but only at 83% and only because the competitors are further off; the 32-point miss on Tradition (35 vs 67) is the single largest error and cannot be closed by any honest Lutheran answer set (reaching 35 requires S15 'Agree' or S14 'Unsure', both of which contradict FC Ep Rule and Norm). Fragility check, a plausible LCMS layperson wary of decretal wording and unsure on the gifts (S1 +1, S3 +1, S7 -1, S8 0, S9 -1, S13 +2): scores [50,0,67,8,58,8], Lutheran 43.1 vs Anglican 47.8, a 4.7 margin; with Spirit answered Unsure on all three ([50,0,50,8,67,8]) it flips: Anglican sqrt(2407) = 49.1 beats Lutheran sqrt(2742) = 52.4. Control: an informed Presbyterian (S1 +2, S2 -2, S3 +2, S4 +2, S5 -2, S6 +2, S7 -1, S8 +1, S9 -1, S10 -2, S11 +2, S12 -2, S13 +1, S14 +2, S15 -1, S16 +1, S17 -2, S18 0) scores [0,0,75,0,67,25] and lands on Lutheran (43.9) ahead of Presbyterian (49.3). Proposed fix: Lutheran coords [30,8,75,10,60,15] -> typical Lutheran d = sqrt(9+64+64+4+49+49) = sqrt(239) = 15.5 (94%), wary Lutheran 24.2 (90%); with Presbyterian also recalibrated to [10,10,80,10,60,25] the Presbyterian control returns home (19.3 vs Lutheran 34.8) and the typical Lutheran still lands Lutheran (15.5 vs Presbyterian 31.3), the separator being S2 (resistible grace) and S18 (weekly Supper), which is exactly the historical fault line.

findings.claim: "A person can genuinely resist God's grace and refuse salvation to the very end" is scored (+1) as a synergist statement, but confessional Lutherans affirm it for monergist reasons, so every Lutheran is pushed two notches toward "Synergist" for confessing that the lost are lost by their own resistance and not by a decree.
findings.evidence: FC SD II: before conversion the will is purely passive and can only resist (Acts 7:51 is the proof text); FC SD XI.41: those who are lost perish by their own wilful contempt of the Word, not because God did not will their salvation; FC SD XI rejects any decree of reprobation. A Lutheran therefore answers S1 +2, S2 +2, S3 +2, the most monergist honest set available, and receives Grace 33 = "Reformed-leaning". If S1 is softened to +1 the score is 42 = "balanced on grace". Neither describes a tradition whose founding text is The Bondage of the Will (which the quiz's own history cites).
findings.fix: Keep S2 (it is the only thing separating Wittenberg from Geneva in the instrument) but (a) reword the Grace fair summary so monergism is not defined by irresistibility, (b) drop the "Reformed-leaning" band name, and (c) move the Lutheran grace coordinate to 30. If the axis is meant to be a pure monergism test instead, replace S2 with: "Coming to faith requires a person's own free cooperation with God's grace." (Lutheran and Reformed -2; Arminian, Catholic, Orthodox +1/+2) and put Lutheran grace at 12.

findings.claim: "his saving grace cannot finally be refused" defines the Monergist pole as Calvinism and thereby excludes the oldest Protestant monergists from their own pole.
findings.evidence: FC SD II.7, 44, 71-73: conversion is solely the Holy Spirit's work and man contributes nothing, not even non-resistance; yet FC SD II and XI (Matt 23:37, Acts 7:51, Heb 6:4-6) confess that grace can be resisted and that believers can fall away (FC SD XI.42). Lutherans coined "monergism" and "synergism" (the Synergistic Controversy, FC II) precisely as terms about the cause of conversion, not about irresistibility.
findings.fix: Monergists hold that salvation is God's work from beginning to end: he chooses, calls, and keeps his people, and the person contributes nothing to conversion, not even a decision to cooperate. Monergists differ on whether that grace can be resisted: the Reformed say no; Lutherans say yes, so that anyone lost is lost by his own refusal and not by a decree. Synergists hold that God's grace always comes first and makes faith possible, but that each person must freely respond and can decline, so that election follows God's foreknowledge of faith or rests on his choice of a people in Christ.

findings.claim: The 21-40 band is named "Reformed-leaning" and the 60-79 band "Arminian-leaning"; a confessional Lutheran lands at 33 and is told he is Reformed-leaning. No other axis names a rival tradition in a band label.
findings.evidence: Simulation: Grace raw -2 -> 33 -> bands[1] = "Reformed-leaning". FC SD XI explicitly rejects the Reformed decree of reprobation and FC SD VII the Reformed view of the Supper; "Reformed" is the tradition Lutherans have defined themselves against since Marburg (1529). An Eastern Orthodox at 65 is likewise told he is "Arminian-leaning", a 17th-century Dutch label for a 1st-millennium church.
findings.fix: ["firmly monergist", "mostly monergist", "mixed on grace", "mostly synergist", "firmly synergist"]

findings.claim: Coordinates [20, 15, 70, 15, 35, 20] do not match what an informed confessional Lutheran scores on these eighteen statements; Tradition 35 in particular places Lutherans left of center ("tradition-friendly"), which contradicts the Formula of Concord and cannot be reached by any honest Lutheran answer set.
findings.evidence: Honest simulation scores [33, 0, 83, 8, 67, 8]; distance to the current coords = sqrt(13^2+15^2+13^2+7^2+32^2+12^2) = 42.2, only 83%. Tradition: FC Ep Rule and Norm 1-8 ("Holy Scripture alone remains the only judge, rule, and norm... other writings are not judges but witnesses") and AC XXVIII.34-35 (traditions cannot bind conscience) give S14 +2 and S15 -1, so the floor is 58 even with S13 +2. Table 15 vs Rome's 5 is a distinction the three Table statements cannot measure (all five paedobaptist traditions score 0). A lay Lutheran wary of decretal wording and unsure on the gifts ([50,0,50,8,67,8]) is placed Anglican: sqrt(2407) = 49.1 vs Lutheran sqrt(2742) = 52.4.
findings.fix: {"grace": 30, "table": 8, "spirit": 75, "kingdom": 10, "tradition": 60, "worship": 15}. Check: typical Lutheran d = sqrt(3^2+8^2+8^2+2^2+7^2+7^2) = sqrt(239) = 15.5 (94%); wary variant d = 24.2 (90%); the Anglican flip case becomes Lutheran 35.0 vs Anglican 49.1.

findings.claim: An informed Presbyterian lands on "Lutheran (confessional)" rather than on his own tradition, so the Lutheran label is being handed to Calvinists, which a Lutheran will find as objectionable as the reverse.
findings.evidence: Presbyterian control answers (S1 +2, S2 -2, S3 +2, S4 +2, S5 -2, S6 +2, S7 -1, S8 +1, S9 -1, S10 -2, S11 +2, S12 -2, S13 +1, S14 +2, S15 -1, S16 +1, S17 -2, S18 0) score [0, 0, 75, 0, 67, 25]; distance to Lutheran [20,15,70,15,35,20] = sqrt(400+225+25+225+1024+25) = 43.9, to Presbyterian [10,35,75,15,45,45] = sqrt(100+1225+0+225+484+400) = 49.3. The Presbyterian Table 35, Tradition 45 and Worship 45 are each 20-35 points from what WCF-confessing paedobaptists actually score.
findings.fix: {"grace": 10, "table": 10, "spirit": 80, "kingdom": 10, "tradition": 60, "worship": 25}. Check: Presbyterian control d = sqrt(100+100+25+100+49+0) = 19.3 vs proposed Lutheran 34.8; typical Lutheran stays Lutheran (15.5 vs 31.3). More generally, set every tradition's coordinates by running an informed member through the eighteen statements rather than by hand.

findings.claim: The Table coordinates spread Roman Catholic 5, Eastern Orthodox 5, Lutheran 15, Anglican 25, Presbyterian 35, but the three Table statements are answered identically (+2, -2, +2 -> 0) by informed members of all five, so the spread is noise that penalizes the Lutheran match by 15 points for a difference (transubstantiation vs sacramental union vs spiritual presence) the instrument never asks about. The same is true of Kingdom (RC 15, EO 15, Lutheran 15, Anglican 20, Presbyterian 15 vs an honest 0-8 for all).
findings.evidence: S4 "truly present in a way that goes beyond a symbol" is affirmed by Calvin (Inst. IV.17) as readily as by AC X and Trent; S5 and S6 are both baptism questions all five answer the same way. Nothing in the axis separates FC SD VII.54-60 (oral reception by all communicants, 1 Cor 10:16) from Reformed reception by faith alone.
findings.fix: Either set all five paedobaptist, real-presence traditions to Table 5-10 and Kingdom 5-10, or add the statement that actually divides them: "In the Supper, Christ's body and blood are received with the mouth by every communicant, believing or not." (Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox +2; Reformed -2; memorialist -2).

findings.claim: "The church, not the individual reader, is the final interpreter of Scripture" is a false dichotomy written in Roman Catholic apologetic vocabulary ("private judgment"); the Lutheran answer is that Scripture is its own interpreter and neither the magisterium nor the private reader is "final".
findings.evidence: FC Ep Rule and Norm 1: Scripture is "the only judge, rule, and norm"; Luther, Bondage of the Will, on the claritas Scripturae; Scriptura sui ipsius interpres is the standard Lutheran formula. A Lutheran who disagrees is not thereby asserting individualism, yet that is what the statement makes him affirm; a Lutheran who is bound to the Book of Concord by subscription may even hesitate toward Unsure, pulling the score the wrong way.
findings.fix: When Christians disagree about what a passage means, the church's teaching office has the final say. (direction -1)

findings.claim: "The creeds and councils of the early church carry real authority" bundles two things Lutherans answer differently: the three ecumenical creeds are confessed in the Book of Concord as binding (derived) norms, but councils can err and cannot make new articles of faith, so the informed Lutheran softens to Agree rather than Strongly agree.
findings.evidence: The Apostles', Nicene and Athanasian Creeds open the Book of Concord (1580); FC Ep Rule and Norm 2-3 receives them "as witnesses"; Luther, On the Councils and the Church (1539), denies councils the power to establish new articles; Second Nicaea on images is not received.
findings.fix: The ancient creeds (Apostles', Nicene, Athanasian) carry real authority for the church today, not just historical interest.

findings.claim: Neither pole describes the confessional position held by three of the twelve listed traditions (Lutheran, Presbyterian, confessional Anglican): Scripture is the only infallible norm (norma normans) while creeds and confessions carry real, derived, binding authority (norma normata). The right pole reduces tradition to "a valuable guide", which understates quia subscription; the left pole gives the creeds "real authority" only as part of a teaching office.
findings.evidence: FC Ep Rule and Norm 7-8: other writings "are not judges like Holy Scripture, but only witnesses and explanations of the faith"; LCMS and WELS pastors subscribe to the Book of Concord unconditionally because (quia), not insofar as (quatenus), it agrees with Scripture, so on the ground the confessions bind teachers. The current wording forces such a person to split S13 against S14, landing in "balanced on authority" or "Scripture-first", neither of which is what he would call himself.
findings.fix: Those who hold to Scripture alone agree that creeds and confessions can carry real, derived authority, binding on teachers because and insofar as they agree with Scripture, but insist that only Scripture is infallible and that no council or teacher can bind the conscience where Scripture is silent or says otherwise.

findings.claim: The Protestant slot in the Tradition history is given to Westminster (1646) alone; the two Lutheran sola Scriptura moments, Worms (1521) and the Formula of Concord's Rule and Norm (1577), which coined the judge/witness distinction the whole axis turns on, are absent.
findings.evidence: Luther at Worms, 1521: "unless I am convinced by Scripture and plain reason... popes and councils have often erred"; FC Ep Rule and Norm 1-8 (1577) predates WCF ch. 1 by seventy years and is its direct model for "Scripture alone is judge".
findings.fix: Insert before the Westminster entry: {"when": "1577", "what": "Formula of Concord, Rule and Norm: Scripture alone is judge; creeds and confessions are witnesses to be judged by it, not judges themselves."} (optionally also {"when": "1521", "what": "Luther at Worms: conscience bound by Scripture, since popes and councils have erred."})

findings.claim: The Table history states transubstantiation (1215) and Calvin's spiritual presence (1559) but never states the Lutheran doctrine of the Supper, the view of the tradition placed at 15 on the axis; the Marburg line says Luther and Zwingli "part over the Supper" without saying what Luther held.
findings.evidence: AC X (1530): "the body and blood of Christ are truly present and are distributed to those who eat"; FC SD VII (1577): sacramental union "in, with, and under" the bread and wine, oral reception by all communicants, explicitly without transubstantiation (SD VII.35-38).
findings.fix: Either amend the 1529 line to "Marburg Colloquy: Luther and Zwingli agree on fourteen articles and part over whether Christ's body is bodily present in the bread ('This is my body')", or add {"when": "1530", "what": "Augsburg Confession X: Christ's body and blood are truly present under the bread and wine and given to all who eat, with no theory of transubstantiation."}

findings.claim: John 6:53-58 heads the list as a sacramental proof text, but Lutherans do not read John 6 as about the Supper, and 1 Corinthians 10:16, the passage the Formula of Concord makes decisive for the real presence, is missing; the baptism texts Lutherans actually cite (1 Peter 3:21, Titus 3:5) are missing while Colossians 2:11-12 (the Reformed circumcision argument) is present.
findings.evidence: FC SD VII.61-62: the eating of John 6 "is nothing else than faith", a spiritual eating distinct from the sacrament; FC SD VII.54-59 builds the real presence on 1 Cor 10:16; SC IV cites Titus 3:5, 1 Pet 3:21, Mark 16:16 for what baptism gives.
findings.fix: ["1 Corinthians 10:16", "1 Corinthians 11:23-29", "Matthew 26:26-28", "John 6:53-58", "Acts 2:38-39", "1 Peter 3:21", "Titus 3:5", "Romans 6:3-4"] (drop Colossians 2:11-12 if a slot must go).

findings.claim: "and so the children of believers are baptized" grounds infant baptism in the parents' faith, which is the Reformed covenant rationale; Lutherans, Catholics and Orthodox, three of the four paedobaptist traditions at this pole, baptize infants because baptism itself regenerates and infants need it.
findings.evidence: SC IV.2: baptism "works forgiveness of sins, rescues from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation"; LC IV.47-63 on infant faith; John 3:5, Titus 3:5. Statement 6's "infants of believing parents" has the same covenantal tilt, though a Lutheran still answers +2.
findings.fix: ...baptism joins a person to Christ and his church and gives forgiveness and new birth, and so infants too are baptized.

findings.claim: The sacramental reading list is Orthodox (Schmemann) plus Reformed (Mathison); no Lutheran, although the history's hinge event (Marburg) is Luther's.
findings.evidence: Standard Lutheran references: Sasse, This Is My Body (1959); Luther, Large Catechism V; Chemnitz, The Lord's Supper.
findings.fix: left: ["Schmemann, For the Life of the World", "Sasse, This Is My Body"]

findings.claim: The Monergist reading list is Calvin and Sproul only; the book the quiz's own history names as the Reformation's monergist manifesto (1525, The Bondage of the Will) is not listed, which reinforces the equation monergist = Calvinist.
findings.evidence: Grace history entry index 2 cites Luther's Bondage of the Will; read_more.left omits it.
findings.fix: left: ["Luther, The Bondage of the Will", "Calvin, Institutes III"] (or add "Formula of Concord, Article XI" as a third).

findings.claim: The history runs Augustine, Orange, Luther, Dort, Wesley, so Luther reads as a prelude to Dort; the Formula of Concord (1577), which fixed the Lutheran third position (conversion God's work alone, grace resistible, no decree of reprobation, election known only in Christ through the gospel), is missing.
findings.evidence: FC SD II (free will) and XI (election), esp. SD XI.28 (Christ died for all), 41 (the lost resist), 65-66 (election in Christ), and the rejection of a decree to damnation; this is the position of the tradition listed at Grace 20.
findings.fix: Insert before the Dort entry: {"when": "1577", "what": "Formula of Concord (arts. II, XI): conversion is God's work alone, yet grace can be resisted and there is no decree of reprobation; election is known only in Christ through the gospel."}

findings.claim: The texts Lutherans reach for on both halves of their position, Ephesians 2:8-9 (faith a gift) and Matthew 23:37 / Acts 7:51 (grace resisted), are absent.
findings.evidence: SC, Third Article explanation ("I cannot by my own reason or strength believe"); FC SD II cites Acts 7:51 and Matt 23:37 for resistance; Eph 2:8-9 is the standard sola gratia text in Ap IV.
findings.fix: Add "Ephesians 2:8-9" and "Matthew 23:37" (drop 2 Peter 3:9 or Hebrews 6:4-6 if the list must stay at six).

findings.claim: "God has already chosen who will be saved" can be read as a symmetrical decree over the saved and the lost; a Lutheran affirms election unto salvation strongly but confesses no decree of reprobation, so some informed Lutherans will soften to Agree, dropping Grace from 33 to 42 ("balanced on grace").
findings.evidence: FC SD XI.5 (election "a cause which procures, works, helps and promotes our salvation") supports Strongly agree; FC SD XI's rejection of predestination to damnation is what makes the wording pause-worthy.
findings.fix: Before the world began God chose his people in Christ, and none of them will finally be lost.

findings.claim: "Covenantal" is Reformed federal-theology vocabulary (covenant of works / covenant of grace); Lutherans, Catholics and Orthodox, three of the five traditions placed at 15-20 on this axis, do not hold covenant theology. A confessional Lutheran's headline reads "Sacramental, covenantal, liturgical", another tradition's name in his own label.
findings.evidence: Lutheran dogmatics organizes Scripture by Law and Gospel, not by covenants (FC V; Walther, Law and Gospel); the Lutheran stake in this axis is amillennialism, AC XVII.5 rejecting the opinion "that before the resurrection of the dead the godly shall take possession of the kingdom of the world". The three statements actually test one people of God, promises fulfilled in Christ, and no pretribulation rapture, none of which requires covenant theology.
findings.fix: Minimal: keep the pole name but define it in the summary as "one covenant people of God across both testaments (a view Lutherans, Catholics and Orthodox hold without the Reformed covenant-of-works framework)". Better: rename the left pole "One people of God" with bands ["one people of God", "leaning to one people of God", "centered on the kingdom", "dispensational-leaning", "dispensational"].

findings.claim: "1646 Westminster Confession sets out the covenant of works and the covenant of grace" defines the left pole by a system four of its five occupying traditions reject, while the Lutheran amillennial anchor, Augsburg XVII (1530), is absent.
findings.evidence: AC XVII (1530) condemns chiliasm 116 years before Westminster; Rome (Trent) and the Orthodox have no covenant-of-works doctrine either.
findings.fix: Replace with or add before it: {"when": "1530", "what": "Augsburg Confession XVII rejects a reign of the saints on earth before the resurrection: the kingdom is present now and consummated at Christ's return."}

findings.claim: The cessationist pole is described only with Warfield's rationale ("authenticated the apostles... New Testament was complete"); Lutheran caution about the gifts rests on a different ground, that the Spirit binds himself to Word and sacrament so that no new revelation is to be expected, and Lutherans do not deny that God still heals in answer to prayer.
findings.evidence: SA III.viii.3-13: "God gives no one his Spirit or grace except through or with the external Word"; whatever is claimed of the Spirit apart from Word and sacrament "is of the devil". LCMS CTCR, The Lutheran Church and the Charismatic Movement (1977): the extraordinary gifts are not to be expected as normative, while refusing to say God cannot work miracles. A Lutheran scoring 75-83 is thus described in words he would not use.
findings.fix: Cessationists hold that the sign gifts authenticated the apostles and their message and passed away once that foundation was laid, or that the Spirit has bound himself to Word and sacrament so that no new revelation is to be expected; God may still heal in answer to prayer, but the gifts of Acts are not the church's ordinary pattern.

findings.claim: The history makes caution about the gifts a 1918 Reformed innovation (Warfield) restated in 2013; the Lutheran rejection of the Spirit apart from the external Word, against the Zwickau prophets and Muntzer, dates to the 1520s and was confessed in 1537.
findings.evidence: Smalcald Articles III.viii (1537), "Of Confession", against "enthusiasm" (Schwarmerei); Luther, Against the Heavenly Prophets (1525).
findings.fix: Insert before the Warfield entry: {"when": "1537", "what": "Smalcald Articles III.viii: against 'enthusiasm', Luther holds that the Spirit comes only through the external Word and sacraments, not by new revelation."}

findings.claim: "Communion should be celebrated every week as the center of the service" is double-barreled: Lutherans confess every-Sunday celebration but hold that the Divine Service has two centers, Word and Sacrament, so many informed Lutherans will drop to Agree or Unsure.
findings.evidence: AC XXIV.34 and Ap XXIV.1: Mass "celebrated every Sunday and on other festivals"; but AC V and VII make preaching and sacraments jointly the marks of the church, and much LCMS practice is still twice-monthly.
findings.fix: Communion should be celebrated every Sunday.

findings.claim: "the participation of the whole congregation" is listed as a distinctive of free worship, implying liturgical worship is not participatory; congregational hymnody and the sung ordinary are Lutheran inventions. The liturgical rationale "prays with the historic church" is the Anglican/Webber reason, not the Lutheran one (in the Divine Service God serves the congregation with Word and Sacrament).
findings.evidence: Luther, Deutsche Messe (1526), replaced choir propers with congregational chorales; LC and AC XXIV.2-3 on singing in the vernacular "for the instruction of the people". The Free summary also lumps regulative-principle Presbyterians (who reject "led in the moment") with Pentecostals, which is unfair to that side too.
findings.fix: Free worship keeps the form open, whether so that the Spirit can lead in the moment or so that each service can take its own shape, with an emphasis on spontaneity and sincerity.

findings.claim: The history jumps from Justin Martyr (155) to Cranmer (1549), skipping the first Protestant liturgies, Luther's Formula Missae (1523) and Deutsche Messe (1526), which kept the historic order of the Mass in the vernacular and added congregational hymns, the pattern the tradition at Worship 20 still follows.
findings.evidence: Luther, Formula Missae (1523), Deutsche Messe (1526); AC XXIV.1: "we keep the Mass"; the Lutheran Divine Service (LSB, CW) is a direct descendant.
findings.fix: Insert before the Cranmer entry: {"when": "1526", "what": "Luther's German Mass keeps the historic order of the Mass in the vernacular and adds congregational hymns."}

findings.claim: As a system the band adjectives are inconsistent and several are loaded: two name rival traditions ("Reformed-leaning", "Arminian-leaning"), "balanced on grace" and "balanced on authority" imply the poles are unbalanced, "centered on the sacraments" for the Table midpoint reads as more sacramental than "sacramental-leaning", and "undecided on the gifts" mislabels the deliberate open-but-cautious position (LCMS CTCR 1977, many Anglicans) as indecision.
findings.evidence: Compare the six band arrays: only Grace uses tradition names; the Kingdom and Table midpoints ("centered on the kingdom", "centered on the sacraments") describe an emphasis, not a midpoint.
findings.fix: Grace: ["firmly monergist", "mostly monergist", "mixed on grace", "mostly synergist", "firmly synergist"]; Table midpoint: "between sacrament and symbol"; Spirit midpoint: "open but cautious on the gifts"; Tradition midpoint: "mixed on authority"; Kingdom midpoint: "between the two on Israel and the church".

findings.claim: A confessional Lutheran can take the whole quiz and never once see his own confession described: on Grace, Kingdom and Tradition the Lutheran position is a documented third way (FC XI; AC XVII; FC Rule and Norm) and the poles, summaries, histories and reading lists are written in Reformed, Catholic or evangelical vocabulary; no Lutheran author appears in any of the twelve read-more lists and no Book of Concord text in any of the thirty-three history lines, though "Lutheran (confessional)" is a listed tradition.
findings.evidence: Only two history entries mention Luther (1525 Bondage of the Will, 1529 Marburg) and neither states what he held; the Lutheran coordinates are hand-set in a way no honest Lutheran answer set reaches (Tradition 35).
findings.fix: Apply the summary clauses and three history insertions proposed above (FC 1577 on Grace, AC XVII 1530 on Kingdom, FC Rule and Norm 1577 on Tradition), add Luther's Bondage of the Will and Sasse to the reading lists, and recalibrate the Lutheran and Presbyterian coordinates by simulation.

findings.claim: The Catholic apologist and the Orthodox convert get the same screenshot from opposite sides: a Catholic who answers exactly as Trent and the Catechism require lands on 'Closest traditions: Eastern Orthodox, Roman Catholic', and an Orthodox convert's card says 'Roman Catholic 85%'. Caption: 'lol, this quiz was written by a Baptist — it cannot tell Rome from Constantinople.' The six axes are the intra-evangelical arguments (Calvinism, baptism, gifts, rapture, sola scriptura, worship style); nothing on the compass measures the papacy, the filioque, or justification, so the two largest Christian bodies are coordinates 13 units apart in a 245-unit space.
findings.evidence: Roman Catholic [55,5,40,15,10,10] vs Eastern Orthodox [65,5,35,15,5,5]: distance 13.2, the smallest gap between any two traditions. A Catholic answer set (Strongly agree on resistible grace per Trent VI canon 4, real presence, infant baptism, creeds, church as final interpreter, liturgy, weekly Eucharist) scores [83,0,25,17,0,0]: Orthodox 22.4 (91%), Catholic 35.2 (86%). An Anglo-Catholic answer set [67,0,33,17,17,0] lands Orthodox 94%, Catholic 92%, Anglican 81%.
findings.fix: Either add a seventh axis 'Church' (statements: 'The bishop of Rome holds a Christ-given authority over the whole church'; 'The church is governed by bishops in succession from the apostles'; 'A local congregation is complete in itself and answers to no higher church body') which also separates episcopal, presbyterian, and congregational Protestants; or, as a minimum, when the two nearest traditions are within 15 units of each other, render them as one tied line: 'Roman Catholic / Eastern Orthodox — tied: what divides them (the papacy, the filioque) is not on this compass.'

findings.claim: The Grace bands name parties, not positions: 'Reformed-leaning' and 'Arminian-leaning' on an axis whose poles are Monergist/Synergist. The Orthodox convert screenshots 'Arminian-leaning' with 'lol, this quiz thinks St John Cassian was a Dutch Remonstrant'; the confessional Lutheran screenshots 'Reformed-leaning' with 'written by a Presbyterian'. The quiz's own map already does this to them.
findings.evidence: The Eastern Orthodox coordinate grace=65 sits in band 3, i.e. the quiz labels the Orthodox Church 'Arminian-leaning'. A Lutheran answering per Formula of Concord SD XI (election cannot fail: Strongly agree on 1 and 3; grace resistible: Strongly agree on 2) scores 33, band 1 'Reformed-leaning'; the Formula of Concord explicitly rejects the Reformed doctrine of predestination. A Catholic Molinist who is Unsure on 1 scores 67, 'Arminian-leaning'.
findings.fix: bands: ['firmly monergist', 'monergist-leaning', 'balanced on grace', 'synergist-leaning', 'firmly synergist']. Keep 'firmly' — it is symmetric and nobody minds it.

findings.claim: The middle band is 'centered on the sacraments' — on the sacramental-vs-memorial axis, the midpoint is labeled with the left pole's word and reads as a theological position (sacrament-centered). A Baptist at 50 gets a headline like 'Cessationist, centered on the sacraments, dispensational-leaning' and screenshots it: 'lol, I said ordinances and the quiz made me sacrament-centered.'
findings.evidence: Score 50 on Table (e.g. Agree on 4, Agree on 5, Unsure on 6) yields bands[2] = 'centered on the sacraments'; headline() concatenates it verbatim. The memorial pole's own summary says 'ordinances ... rather than channels of grace', so the word 'sacraments' is contested on this very axis.
findings.fix: bands: ['sacramental', 'sacramental-leaning', 'between sacramental and memorial', 'memorial-leaning', 'memorialist']

findings.claim: Two problems. 'centered on the kingdom' for the midpoint reads as a position (kingdom-centered, i.e. Ladd's 'already/not yet', which is the left pole). And 'covenantal' is stamped on every non-dispensationalist: the Catholic apologist gets 'Sacramental, liturgical, covenantal' and screenshots 'lol, written by a Presbyterian — I'm apparently a Westminster federalist'; the Lutheran and the Mennonite get the same word and both reject covenant theology by name.
findings.evidence: Quiz coordinates: Roman Catholic kingdom=15 and Lutheran (confessional) kingdom=15 are band 0 'covenantal'; Anabaptist / Mennonite kingdom=30 is 'covenantal-leaning' — the Anabaptists split from Zwingli precisely over his covenant argument for infant baptism. My Lutheran and Anglo-Catholic answer sets both produced headlines ending in 'covenantal'. The fair summary already has the neutral phrase: 'one people of God'.
findings.fix: bands: ['one people of God', 'leaning to one people of God', 'between covenantal and dispensational', 'dispensational-leaning', 'dispensational']. Pole names can stay ('covenant theology' is the antonym dispensationalists themselves use) once the bands stop branding Catholics and Lutherans.

findings.claim: The share bar is a fill gauge under the axis name, so it reads as a score of the virtue named. The Orthodox convert's text says '📜 Tradition · With tradition ○○○○○○○○○○ Scripture alone' (zero Tradition); the Pentecostal pastor's says '🔥 Spirit ○○○○○○○○○○'; the Reformed blogger's says '⚖️ Grace ●●○○○○○○○○'. Caption writes itself: 'The Calvinist scored 2/10 on Grace and the Pentecostal 0/10 on Spirit.' The page's own caption admits it: 'a monergist shows few filled circles on Grace'.
findings.evidence: shareText(): f = round(score/10) filled circles from the left, so the left-pole holder on every axis gets an empty bar, and on Grace, Table, Spirit, Tradition, and Worship the left pole is the group most likely to read the axis name as their own virtue. The emoji compound it: 🎵 for Worship (worship = music, the exact thing liturgical and Reformed readers mock), ⚖️ scales for Grace, 🍞 a loaf for the Eucharist.
findings.fix: Replace the gauge with a position marker: 'Monergist ━━●━━━━━━━ Synergist' (one ● at the score position, box-drawing dashes elsewhere). Rewrite the caption: 'The dot marks where you sit between the two poles.' Replace the emoji with the six axis-colour squares already on the card (🟦 🟥 🟧 🟩 🟨 🟪) or drop them.

findings.claim: A PCA elder answering straight from the Westminster Standards gets 'Closest traditions: Lutheran (confessional), Presbyterian / Reformed', both at 87%, Lutheran listed first. Screenshot: 'lol, the quiz says Westminster is Wittenberg.' The cause is table=35, which puts the Reformed a third of the way to memorialism.
findings.evidence: Answers: 1 SA, 2 SD, 3 SA; 4 A, 5 D, 6 SA; 7 D, 8 A, 9 D; 10 D, 11 A, 12 SD; 13 A, 14 A, 15 D; 16 A, 17 SD, 18 U → scores [0,17,75,17,58,25]. Distance to Lutheran (confessional) 31.4, to Presbyterian / Reformed 31.6. WCF 27.3 (grace 'conferred' by the sacraments), 28.6 (efficacy of baptism), 29.7 (Christ 'really, but spiritually, present') put Presbyterians near the sacramental end, not at 35.
findings.fix: Presbyterian / Reformed: table 35 → 20, worship 45 → 35. With those values the same answer set is 19.5 from Presbyterian and 31.4 from Lutheran; the Lutheran answer set still lands Lutheran (37.6 vs 54.5).

findings.claim: There is no home for the Reformed charismatic (Sovereign Grace, Newfrontiers, Piper/Grudem/Storms readers) — the very people whose books the quiz lists under Spirit and Worship. The Pentecostal pastor screenshots the reading list beside the tradition list: 'The quiz's favourite authors don't exist on its own map.'
findings.evidence: Answer set 1 SA, 2 SD, 3 SA; 4 U, 5 SA, 6 SD; 7 SA, 8 SD, 9 SA; 10 D, 11 A, 12 D; 13 A, 14 A, 15 D; 16 D, 17 A, 18 U → [0,83,0,25,58,67]. Nearest: Reformed Baptist 81.9 (67%), Charismatic non-denominational 86.1 (65%). No other realistic answer set in my runs failed to reach 85%.
findings.fix: Add { name: 'Reformed charismatic', position: {grace:10, table:75, spirit:10, kingdom:30, tradition:55, worship:70} } — the answer set above lands 17.5 away (93%) and Pentecostal / Assemblies of God and Charismatic non-denominational stay far (>75).

findings.claim: The continuationist reading list contains zero Pentecostals (Grudem and Storms are both Reformed charismatics) while the cessationist list leads with Strange Fire, the one book that calls Pentecostal worship blasphemous. The Pentecostal pastor screenshots both lines: 'lol, my side is represented by two Calvinists and the other side by the book that says I offend the Holy Spirit.' The Reformed blogger enjoys it, which is the problem.
findings.evidence: Grudem (formerly Vineyard, Reformed) and Storms (Bridgeway, Reformed) vs MacArthur, Strange Fire (subtitle: 'The Danger of Offending the Holy Spirit with Counterfeit Worship'). Every other axis pairs a primary source with a measured modern defence; this is the only axis whose modern pick on one side is a polemic.
findings.fix: left: ['Fee, Paul, the Spirit, and the People of God', 'Grudem, The Gift of Prophecy']  (Fee is an Assemblies of God minister); right: ['Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles', 'Gaffin, Perspectives on Pentecost'] (or Schreiner, Spiritual Gifts). Drop Strange Fire from the list; it stays in the timeline.

findings.claim: Continuationism's ancestry on the timeline is Montanist heretics, then Chrysostom saying the gifts ceased, then nothing for 1,500 years until Azusa Street. The Pentecostal pastor screenshots the whole list: 'lol, written by a cessationist — my family tree is Montanus and a gap.' The cessationist side gets Chrysostom, Warfield, and Strange Fire.
findings.evidence: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.32.4 and 5.6.1 (c. 180): brethren in the church prophesy, heal, speak in tongues, and 'the dead even have been raised'. Augustine, City of God 22.8 (c. 426) records healings at Hippo and Retractationes 1.13.7 withdraws his earlier claim that miracles had ceased — the standard continuationist patristic citations, both absent.
findings.fix: Prepend ['c. 180', 'Irenaeus, Against Heresies: brethren in the church still prophesy, heal, and speak in tongues.'], keep the Montanist entry second, and insert after Chrysostom ['c. 426', 'Augustine, City of God XXII.8, withdraws his earlier view that miracles had ceased and records healings at Hippo.']

findings.claim: 'Chrysostom ... notes that the sign gifts had ceased' — 'notes' reports his claim as an observed fact. Pentecostal caption: 'the quiz notes it too.'
findings.evidence: Homily 29 on 1 Corinthians (c. 392): the passage is obscure 'by their cessation, being such as then used to occur but now no longer take place' — his assertion about his own day.
findings.fix: 'Chrysostom, preaching on 1 Corinthians, says the gifts of that chapter had ceased in his day.'

findings.claim: 'Charismatic renewal carries the gifts into mainline and Catholic churches' implies the gifts were absent from the Catholic Church for nineteen centuries. The Catholic apologist screenshots it beside Padre Pio and the miracle requirement for canonization.
findings.evidence: Catholic canonization has required attested miracles since Urban VIII (1625–34); Lourdes cures are formally investigated. The 1967 Duquesne weekend brought Pentecostal-style tongues and prophecy, not 'the gifts' as such.
findings.fix: 'Charismatic renewal brings Pentecostal-style tongues and prophecy into mainline Protestant and Catholic congregations.'

findings.claim: 'informal in worship' for band 3. The Pentecostal pastor screenshots his headline 'Continuationist, memorialist, informal in worship': 'lol, informal — written by someone in a cassock.' 'Informal' is what liturgical people call free worship; free-worship people call it Spirit-led or free.
findings.evidence: The pole name is 'Free' and the fair summary uses 'free worship'; the band system elsewhere uses the pole word with '-leaning'. 'Informal' is the only band on any axis that describes a position with an outsider's word.
findings.fix: bands: ['liturgical', 'liturgy-leaning', 'between liturgical and free', 'leaning to free worship', 'free in worship']

findings.claim: The six midpoint bands use four different words for the same thing — 'balanced on grace', 'centered on the sacraments', 'undecided on the gifts', 'centered on the kingdom', 'balanced on authority', 'flexible in worship' — and only one of them is a put-down. 'Undecided on the gifts' is screenshotted by the Baptist who holds the 'open but cautious' view as a settled position: 'lol, I've had this view for twenty years and the quiz calls it undecided.'
findings.evidence: 'Open but cautious' is the named middle view (Saucy) in Grudem, ed., Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views (1996); it is a position, not an absence of one. The band 3 label 'cautious about the gifts' borrows half of that name for the cessationist lean, which muddles it further.
findings.fix: spirit bands: ['continuationist', 'continuationist-leaning', 'open but cautious on the gifts', 'cessationist-leaning', 'cessationist']. Across axes, use one pattern for the midpoint: 'balanced on grace', 'between sacramental and memorial', 'open but cautious on the gifts', 'between covenantal and dispensational', 'balanced on authority', 'between liturgical and free'.

findings.claim: 'A theological centrist' is the Reformed blogger's easiest screenshot: 'Centrist = answered Unsure eighteen times. Rev 3:16.' It has a political ring and presents the middle as a party, which is exactly what discernment readers accuse the middle of.
findings.evidence: headline(): all six within 10 of 50 → only scores 42/50/58 are possible there, i.e. raw −1..+1 on every axis, which an all-Unsure answer set produces; that answer set then shows 'Wesleyan / Methodist 83%' (see scoring).
findings.fix: 'Near the center on every axis' as the headline, with the sub-line 'Your answers sit close to the midpoint on all six axes, so read the nearest traditions loosely.'

findings.claim: Match percentages are inflated, ties are hidden, and the note describing the formula is wrong. An all-Unsure answer set gets 'Wesleyan / Methodist 83%' — screenshot: 'Know nothing about theology? Congratulations, you're a Methodist.' My Catholic answer set shows Orthodox 91%, Catholic 86%; my PCA set shows two traditions at 87% with the wrong one first.
findings.evidence: match = 100 − d/245·100, where 245 is corner-to-corner; the all-Unsure vector [50]*6 is 42.1 from Wesleyan/Methodist → 83%. PCA set: 31.4 vs 31.6, both round to 87%, order decided by 0.2 units — less than one answer step on one axis (8.3). The permalink encoder rounds scores to multiples of 4, so a reopened link can reorder such near-ties. The on-page note 'Match is 100 minus your distance across all six axes' omits the scaling.
findings.fix: match = max(0, round(100 − d/140·100)) (all-Unsure → 70%, Catholic set → 84%/75%). If d2 − d1 < 8, show the pair as 'tied'. Note: 'Match is 100 minus your distance from that tradition's position, scaled so that a wholly different set of answers scores near 0.'

findings.claim: 'With tradition' vs 'Scripture alone' and the band 'Scripture-first' hand the Catholic apologist his line: 'So my side is Scripture-last? Dei Verbum 21 says we venerate the Scriptures as we venerate the Lord's Body.' The right pole gets its own slogan; the left pole gets a description with 'Scripture' removed from it.
findings.evidence: Dei Verbum 9–10: 'Sacred Tradition and Sacred Scripture' together; the Catholic name for the position is 'Scripture and Tradition', the Orthodox 'Scripture within Tradition' (Florovsky, whose book the quiz itself lists). 'Scripture-first' as a band implies an ordering the other side denies rather than a difference the other side would state.
findings.fix: left_pole: 'Scripture and Tradition'; right_pole: 'Scripture alone'. bands: ['Scripture within tradition', 'tradition-leaning', 'balanced on authority', 'Scripture over tradition', 'Scripture alone']. Rename the axis 'Authority' (the band already says 'balanced on authority'); an axis named 'Tradition' is named after one pole.

findings.claim: 'The church, not the individual reader, is the final interpreter of Scripture' makes the only alternative to Rome 'the individual reader'. The Reformed blogger screenshots it: 'lol, written by a Catholic — the options are the Magisterium or me alone in my bedroom.'
findings.evidence: WCF 1.10: the supreme judge is 'the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture', not the reader; WCF 31.3: councils 'may err ... to be used as a help'. Protestants deny the statement without affirming individualism, and the wording denies them that.
findings.fix: 'When the church has defined a doctrine, that definition settles the meaning of Scripture for every believer.' Catholics (CCC 85, 100) and Orthodox (the ecumenical councils) agree; confessional Protestants disagree on the record without being cast as lone readers.

findings.claim: Two of the three Table statements are about baptism, so a Reformed Baptist who holds Calvin's spiritual presence is pushed to 'memorial-leaning' or 'memorialist' for being credobaptist. Screenshot from a 1689 elder: 'I confess that we really and indeed, spiritually, receive and feed upon Christ, and the quiz calls me a memorialist.'
findings.evidence: 1689 LBCF 30.7 copies WCF 29.7 on the Supper. Answer set 4 Agree, 5 Strongly agree, 6 Strongly disagree → table 75, band 'memorial-leaning'; the quiz's own Reformed Baptist coordinate table=70 is in that band. Statement 5 measures baptismal candidacy, which statement 6 already measures.
findings.fix: Statement 5 (direction +1): 'Baptism and the Supper are signs of a grace already received, not means by which God gives it.' That measures the actual pole; a Reformed Baptist (Agree 4, Unsure 5, Strongly disagree 6) then lands 58, 'between sacramental and memorial', and a Zwinglian Baptist still lands 83, 'memorialist'.

findings.claim: Free worship is defined as 'spontaneity ... the Spirit can lead in the moment', which is Pentecostal worship only. The Reformed blogger, whose church has no liturgy and no spontaneity, screenshots it with the Puritan entry from the same timeline: 'The quiz's two options are the Prayer Book and Hillsong. The regulative principle is in its own history and nowhere on its axis.' The liturgical side also reads 'the Spirit can lead' as claiming the Spirit for one pole.
findings.evidence: A regulative-principle Presbyterian answers Disagree on 16 and Disagree on 17 and cancels to the midpoint; the history entry '1600s Puritans articulate the regulative principle' describes a position the axis cannot place. 'Free worship' in worship studies (e.g. James F. White, Protestant Worship) covers Reformed, Baptist, and Pentecostal non-liturgical worship alike.
findings.fix: 'Free worship keeps the form open — from the plain, Scripture-ordered service of Reformed and Baptist churches to the spontaneity of Pentecostal worship — so that the service is shaped by the congregation and its leaders rather than by a fixed text, with an emphasis on sincerity and the participation of everyone present.'

findings.claim: The Grace timeline is Augustine, Orange, and then Protestants arguing with each other (Luther, Dort, Wesley). The Catholic apologist screenshots it: 'lol, written by an evangelical — Trent Session VI, the biggest statement on grace since Orange, isn't on the list.' The Orthodox convert adds that his side has no patristic ancestor at all, so 'synergist' looks like a 17th-century Dutch invention.
findings.evidence: Council of Trent, Decree on Justification (1547), canon 4: the will, moved by God, 'can also refuse its assent if it wishes'; canons 15–16: no one may presume certainty of predestination. John Cassian, Conferences XIII (c. 426), is the classic Eastern statement of grace and free will cooperating, and Cassian is a saint in the East.
findings.fix: Insert after Augustine: ['c. 426', 'John Cassian, Conferences XIII: grace and free will work together — the Eastern "synergy" against both Pelagius and hard predestination.'] and after Luther: ['1547', 'Council of Trent, Decree on Justification: grace goes first and enables the will, which can still refuse it; no one may presume to know he is among the predestined.']

findings.claim: '1740s' is loose for the Wesley–Whitefield split.
findings.evidence: Wesley's sermon 'Free Grace' was preached and printed in 1739; Whitefield's public reply, 'A Letter to the Rev. Mr John Wesley', is dated December 1740 and published 1741.

findings.claim: '1646 Westminster Confession sets out the covenant of works and the covenant of grace' has nothing to do with Israel and the church, and it makes the left pole's founding document a Presbyterian confession — the Catholic's, Lutheran's, and Mennonite's eschatology apparently begins at Westminster. Meanwhile the dispensational side's history starts in 1830, which is the covenantalist's favourite jab ('your theology was invented by Darby').
findings.evidence: Justin Martyr, Dialogue 80–81 (c. 155) and Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.32–36 (c. 180) expect a literal thousand-year reign on earth; Papias is cited for the same by Eusebius. Dispensationalists (Ryrie, Dispensationalism, ch. 4) claim exactly these as the premillennial root; so does Ladd.
findings.fix: Replace the 1646 entry with ['c. 155–180', 'Justin Martyr and Irenaeus expect a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth — the early premillennialism both Ladd and the dispensationalists claim.'] and move it to the front of the list.

findings.claim: The 'with tradition' side of the timeline is Vincent, then three Roman entries (Trent, Newman, Vatican II) and no Orthodox one. The Orthodox convert screenshots Newman: 'lol, written by a Catholic — we reject Newman's development theory, and our Fathers aren't on the list.' The Protestant side is also missing its own founding moment.
findings.evidence: Basil, On the Holy Spirit 27.66 (c. 375): some teachings come from written Scripture, others from unwritten apostolic tradition — the standard Orthodox citation (used by Florovsky, whom the quiz lists). Luther at Worms, 1521 ('unless I am convinced by Scripture and plain reason'), is the sola scriptura moment the timeline skips in favour of 1646.
findings.fix: Insert before Trent: ['c. 375', 'Basil the Great, On the Holy Spirit: some teachings come from written Scripture, others from the unwritten tradition of the apostles.'] and ['1521', 'Luther at Worms: bound by Scripture and plain reason, he will not recant on the authority of popes and councils alone.']

findings.claim: 'the church's teaching office' is Roman vocabulary (magisterium). The Orthodox convert: 'We have no teaching office; we have the Church, the Fathers, and the councils.'
findings.evidence: Lumen Gentium 25 and CCC 85 use 'teaching office'; Orthodox writers (Florovsky, Ware) speak of the consensus of the Fathers and the councils received by the whole Church.
findings.fix: 'the creeds, the councils, and the church's living teaching are God's appointed means...'

findings.claim: table=40 puts Methodists nearly halfway to memorialism. A United Methodist who baptizes infants and holds Wesley's means-of-grace view lands 17 and still matches, but the coordinate itself is a screenshot for the Methodist: 'Wesley preached The Duty of Constant Communion and the quiz put him next to Zwingli.'
findings.evidence: Wesley, 'The Duty of Constant Communion' (1732/1787); Methodist Articles of Religion XVIII (the Supper is 'a sacrament of our redemption'); UMC 'This Holy Mystery' (2004) affirms real presence and infant baptism.

The Pentecostal pastor: 'Free worship, as explained by two Presbyterians.' The Catholic apologist: 'Schmemann twice, Newman once, and not one Catholic liturgist.'

findings.claim: Cessationists get three texts (1 Cor 13:8–12, Eph 2:20, Heb 2:3–4); continuationists get two (Acts 2, Joel 2) plus the shared 1 Cor 12–14. The Pentecostal's first citation is absent.
findings.evidence: 1 Thessalonians 5:19–21 ('do not despise prophecies, but test everything') and 1 Corinthians 14:1 ('earnestly desire ... that you may prophesy') are the texts behind 'sought and tested' in the quiz's own fair summary.

findings.claim: 'A person can genuinely resist God's grace and refuse salvation to the very end' — a Calvinist can agree (Acts 7:51: everyone resists the Spirit; what is irresistible is effectual calling), which blunts the statement. A Lutheran agrees with it and with statements 1 and 3, and cancels to the middle.
findings.evidence: Canons of Dort III/IV.16 vs Remonstrance article 4 turn on whether saving grace in the elect can be finally refused; Formula of Concord SD XI holds unconditional election and resistible grace together.
findings.fix: 'A person whom God is drawing to salvation can still refuse his grace, even to the very end.'

findings.claim: 'The infants of believing parents' is Reformed covenant-household idiom. Catholic apologist: 'lol, written by a Presbyterian — we baptize infants, full stop.'

findings.claim: Axis names 'Spirit' and 'Tradition' are named after the left pole's key word, so the share bar and the headline read as if the cessationist has no Spirit and the Protestant no tradition (and vice versa). Both discernment sides screenshot the axis name alone.

findings.fix: name: 'Gifts' for the spirit axis; name: 'Authority' for the tradition axis. Leave 'Grace', 'Table', 'Kingdom', 'Worship'.

findings.claim: Do not touch these — they are the reason the quiz survives at all, and 'fixing' them would produce blandness: the pole names Monergist/Synergist (the Orthodox convert is delighted to be called a synergist; only the bands spoil it); 'A map, not a grade. No answer is the right one.'; 'Approximate positions of typical adherents, not official teaching.'; statements 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16 are each in the holder's own words; the fair summaries on Grace, Spirit, and Kingdom use each side's vocabulary ('ordinances' vs 'sacraments', 'sought and tested', 'usually preceded by'); the Grace history's Orange entry conceding the condemnation of predestination to evil; the Table history giving Calvin his own entry apart from Zwingli; the Kingdom history including Ladd and progressive dispensationalism; the 3–3 passage balance on Grace and Tradition; the primary-source-plus-modern pairing on Grace, Kingdom, and Tradition; 'firmly' on both ends of Grace; the footer admitting the positions are approximate.

simulation.headline: Sacramental, covenantal, rooted in tradition
simulation.comment: Answers (statements 1-18): -2,+2,-1 | +2,-2,+2 | +1,-2,+1 | -2,+2,-2 | +2,-2,+2 | +2,-2,+2. Raw = sum(direction x answer): Grace (-1)(-2)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-1)=5 -> round(11/12x100)=92; Table (-1)(2)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(2)=-6 -> 0; Spirit (-1)(1)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(1)=-4 -> round(2/12x100)=17; Kingdom (1)(-2)+(-1)(2)+(1)(-2)=-6 -> 0; Tradition (-1)(2)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(2)=-6 -> 0; Worship (-1)(2)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(2)=-6 -> 0.
