Headline: |score-50| = 42,50,33,50,50,50; four axes tie at 50 and the code breaks ties by axis index, so Table (band 0 'sacramental'), Kingdom ('covenantal'), Tradition ('rooted in tradition') -> 'Sacramental, covenantal, rooted in tradition'; 'liturgical' and 'firmly synergist' never appear. Distances (sum of squares -> sqrt -> match%): Eastern Orthodox 729+25+324+225+25+25=1353 -> 36.78 -> 85%; Roman Catholic 1369+25+529+225+100+100=2348 -> 48.46 -> 80%; Anglican 5813 -> 76.24 -> 69%; Wesleyan 6778 -> 82.33 -> 66%; Lutheran 10068 -> 100.34; Presbyterian 15588 -> 124.85; Anabaptist 18358 -> 135.49; Reformed Baptist 23743 -> 154.09; Charismatic 25953 -> 161.10; Pentecostal 28463 -> 168.71; Southern Baptist 29823 -> 172.69; Dispensational 38883 -> 197.19. So it lands, but 729 of the 1353 comes from the Grace coordinate (65 vs my 92), and the margin is fragile. Sensitivity: an equally defensible Orthodox pattern (S1 Unsure, since predestination-according-to-foreknowledge is eternal; S2 Agree; S3 Agree, since faith is a gift; S7/S9/S12 Unsure) gives [50,0,33,17,0,0] and lands ROMAN CATHOLIC first: RC 25+25+49+4+100+100=303 -> 17.41 (93%), EO 225+25+4+4+25+25=308 -> 17.55 (93%). Moving the EO coordinate alone does not rescue that case (EO grace 85 makes it 1368 -> 36.99). Rewriting statements 1 and 3 as proposed (an Orthodox then answers -2 to both) turns that pattern into [92,0,33,17,0,0]: EO 812 -> 28.50 vs RC 1647 -> 40.58 with current coordinates; with EO moved to grace 85 / spirit 25, EO 192 -> 13.86 (94%) vs RC 40.58. My main pattern against the proposed EO coordinates: 4+25+64+225+25+25=413 -> 20.32 (92%).

findings.claim: Double-barreled: an informed Orthodox agrees with the first clause (faith is God's gift) and rejects the second (election without regard to foreseen faith); agreeing is scored monergist, and that alone can flip the nearest tradition to Roman Catholic.
findings.evidence: Text: "Saving faith is itself a gift God gives to those he has chosen, not the reason he chose them." Eph 2:8 and Chrysostom, Hom. 4 on Ephesians, call faith God's gift; the Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem 1672), Decree 3, says God predestined "since He foreknew the one would make a right use of their free-will" and anathematizes election without regard to that. Arithmetic: S1 Unsure, S2 Agree, S3 Agree gives Grace 50; with S7/S9/S12 Unsure the vector is [50,0,33,17,0,0]; distance to Roman Catholic sqrt(303)=17.41, to Eastern Orthodox sqrt(308)=17.55, so the card lists Roman Catholic first.
findings.fix: Faith is the result of God's choice, not the reason for it.

findings.claim: "Before anyone does anything, God has already chosen who will be saved" asserts eternal priority, which the Orthodox affirm (predestination according to foreknowledge), so a synergist can honestly answer Unsure or Agree; only "his choice cannot fail" carries the monergist content.
findings.evidence: Rom 8:29 ("those whom he foreknew he also predestined"); John of Damascus, Exact Exposition II.30: God foreknows all things but does not predestine all things; Dositheus, Decree 3, affirms that God "from eternity predestinated unto glory" those he foreknew.
findings.fix: God's choice of who will be saved does not rest on anything he foresaw in them, and it cannot fail.

findings.claim: Triple-barreled ("Tongues, prophecy, and healing" plus "as they did in Acts"): the Orthodox affirm healing and prophecy in the lives of the saints, have no practice of tongues, and do not claim an Acts-style congregational pattern, so an honest answer is Unsure or Disagree, which is scored cessationist, a position the Orthodox flatly reject.
findings.evidence: Text: "Tongues, prophecy, and healing continue in the church today, as they did in Acts." Anointing for healing is one of the seven mysteries; the Church canonizes wonderworkers and elders with foresight (Seraphim of Sarov, d. 1833; Paisios of Mount Athos, canonized 2015); glossolalia is absent from Orthodox practice and "as in Acts" is the Pentecostal reading. A parish Orthodox answering 0 here moves Spirit from 17 to 25 for no doctrinal reason.
findings.fix: Miraculous gifts such as healing and prophecy still occur in the church today. (Tongues stays covered by statement 8's "sign gifts".)

findings.claim: Leads with "caught up to meet Christ", which every tradition affirms from 1 Thess 4:17; the dispensational content is only the final clause, and an Orthodox, who has no doctrine of a rapture at all, may hesitate at the first clause.
findings.evidence: Text: "Believers will be caught up to meet Christ before a seven-year tribulation." The Orthodox reading of 1 Thess 4:17 is the general resurrection at the Parousia (Chrysostom, Hom. 8 on 1 Thessalonians); no Orthodox text knows a seven-year tribulation.
findings.fix: The church will be taken out of the world before a final seven-year tribulation.

findings.claim: "Reformed-leaning" and "Arminian-leaning" pin Protestant party names on everyone in the 21-40 and 60-79 bands; the quiz's own Eastern Orthodox coordinate (grace 65) sits inside the "Arminian-leaning" band, so the data file labels the Orthodox Church a leaning-Arminian body.
findings.evidence: Bands: ["firmly monergist","Reformed-leaning","balanced on grace","Arminian-leaning","firmly synergist"]. Orthodox synergism (Cassian, Conferences 13; Maximus the Confessor; John of Damascus, Exact Exposition II.29-30; Synod of Jerusalem 1672) predates Arminius (1560-1609) by a millennium and rests on a different anthropology: no total depravity, no prevenient-grace scheme, salvation as theosis. An Orthodox landing 60-79 sees "Arminian-leaning" on the share card.
findings.fix: ["firmly monergist", "leaning monergist", "balanced on grace", "leaning synergist", "firmly synergist"]

findings.claim: The monergist half states the Reformed position only ("his saving grace cannot finally be refused") and so excludes confessional Lutherans, whom the quiz places at grace 20 ("firmly monergist"); the synergist half is acceptable to the Orthodox but never names the Eastern framing (synergy, theosis), so the axis reads as an intra-Protestant quarrel.
findings.evidence: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration II (Free Will), teaches that the unconverted can resist the Holy Spirit (Acts 7:51) while conversion remains God's work alone; a Lutheran therefore answers statement 2 Agree and is pushed synergist. On the Orthodox side, synergeia is the tradition's own word (1 Cor 3:9; Phil 2:12-13) and salvation is theosis (2 Pet 1:4; Athanasius, On the Incarnation 54).
findings.fix: Monergists hold that salvation is God's work from beginning to end: he chooses, calls, and keeps his people, and no one contributes anything to it, not even the decision to believe (the Reformed add that his saving grace cannot finally be refused; Lutherans hold that it can be resisted but never merited). Synergists hold that God's grace always comes first and makes faith possible, but that each person must freely respond and can decline, so that election follows God's foreknowledge of faith or rests on his choice of a people in Christ; the Christian East calls this cooperation synergy and sees salvation as a lifelong growth into God's likeness (theosis).

findings.claim: All five entries are Western, and the synergist side is anchored only to the Remonstrants and Wesley, implying the Orthodox position is a Protestant variant; the East's own conciliar answer to Calvinism is absent.
findings.evidence: Patriarch Cyril Lucaris published a Calvinist confession in 1629; the Synod of Jerusalem (1672, Confession of Dositheus) rejected it, Decree 3 teaching predestination according to foreknowledge of each person's free use of the will.
findings.fix: Insert after the Dort entry: {"when": "1672", "what": "Synod of Jerusalem rejects Patriarch Cyril Lucaris's Calvinist confession: God predestines according to his foreknowledge of each person's free response."}

findings.claim: The two texts the synergist tradition reaches for first are absent.
findings.evidence: Rom 8:29-30 ("those whom he foreknew he also predestined") is the locus of the Orthodox and Arminian doctrine of election on foreknowledge; Phil 2:12-13 ("work out your own salvation... for it is God who works in you") is the classic synergy text (Chrysostom, Hom. 8 on Philippians).
findings.fix: Add "Romans 8:29-30" and "Philippians 2:12-13".

findings.claim: The right pole's list is Arminius and Olson only, so an Orthodox or Catholic scoring synergist is sent to Arminian sources.
findings.evidence: read_more.right: ["Arminius, Works", "Olson, Arminian Theology"]; the quiz itself coordinates Orthodox (65) and Catholics (55) on this side.
findings.fix: Add "Ware, The Orthodox Way" (or "John of Damascus, Exact Exposition II.29-30").

findings.claim: grace 65 and spirit 35 sit too far toward the monergist and cessationist poles; grace 65 even places the Orthodox coordinate in the "Arminian-leaning" band, and the Orthodox are at least as synergist as the Wesleyans, who are given 80.
findings.evidence: Informed simulation [92,0,17,0,0,0]: current distance sqrt(1353)=36.78 (85%), of which 729 comes from grace alone; with grace 85 / spirit 25 the distance is sqrt(413)=20.32 (92%). Doctrine: Dositheus Decree 3 (free response foreknown); Spirit 35 puts the Church one point from "undecided on the gifts" despite healing unction, canonized wonderworkers, and myrrh-streaming icons; a typical adherent answering statement 7 Unsure scores 25. Caveat: with statement 3 as currently worded, moving the coordinate alone does not rescue the soft pattern (grace 50 case: EO distance rises to 36.99); fix statements 1 and 3 first, then move the coordinate.
findings.fix: {"grace": 85, "table": 5, "spirit": 25, "kingdom": 15, "tradition": 5, "worship": 5}

findings.claim: "should be sought" is not the Orthodox (or Catholic) view of the gifts, yet the Orthodox coordinate is on the continuationist side; the summary describes only the Pentecostal form of continuance.
findings.evidence: Text: "remain available to the church until Christ returns, and should be sought and tested." Orthodox ascetic teaching warns against seeking visions or gifts as the road to prelest (Ignatius Brianchaninov, The Arena; the Philokalia on discernment); the gifts are received unsought in the lives of the saints; 1 Cor 12:31 is read as pointing to love (Chrysostom, Hom. 32 on 1 Corinthians).
findings.fix: Continuationists hold that the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12, including tongues, prophecy, and healing, remain in the church until Christ returns: Pentecostals and charismatics actively seek them, while Orthodox and Catholics expect them chiefly in the lives of the saints and warn against seeking them; all agree they must be tested.

findings.claim: The only patristic entry on this axis is deployed as a cessationist proof, and the continuationist side's first entry (index 0) is a condemned movement, so the sequence reads heresy, then a Father says the gifts ceased, then Pentecostalism; the patristic evidence for continuance is omitted.
findings.evidence: Text: "Chrysostom, preaching on 1 Corinthians, notes that the sign gifts had ceased." Hom. 29 on 1 Corinthians (Antioch, c. 392) does say the Corinthian gifts "no longer take place", but the same preacher proclaims ongoing miracles at the martyrs' tombs (Hom. on St Babylas; Hom. on the Holy Martyrs). Augustine, Retractationes I.13.7, withdrew his earlier claim that miracles had ceased, and City of God XXII.8 (426) records nearly seventy healings at Hippo in under two years.
findings.fix: Reword entry 1 to "c. 392 — Chrysostom, Homilies on 1 Corinthians, observes that the Corinthian gifts 'no longer take place', while preaching miracles at the martyrs' shrines." and insert after it {"when": "426", "what": "Augustine, City of God XXII.8, withdraws his earlier view that miracles had ceased and records some seventy recent healings at Hippo."}

findings.claim: The text the older churches use for both continuance and testing is absent.
findings.evidence: 1 Thess 5:19-21 ("Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything") is the Orthodox and Catholic rule for the gifts; the present list has no text that unites the two poles.
findings.fix: Add "1 Thessalonians 5:19-21".

findings.claim: The left list is entirely charismatic-Protestant; the Orthodox and Catholics coordinated on that pole have no entry.
findings.evidence: read_more.left: ["Grudem, The Gift of Prophecy", "Storms, Practicing the Power"].
findings.fix: Add "Seraphim of Sarov, On the Acquisition of the Holy Spirit (Conversation with Motovilov)".

findings.claim: "Covenantal" is the Reformed technical term for federal theology (covenant of works / covenant of grace), which the Orthodox do not hold; because Kingdom sits at maximum distance and ties break by axis index, every Orthodox and Catholic headline and share card reads "Sacramental, covenantal, rooted in tradition".
findings.evidence: Simulation headline above. Westminster Confession ch. 7 defines the covenants of works and grace; Orthodox theology has neither and simply calls the Church the New Israel (Justin, Dialogue with Trypho 11; the Paschal hymnography). "Theology Compass says the Orthodox are covenantal" is the screenshot this product is trying to avoid. The share text likewise prints "Covenantal ○○○○○○○○○○ Dispensational".
findings.fix: Rename left pole "One people of God" and bands to ["one people of God", "leaning to one people of God", "centered on the kingdom", "dispensational-leaning", "dispensational"]. Minimal alternative: keep the name and append to the fair summary: "Though the name comes from Reformed covenant theology, this is also the historic reading of the Orthodox, Catholic, Lutheran, and Anglican churches."

findings.claim: The one-people side begins with Augustine (413) and jumps to Westminster (1646), making the ancient consensus look Augustinian-Reformed; the second-century witness that the Church is Israel is absent.
findings.evidence: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 11 and 135 (c. 155-160): Christians are "the true spiritual Israel" and "the true Israelite race"; this is the reading the Orthodox liturgy assumes.
findings.fix: Insert before the Augustine entry: {"when": "c. 160", "what": "Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho: the church of Jews and Gentiles is 'the true, spiritual Israel'."}

findings.claim: The left list is two Reformed authors; an Orthodox or Catholic at the left pole is sent to covenant theology.
findings.evidence: read_more.left: ["Horton, Introducing Covenant Theology", "Riddlebarger, A Case for Amillennialism"].
findings.fix: Add "Catechism of the Catholic Church §§ 668-682" (§ 676 rejects millenarianism; the Orthodox share the reading) or "Alfeyev, Orthodox Christianity vol. II, on the Last Things".

findings.claim: "the church's teaching office" is the Roman magisterium, which the Orthodox do not have, and "read Scripture with tradition" describes Trent's two-source model rather than the Orthodox view that Scripture lives within Tradition; the Orthodox at the left pole are described in Rome's words.
findings.evidence: Text: "the creeds, councils, and the church's teaching office are God's appointed means of guarding and interpreting his Word". Florovsky, "The Function of Tradition in the Ancient Church" (in Bible, Church, Tradition, the very book in read_more) and Ware, The Orthodox Church, ch. "Holy Tradition": Scripture is the heart of Tradition, not a source beside it; authority is the ecumenical councils received by the whole Church and the consensus of the Fathers (Vincent, Commonitorium 2).
findings.fix: Those who read Scripture within the Church's tradition hold that Scripture was written, recognized, and is rightly interpreted inside the life of the Church, so that the creeds, the ecumenical councils, the consensus of the Fathers, and (for Roman Catholics) the papal teaching office carry real authority in guarding and interpreting God's Word.

findings.claim: Three of the five entries are Roman (Trent, Newman, Dei Verbum) and none is Eastern, so an Orthodox at "rooted in tradition" sees the pole defined by councils and theologians the Orthodox Church does not accept; the two classic Eastern statements are missing.
findings.evidence: Basil the Great, On the Holy Spirit 27.66 (c. 375): some teachings come from written teaching, others "from the tradition of the apostles... in a mystery" (facing east, the sign of the cross, the words of the epiclesis). Second Council of Nicaea (787), the last council received by both East and West: "we keep unchanged all the ecclesiastical traditions handed down to us, whether in writing or unwritten."
findings.fix: Insert before Vincent: {"when": "c. 375", "what": "Basil the Great, On the Holy Spirit 27: some teachings come from Scripture, others from unwritten apostolic tradition (facing east, the sign of the cross, the epiclesis)."} and after Vincent: {"when": "787", "what": "Second Council of Nicaea: 'we keep the ecclesiastical traditions handed down to us, whether written or unwritten.'"}

findings.claim: "Christ is truly present in the Supper" describes the sacramental view in the memorialist's vocabulary; no Orthodox or Catholic calls it "the Supper".
findings.evidence: The sacramental side's own word is "Eucharist" (Ignatius, Smyrn. 7, the very source cited in history[0]).
findings.fix: Christ is truly present in the Eucharist (the Lord's Supper)

findings.claim: After Ignatius the sacramental side is represented only by Lateran IV, a council the East does not recognize; the Eastern teaching of the change by the epiclesis, which directly answers statement 4's "beyond a symbol", is absent.
findings.evidence: Cyril of Jerusalem, Mystagogical Catecheses 4-5 (c. 350); John of Damascus, Exact Exposition IV.13 (c. 743): the bread and wine are "not merely figures... but the deified body of the Lord itself", changed "through the invocation and coming of the Holy Spirit".
findings.fix: Insert after Ignatius: {"when": "c. 743", "what": "John of Damascus, Exact Exposition IV.13: the bread and wine are changed by the invocation of the Holy Spirit; not a figure but the very Body."}

findings.claim: The Orthodox anchor texts for baptism and the Eucharist are absent.
findings.evidence: John 3:5 (born of water and the Spirit) is the baptismal text read at every Orthodox baptism; 1 Cor 10:16-17 (the cup a koinonia in the Blood, one bread one body) is the Eucharistic text the Fathers cite alongside John 6.
findings.fix: Add "John 3:5" and "1 Corinthians 10:16-17".

findings.claim: Listing "the participation of the whole congregation" as a free-worship distinctive implies liturgical worship lacks it, and the liturgical description reads as an argument from antiquity, omitting the reason the Orthodox keep a set liturgy: it joins the worship of heaven.
findings.evidence: Text: "with an emphasis on spontaneity, sincerity, and the participation of the whole congregation." Leitourgia means the work of the people; the Orthodox liturgy is sung and answered by all; the Cherubic Hymn and Isaiah 6 / Revelation 4-5 are its rationale.
findings.fix: Liturgical worship follows a set order, the church calendar, and a weekly Eucharist, so that the whole congregation prays and sings with the historic church, in words tested over centuries, and joins the worship of heaven. Free worship keeps the form open so that the Spirit can lead in the moment, with an emphasis on spontaneity, sincerity, and room for any member to contribute.

findings.claim: The liturgical side jumps from Justin (155) to Cranmer (1549), so the first named liturgy in the list is Anglican; the liturgies celebrated every Sunday by the Orthodox Church, coordinated at worship 5, do not appear.
findings.evidence: The Liturgy of St Basil (4th c., Cappadocia) and the Liturgy of St John Chrysostom (Antioch/Constantinople, 4th-5th c.) are the ordinary eucharistic rites of Orthodoxy and the oldest liturgies in continuous use.
findings.fix: Insert after Justin: {"when": "4th-5th c.", "what": "The Liturgies of St Basil and St John Chrysostom take the shape still celebrated every Sunday in the Orthodox Church."}

findings.claim: The texts the liturgical side actually reaches for, the heavenly liturgy, are absent; the list is weighted to the free side's proof texts (John 4, 1 Cor 14, Psalm 150).
findings.evidence: Isaiah 6:1-3 and Revelation 4-5 supply the Trisagion and the Sanctus; Hebrews 8:1-5 grounds earthly worship in the heavenly sanctuary.
findings.fix: Add "Revelation 4-5" and "Hebrews 8:1-5".

findings.claim: All six axes are controversies internal to Western Christianity; the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox coordinates differ by at most 10 points on any axis and the quiz cannot separate the two largest non-Protestant communions, so the intro's "Tradition-neutral" promise is overstated for them.
findings.evidence: RC [55,5,40,15,10,10] vs EO [65,5,35,15,5,5]; no axis touches the papacy, the filioque, doctrinal development, purgatory, or theosis, the matters that actually divide Rome and the East. Soft-pattern arithmetic: [50,0,33,17,0,0] gives RC 17.41 vs EO 17.55, both shown as 93% match. Intro text: "Tradition-neutral: every position is described in words its holders would accept."
findings.fix: Add one distance-only statement, "The bishop of Rome has, by Christ's appointment, authority over the whole church", scored as a seventh coordinate used only in nearest-tradition matching (Roman Catholic 95, Anglican 10, all others 5); or, at minimum, add to the intro: "The six axes are the questions that divided the Western churches; Orthodox and Catholic readers will land close together."

findings.claim: "Unsure" is the only middle answer, so "I have no view" and "my tradition does not frame the question this way" score identically; on the Spirit and Kingdom statements an Orthodox reader needs the second.
findings.evidence: Answer buttons: Strongly disagree / Disagree / Unsure / Agree / Strongly agree; statements 7, 8, 10, 12 use Pentecostal and dispensational vocabulary ("sign gifts", "completion of the New Testament", "national Israel", "seven-year tribulation") that has no Orthodox equivalent.
findings.fix: Add a one-line note above the quiz: "If a statement is not how your tradition frames the question, choose Unsure." (or a fourth option "Not how I'd put it" scored 0).

findings.claim: The middle-band names "centered on the sacraments" and "centered on the kingdom" read as substantive positions rather than midpoints; a 50 on Table is told they are "centered on the sacraments", which is what the 0 end believes.
findings.evidence: Table bands[2] = "centered on the sacraments"; Kingdom bands[2] = "centered on the kingdom"; the other four axes use genuinely neutral midpoints ("balanced on grace", "undecided on the gifts", "balanced on authority", "flexible in worship").
findings.fix: Table bands[2]: "between sacrament and symbol"; Kingdom bands[2]: "mixed on Israel and the church".

findings.claim: The share bar fills from the left pole, so a fully sacramental Orthodox posts "Sacramental ○○○○○○○○○○ Memorial", which reads at a glance as zero on sacramental; four of my six lines render as empty bars.
findings.evidence: shareText(): f = round(score/10) filled circles, so a score of 0 prints ten empty circles next to the pole the person holds most strongly.
findings.fix: Mark position instead of filling: place ● at slot round(score/100*9) and ○ elsewhere, so 0 renders "Sacramental ●○○○○○○○○○ Memorial" and 100 renders "Sacramental ○○○○○○○○○● Memorial".

lens: Pentecostal (Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths)

simulation.headline: Continuationist, firmly synergist, memorialist
simulation.comment: Answers S1..S18 as an informed AG member: -2,2,-1 | -1,2,-2 | 2,-2,2 | 1,-1,2 | -1,2,-1 | -2,2,-1. Raw: grace (-1)(-2)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-1)=5 -> round(11/12*100)=92; table (-1)(-1)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-2)=5 -> 92; spirit (-1)(2)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(2)=-6 -> 0; kingdom (1)(1)+(-1)(-1)+(1)(2)=4 -> round(10/12*100)=83; tradition (-1)(-1)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-1)=4 -> 83; worship (-1)(-2)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-1)=5 -> 92. |score-50|: spirit 50, grace 42, table 42, worship 42, kingdom 33, tradition 33; sort by distance then index gives spirit, grace, table -> bands 'continuationist', 'firmly synergist', 'memorialist' -> 'Continuationist, firmly synergist, memorialist'. Per-axis bands: kingdom 83 = 'dispensational', tradition 83 = 'Scripture alone', worship 92 = 'free in worship'. Distances (squares summed): Pentecostal/AoG 144+49+25+64+4+4=290 -> 17.03 (93%); Charismatic non-denom 484+144+25+529+4+4=1190 -> 34.50 (86%); Anabaptist 85.82; Southern Baptist 92.41; Dispensational Bible church 106.25; Wesleyan 111.29; Reformed Baptist 133.90; Anglican 145.53; Presbyterian 154.52; Roman Catholic 164.97; Eastern Orthodox 166.73; Lutheran 167.71. Lands correctly. Sensitivity: (a) an AG member who reads S1 as foreknowledge and agrees (+1) with S3 unsure gets grace 58 ('balanced on grace') yet still lands AoG (25.10 vs 29.15); (b) an AG member agnostic on the pretrib rapture (S10=0, S11=-1, S12=-1) gets kingdom 50 and flips to Charismatic non-denom 27.59 vs AoG 29.17 -- the nearest-tradition call between the two Pentecostal-type entries is decided entirely by eschatology and election because both sit at spirit=5 and the axis has no statement on Spirit baptism or initial evidence; (c) S4 answered +1 from experience of Christ's presence at the Table gives table 75 but still AoG nearest (18.47).

findings.claim: The quiz lists 'Pentecostal / Assemblies of God' and 'Charismatic non-denominational' as separate traditions but contains no statement on the one doctrine that separates them, so it cannot place a Pentecostal as a Pentecostal; the two entries sit at identical spirit=5 and differ only on grace (80/70), table (85/80) and kingdom (75/60). Statement 9 is also nearly redundant with statement 7 (both test whether prophecy continues), so the Spirit axis is effectively two items.
findings.evidence: AG Statement of Fundamental Truths art. 7: the baptism in the Holy Spirit 'is distinct from and subsequent to the experience of the new birth'; art. 8: it 'is witnessed by the initial physical sign of speaking with other tongues' (Acts 2:4). Reformed continuationists (Grudem, Storms, Sovereign Grace, most non-denominational charismatics) reject both. Arithmetic: an AG member agnostic on the pretrib rapture (S10=0, S11=-1, S12=-1) scores [92,92,0,50,83,92] and lands on Charismatic non-denominational (27.59) ahead of AoG (29.17): the Pentecostal/charismatic call flips on eschatology alone.
findings.fix: Replace statement 9 with: 'The baptism in the Holy Spirit is an experience distinct from conversion, and speaking in tongues is normally its first sign.' (axis spirit, direction -1). Then set Charismatic non-denominational spirit to 20 and keep Pentecostal / AoG at 5. If the owners prefer to keep the axis purely cessationist/continuationist, merge the two entries into one 'Pentecostal / charismatic' tradition, because the current pair is a distinction the instrument cannot measure.

findings.claim: 'Before anyone does anything, God has already chosen who will be saved, and his choice cannot fail' is affirmable by a foreknowledge Arminian, which is the AG position, so a convinced Arminian who agrees is scored toward the monergist pole.
findings.evidence: Arminius, Declaration of Sentiments (1608), fourth decree: God decreed to save 'certain particular persons' on the basis of his foreknowledge of faith; AG position paper 'The Security of the Believer' and standard AG teaching ground election in foreknowledge (Rom 8:29; 1 Pet 1:2). Such a person believes God chose from eternity and that his foreknowledge cannot fail. Arithmetic: S1=+1 with S3=0 gives grace raw 1 -> 58, 'balanced on grace', for someone who is firmly Arminian.
findings.fix: 'God chose who will be saved without regard to anything he foresaw they would do, and his choice cannot fail.'

findings.claim: The continuationist reading list ('Grudem, The Gift of Prophecy', 'Storms, Practicing the Power') is written entirely by Reformed continuationists who explicitly reject the Pentecostal doctrines of subsequence and initial evidence; not one Pentecostal author represents the pole Pentecostals defined.
findings.evidence: Grudem, Systematic Theology ch. 39, argues against a second-stage baptism in the Spirit; Storms writes the Third Wave essay in Grudem (ed.), Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views (1996), where the Pentecostal view is a separate chapter by Douglas Oss. The AG's own systematic works (Stanley Horton, ed., Systematic Theology: A Pentecostal Perspective; Menzies & Menzies, Spirit and Power; Stronstad, The Charismatic Theology of St. Luke; Macchia, Baptized in the Spirit) are absent.
findings.fix: left: ['Stronstad, The Charismatic Theology of St. Luke', 'Grudem (ed.), Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views'] -- the second volume contains Pentecostal, Third Wave, open-but-cautious and cessationist essays side by side and is the fairest single title for either pole. Alternatively keep Grudem and add 'Macchia, Baptized in the Spirit'.

findings.claim: The continuationist paragraph ('Continuationists hold that the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12, including tongues, prophecy, and healing, remain available to the church until Christ returns, and should be sought and tested') describes the Third Wave position and omits the baptism in the Holy Spirit, which for Pentecostals is the heart of the matter, not the continuation of gifts as such.
findings.evidence: AG Statement of Fundamental Truths art. 7: 'All believers are entitled to and should ardently expect and earnestly seek the promise of the Father, the baptism in the Holy Spirit and fire ... This was the normal experience of all in the early Christian Church'; art. 8 on tongues as initial physical evidence. The summary's 'sought and tested' is acceptable (1 Cor 14:1; 1 Thess 5:21).
findings.fix: Append: 'Pentecostals go further: the baptism in the Holy Spirit is a distinct experience promised to every believer (Acts 2:39), and classical Pentecostal bodies such as the Assemblies of God hold that speaking in tongues is its first sign.'

findings.claim: The only pre-modern datum on the continuationist side is 'Montanist "new prophecy" in Phrygia; the wider church grows wary of ongoing prophecy' -- a movement the church condemned. That is Warfield's genealogy (charismata = Montanist aberration), not a neutral history; the orthodox second-century witness to continuing gifts is omitted.
findings.evidence: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.32.4 (healings and raisings of the dead in the churches) and 5.6.1 ('we do also hear many brethren in the Church, who possess prophetic gifts, and who through the Spirit speak all kinds of languages'); also Tertullian, Against Marcion 5.8, and Novatian, On the Trinity 29. Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles, is the source of the Montanist framing.
findings.fix: '2nd c. -- Irenaeus reports prophecy, tongues, and healings in the churches (Against Heresies 2.32; 5.6); the Montanist "new prophecy" in Phrygia makes the wider church wary of unregulated prophecy.'

findings.claim: The passage list carries the same text twice (Joel 2:28–29 and Acts 2:17–18, which quotes it) while the AG's central continuation text, Acts 2:38–39, appears only under the Table axis as a paedobaptist proof, and the Lukan evidence texts (Acts 10:44–46; 19:1–7) and the text behind statement 9 (1 Thess 5:19–21) are absent.
findings.evidence: AG Statement of Fundamental Truths art. 7–8 cite Luke 24:49, Acts 1:4,8, 2:4, 2:38–39, 10:44–46, 15:7–9, 19:1–7. Acts 2:39, 'the promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off, for all whom the Lord our God will call', is the verse every AG preacher reaches for against cessationism.
findings.fix: Replace 'Joel 2:28–29' with 'Acts 2:38–39' and add 'Acts 10:44–46' and '1 Thessalonians 5:19–21'.

findings.claim: An informed AG member scores 75–92 on this axis and is labelled 'dispensational-leaning' or 'dispensational' in the headline, a system name the AG Statement never uses and which many Pentecostal theologians expressly reject, because classical dispensationalism confines Joel 2 / Acts 2 to Israel and treats the gifts as belonging to a past dispensation -- the opposite of Pentecostal hermeneutics.
findings.evidence: AG Statement of Fundamental Truths art. 13–14 confess the rapture, the earthly millennial reign and 'the salvation of national Israel' without the word 'dispensation'; the AG requires its credentialed ministers to hold a pretribulational rapture (General Council Bylaws Art. IX.B, 'Eschatological Errors'). Sheppard, 'Pentecostals and the Hermeneutics of Dispensationalism: The Anatomy of an Uneasy Relationship', Pneuma 6 (1984); Scofield's Acts 2 note and the Dallas Seminary doctrinal statement (art. XII) treat the sign gifts as temporary. Simulation: kingdom 83 -> 'dispensational'.
findings.fix: bands: ['covenantal', 'covenantal-leaning', 'centered on the kingdom', 'premillennial-leaning', 'dispensational'] and add to the fair_summary: 'Pentecostal bodies such as the Assemblies of God hold the pretribulational, premillennial hope of this pole without the wider dispensational system.' Optionally lower the AoG kingdom coordinate to 80 so the entry itself sits at the band boundary, and keep 'dispensational' only for those who also affirm the Israel–church distinction (statements 10 and 11) at full strength.

findings.claim: 'The dispensational view keeps Israel and the church distinct' is the defining clause, so the paragraph reads as if everyone at the right pole holds two peoples of God; Pentecostals hold the rapture, tribulation, millennium and salvation of national Israel while typically reading the church as the fulfilment of Joel's promise.
findings.evidence: AG Statement of Fundamental Truths art. 14: 'This millennial reign will bring the salvation of national Israel (Ezekiel 37:21,22; Zephaniah 3:19,20; Romans 11:26,27) and the establishment of universal peace' -- salvation, not a separate programme. See also Sheppard, Pneuma 6 (1984).
findings.fix: After 'a seven-year tribulation.' add: 'Premillennial Pentecostals share this future hope for Israel and the pretribulational rapture without the full dispensational scheme.'

findings.claim: 'In the Lord's Supper, Christ is truly present in a way that goes beyond a symbol' forces a Pentecostal who confesses Christ's real presence by the Spirit among the gathered believers, and who expects healing at the Table, to deny Christ's presence in order to avoid being scored sacramental.
findings.evidence: AG Statement of Fundamental Truths art. 6 calls the Supper 'the symbol expressing our sharing the divine nature of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Peter 1:4); a memorial of His suffering and death' -- so the tradition's confessional answer is Disagree -- yet Pentecostal spirituality prays 'Christ is present here' at the Table (Matt 18:20), and AG theologians such as Chris Green (Toward a Pentecostal Theology of the Lord's Supper, 2012) argue for presence by the Spirit. Arithmetic: S4=+1 moves table from 92 to 75 ('memorial-leaning') on a point unrelated to sacramental theology.
findings.fix: 'In the Lord's Supper, Christ is given to us through the bread and wine themselves, not only remembered.'

findings.claim: The middle band 'centered on the sacraments' (41–59) uses the left pole's vocabulary for the neutral position; a Pentecostal or Baptist at 50–59 who calls the Supper an ordinance is labelled with the word his tradition deliberately avoids, while every other axis has a neutral middle ('balanced on grace', 'undecided on the gifts', 'centered on the kingdom', 'balanced on authority', 'flexible in worship').
findings.evidence: AG Statement of Fundamental Truths art. 6 is titled 'The Ordinances of the Church'; the memorial fair_summary itself says 'both are ordinances ... rather than channels of grace'.
findings.fix: bands[2]: 'between sign and sacrament' (or 'balanced on the Table').

findings.claim: 'so both are ordinances obeyed by believers rather than channels of grace' is the Reformed critic's summary of the memorial view, not the memorialist's own; Pentecostals would say the ordinances confer no saving grace but that Christ is met there by faith and the Spirit.
findings.evidence: AG Statement of Fundamental Truths art. 6: the Supper is 'the symbol expressing our sharing the divine nature of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Peter 1:4)' -- a sharing, not bare obedience; Pentecostal practice pairs the Table with prayer for healing (1 Cor 11:29–30 read positively).
findings.fix: '...so both are ordinances obeyed by believers: Christ is met in them by faith and the Spirit, but the acts themselves do not confer saving grace.'

findings.claim: The 'Free' pole's reading list is 'Frame, Worship in Spirit and Truth' -- a Reformed defence of the regulative principle, i.e. a constraint on worship -- and 'Kauflin, Worship Matters' from Sovereign Grace; the largest free-worship family in the world, Pentecostalism, has no author on its own pole.
findings.evidence: Frame's book argues for the Puritan regulative principle listed at history[3] as a liturgical-side landmark; Kauflin is Sovereign Grace (Reformed charismatic). Standard Pentecostal works: Albrecht, Rites in the Spirit (1999); Ruth & Lim, A History of Contemporary Praise & Worship (Baker Academic, 2021), which traces 'praise and worship' to Pentecostal and Latter Rain roots.
findings.fix: right: ['Albrecht, Rites in the Spirit', 'Ruth & Lim, A History of Contemporary Praise & Worship'] (keep Kauflin as a third if three are allowed; drop Frame).

findings.claim: '1970s– Jesus movement and the contemporary worship movement (Calvary Chapel, Vineyard, Hillsong)' credits modern free worship to the Jesus movement and names Hillsong without noting it was an Assemblies of God church; Pentecostal worship (Azusa 1906, the Black Pentecostal tradition, the 1948 Latter Rain origin of 'praise and worship') is absent from the axis Pentecostals define.
findings.evidence: Hillsong (Hills Christian Life Centre, 1983) belonged to the Assemblies of God in Australia / Australian Christian Churches until it withdrew in 2018. Ruth & Lim (2021) locate the 'praise and worship' theology in the 1948 Latter Rain revival and Pentecostal churches; Azusa Street introduced spontaneous song, tongues and interpretation, and the altar response that the summary describes.
findings.fix: Insert before this entry: '1906– Azusa Street: Pentecostal worship -- spontaneous song, tongues and interpretation, the altar call -- spreads worldwide; the 1948 Latter Rain revival gives "praise and worship" its theology.' and amend this entry to '(Calvary Chapel, Vineyard, and the Pentecostal Hillsong)'.

findings.claim: '1906 Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles launches modern Pentecostalism' is the only mention of the AG's world anywhere in six histories: Warfield and MacArthur are named on the other side but William Seymour is not, Topeka 1901 (where the initial-evidence doctrine of art. 8 was formed) is missing, and the Statement of Fundamental Truths (1916) never appears while Westminster appears twice.
findings.evidence: Parham's Topeka school, 1 Jan 1901 (Agnes Ozman); Seymour's Azusa Street mission, April 1906; General Council of the Assemblies of God, Hot Springs 1914; Statement of Fundamental Truths adopted 1916.
findings.fix: '1901–06 Charles Parham's Topeka school and William Seymour's Azusa Street mission launch modern Pentecostalism, with tongues as the sign of Spirit baptism.' and add '1916 The Assemblies of God adopt the Statement of Fundamental Truths, making Spirit baptism with tongues confessional.'

findings.claim: 'Chrysostom, preaching on 1 Corinthians, notes that the sign gifts had ceased' puts the modern cessationist category 'sign gifts' into a fourth-century mouth.
findings.evidence: Chrysostom, Homily 29 on 1 Corinthians (on 12:1–2): the passage is obscure 'by our ignorance of the facts referred to and by their cessation, being such as then used to occur but now no longer take place' -- he speaks of the gifts Paul lists, not of a class called 'sign gifts', a term from Warfield and later.
findings.fix: 'Chrysostom, preaching on 1 Corinthians 12, remarks that the gifts Paul describes no longer occur in his day.'

findings.claim: 'The miraculous sign gifts ended with the apostles or the completion of the New Testament' adopts the cessationist term 'sign gifts' in the quiz's own voice; Pentecostals speak of the gifts or manifestations of the Spirit given 'for the common good'. The direction is correct and a Pentecostal can still answer Strongly disagree, so this is vocabulary, not scoring.
findings.evidence: 1 Cor 12:7; AG Statement of Fundamental Truths art. 7 ('the bestowment of the gifts and their uses in the work of the ministry'); 'sign gifts' is the vocabulary of Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles, and MacArthur, Strange Fire.
findings.fix: 'The miraculous gifts -- tongues, prophecy, and healing -- ended with the apostles or the completion of the New Testament.'

findings.claim: 'Worship should be free-form and led by the Spirit in the moment' is double-barrelled: Pentecostals affirm the second clause and will answer Agree, but AG services follow a recognisable order (worship set, offering, sermon, altar call), so 'free-form' is a caricature of the pole Pentecostals occupy.
findings.evidence: Albrecht, Rites in the Spirit (1999), documents the stable ritual structure of Pentecostal worship; 1 Cor 14:40 ('decently and in order') is cited in AG worship teaching alongside 14:26.
findings.fix: 'Worship should leave room for the Spirit to lead in the moment rather than follow a fixed order.'

findings.claim: 'with an emphasis on spontaneity, sincerity, and the participation of the whole congregation' claims sincerity for the free side, which implies the liturgical side lacks it; the other pole is described without any such contrast. The paragraph also never mentions the exercise of the gifts, which is what makes Pentecostal worship free.
findings.evidence: The liturgical paragraph is descriptive ('a set order, the church calendar, and a weekly Eucharist'); 'sincerity' is evaluative. AG Statement of Fundamental Truths art. 7 and 1 Cor 14:26 ('each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation').
findings.fix: '...with an emphasis on spontaneity, immediacy, and the participation of the whole congregation, including in Pentecostal churches the exercise of the gifts.'

findings.claim: Coordinates [80, 85, 5, 75, 85, 90] are directionally right but sit low on grace and kingdom relative to how an informed AG member answers; the entry lands nearest in the simulation (17.03) but would fit better at grace 85 and kingdom 80.
findings.evidence: Simulation scores grace 92 and kingdom 83; the AG requires a pretribulational rapture of its ministers (Bylaws Art. IX.B) and rejects unconditional election, so typical members answer S2 and S12 at +2. With grace 85 and kingdom 80 the distance becomes sqrt(49+49+25+9+4+4)=sqrt(140)=11.83 (95%) with no change to any other tradition's nearest result (Charismatic non-denom stays at 34.50).
findings.fix: grace 85, kingdom 80 (leave the rest).

findings.claim: The share text fills circles only toward the right pole, so a Pentecostal's Spirit line prints as 'Spirit · Continuationist ○○○○○○○○○○ Cessationist' -- ten empty circles on the axis named 'Spirit' -- and the same 'empty' look hits every left-pole conviction (monergist, sacramental, covenantal, liturgical). The caption ('a monergist shows few filled circles on Grace') confirms the design rather than fixing it.
findings.evidence: shareText(): 'bar += k < f ? "●" : "○"' with f = round(score/10); a score of 0 yields no filled circle. The result card and radar avoid this by plotting a dot, but the copied text, which is what gets pasted, does not.
findings.fix: Render a single marker at the score position, e.g. 'Continuationist ●○○○○○○○○○ Cessationist' via 'bar += (k === Math.min(9, f) ? "●" : "○")', and change the caption to 'The filled circle marks where you sit between the two poles.'

findings.claim: 'firmly synergist' as a headline adjective for an Arminian uses a term that entered theology as a Lutheran and Reformed charge (the 'synergistic controversy'); AG members self-describe as Arminian or Wesleyan, and the lower band already says 'Arminian-leaning'.
findings.evidence: Formula of Concord, Art. II, condemns 'synergism'; Olson, Arminian Theology: Myths and Realities, accepts only the qualified phrase 'evangelical synergism' and warns the bare word is usually pejorative. The pole names may stay ('Monergist'/'Synergist' is the neutral academic pairing), but the headline is what gets screenshotted.
findings.fix: grace bands[4]: 'firmly Arminian' (mirrors 'Reformed-leaning' / 'Arminian-leaning'); keep 'firmly monergist' or change to 'firmly Reformed' for symmetry.

findings.claim: The entry name 'Pentecostal / Assemblies of God' leaves out the Holiness-Pentecostal bodies that share every one of its coordinates -- Church of God (Cleveland) and the Church of God in Christ, the largest Pentecostal denomination in the United States -- and gives no signal that Oneness Pentecostals (UPCI), who make baptism in Jesus' name essential to salvation, are not covered.
findings.evidence: COGIC and Church of God confess Spirit baptism with tongues, believer's baptism, memorial Supper, Arminian soteriology and premillennial return; their only distinctive (entire sanctification as a second work) is not measured by any axis. UPCI Articles of Faith require water baptism in Jesus' name and Spirit baptism with tongues for the new birth, which the Table axis cannot represent.
findings.fix: Rename the entry 'Pentecostal (Assemblies of God, Church of God, COGIC)' and add to the traditions note: 'Oneness Pentecostal bodies are not represented.'

lens: Presbyterian / Reformed (Westminster Standards, Three Forms of Unity)

simulation.headline: Firmly monergist, covenantal, sacramental
simulation.comment: Persona: confessional Presbyterian, spiritual presence (WCF 29.7), paedobaptist, cessationist (WCF 1.1, 1.6), amillennial, regulative principle, fixed order of worship but no prayer book, monthly communion. Raw sums (direction x answer): Grace (-1)(2)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(2) = -6 -> round(0/12*100) = 0. Table (-1)(1)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(2) = -5 -> round(1/12*100) = 8. Spirit (-1)(-2)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-1) = 5 -> round(11/12*100) = 92. Kingdom (1)(-2)+(-1)(2)+(1)(-2) = -6 -> 0. Tradition (-1)(1)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-1) = 2 -> round(8/12*100) = 67. Worship (-1)(0)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(-1) = -1 -> round(5/12*100) = 42. Headline: |score-50| = 50, 42, 42, 50, 17, 8; top three with index tie-break = grace (firmly monergist), kingdom (covenantal), table (sacramental, index 1 beats spirit index 2 on the tie). Distances: Presbyterian/Reformed sqrt(100+729+289+225+484+9) = sqrt(1836) = 42.85 (83%); Lutheran sqrt(400+49+484+225+1024+484) = sqrt(2666) = 51.63 (79%); Reformed Baptist 75.24; Anglican 79.69; Roman Catholic 101.17; Wesleyan 103.66; Eastern Orthodox 113.67; Anabaptist 118.98; Southern Baptist 119.38; Dispensational 137.74; Charismatic 154.53; Pentecostal 167.78. So this persona lands, but only 83% on its own tradition, and 729 of the 1836 squared distance comes from the Table coordinate (35) sitting 27 points from where honest Reformed answers put a person (0-17). A second, equally typical persona FAILS: a Three Forms of Unity member (URCNA/CRC/RCUS/Canadian Reformed) who answers S4 +2 (Belgic 35: Christ truly gives himself, not a bare sign), S13 +2 (Belgic 9 receives the three creeds), S14 +1, S16 +1 (the Church Order's set liturgical forms for baptism and the Supper), S18 0, everything else as above, scores [0, 0, 92, 0, 50, 25] and gets Lutheran (confessional) at sqrt(400+225+484+225+225+25) = 39.80 ahead of Presbyterian/Reformed at sqrt(100+1225+289+225+25+400) = 47.58. Fix: set the Presbyterian/Reformed table coordinate to 15 (the statements cannot separate bodily from spiritual presence, so the coordinate should not pretend they do). With table=15 alone: Continental persona -> P/R sqrt(1264) = 35.55 beats Lutheran 39.80; main persona -> P/R sqrt(1156) = 34.00 (86%). With table=15, spirit=85, tradition=60: main persona -> P/R sqrt(100+49+49+225+49+9) = 21.93 (91%); Continental -> 33.15 vs Lutheran 39.80; Hodge-style persona [0,17,100,8,42,50] -> 26.96 vs 47.98. Self-check: with the new coordinates every tradition's own coordinate point still maps to itself (nearest other: Lutheran at 39.7).

findings.claim: The Table coordinate 35 is 18-35 points from where honest Reformed answers land, and it makes a Three Forms of Unity member land on Lutheran (confessional).
findings.evidence: WCF 29.7 (Christ 'really, but spiritually, present to the faith of believers'), Belgic 35 (not 'a bare and naked sign'), WCF 28.1 and 28.4 (baptism a sign and seal of the covenant; infants of believers to be baptized) give S4 = +1 or +2, S5 = -2, S6 = +2, i.e. raw -5 or -6, score 8 or 0; even a Hodge-style reader who answers S4 'Unsure' scores 17. Nothing in the three Table statements separates Lutheran bodily presence from Reformed spiritual presence, so the 35 encodes a distinction the quiz cannot measure. Arithmetic: Continental persona [0,0,92,0,50,25] -> Lutheran sqrt(400+225+484+225+225+25) = 39.80 < Presbyterian/Reformed sqrt(100+1225+289+225+25+400) = 47.58. With table = 15: P/R sqrt(100+225+289+225+25+400) = 35.55 < 39.80. Main persona [0,8,92,0,67,42]: distance falls from 42.85 to 34.00.
findings.fix: "table": 15 (Lutheran stays at 15; the two traditions are correctly indistinguishable on this axis as written). If you want them separated, add a fourth Table statement such as 'Christ's body and blood are received with the bread and wine by everyone who eats, believer or not' (Lutheran +2, Reformed -2) rather than faking it in the coordinate.

findings.claim: The Spirit coordinate 75 and the Tradition coordinate 45 both sit at the bottom of the range that informed members actually produce, costing a confessional Presbyterian 8-9 match points and putting the overlay dot in the 'balanced on authority' band.
findings.evidence: Spirit: WCF 1.1 ('those former ways of God's revealing his will unto his people being now ceased') and 1.6 ('whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men') make cessation of revelation confessional; typical answers S7 -2, S8 +2, S9 -1 or -2 give 92-100; only an 'open but cautious' minority gives 67. Tradition: WCF 31.2-3 (councils 'to be received with reverence and submission' yet 'may err; and many have erred'), WCF 1.10 and 20.2 give S13 +1, S14 +2, S15 -1 or -2, i.e. 67-75; even the most creed-friendly Continental answers give 50. A coordinate of 45 places the tradition on the 'with tradition' side of center, which no Reformed confession supports. Arithmetic: main persona distance to P/R with table 15/spirit 85/tradition 60 = sqrt(100+49+49+225+49+9) = 21.93 (91%) versus 42.85 (83%) today.
findings.fix: "spirit": 85, "tradition": 60 (together with "table": 15).

findings.claim: 'Reformed-leaning' names one tradition as the owner of monergism and will be pinned on confessional Lutherans, Augustinian Catholics and Reformed Baptists who explicitly reject the 'Reformed' label; 'Arminian-leaning' does the same to Catholics and Orthodox whose synergism predates Arminius by a millennium.
findings.evidence: Formula of Concord, Epitome XI, rejects the Reformed doctrine of reprobation while affirming that election is by grace alone; a confessional Lutheran who answers S1 +1, S2 +2, S3 +2 scores raw -1-2+... = (-1)(1)+(1)(2)+(-1)(2) = -1 -> round(5/12*100) = 42? No: with S1 +2, S2 +2, S3 +2 the raw is -2+2-2 = -2 -> 33, which is band[1] 'Reformed-leaning'. The Lutheran will screenshot that. Every other axis uses doctrinal adjectives (sacramental-leaning, covenantal-leaning, memorial-leaning); only Grace uses tradition names. From our own side, 'Reformed' is a whole theology (covenant, church, worship), not a synonym for the five points.
findings.fix: bands: ["firmly monergist", "monergist-leaning", "balanced on grace", "synergist-leaning", "firmly synergist"].

findings.claim: The middle band 'flexible in worship' is exactly where regulative-principle Presbyterians land (42-50), and it is the one adjective their tradition cannot bear: the regulative principle is the strictest rule of worship in Protestantism.
findings.evidence: WCF 21.1: the acceptable way of worshipping God 'is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men'. Simulation: S16 0, S17 -2, S18 -1 -> raw -1 -> 42 -> 'flexible in worship'; a Hodge-style reader with S16 -1, S18 -1 -> raw 0 -> 50 -> still 'flexible in worship'. The headline could read 'Firmly monergist, cessationist, flexible in worship' for an OPC elder.
findings.fix: bands: ["liturgical", "liturgy-leaning", "ordered in worship", "informal in worship", "free in worship"]. 'Ordered' is true of both the regulative-principle church and a blended evangelical service, and false of neither pole.

findings.claim: The Reformed position falls off this axis: the liturgical pole is defined as 'a set order, the church calendar, and a weekly Eucharist' and the free pole as 'the Spirit can lead in the moment', and the regulative principle (ordered, Scripture-limited, no prayer book, historically no calendar) is neither. The summary never tells a Reformed reader why they landed in the middle.
findings.evidence: Westminster Directory for the Publick Worship of God (1645) deliberately replaced the Prayer Book with a directory rather than a liturgy; WCF 21.1, 21.5 list the commanded elements; the Puritans rejected the church calendar (Directory, appendix: 'Festival days, vulgarly called Holy-days, having no warrant in the word of God, are not to be continued'). Belgic 32 and HC 96 make the same point for the Continental churches.
findings.fix: Append to fair_summary: "A third stream, the Reformed regulative principle, is neither: worship is simple and ordered, limited to what Scripture commands, but bound to no prayer book or calendar. It usually lands near the middle of this axis."

findings.claim: 'Communion should be celebrated every week as the center of the service' is double-barreled: a Reformed reader who agrees with Calvin on weekly communion must still disagree because the preached Word, not the Supper, is the center of Reformed worship.
findings.evidence: Calvin, Institutes IV.17.43-46, wants the Supper 'at least once a week'; WLC 155 and Belgic 29 make the pure preaching of the Word the first mark and chief means; the Westminster Directory says the Supper is to be celebrated 'frequently'. So the frequency clause and the centrality clause pull a Reformed answer in opposite directions, and 'center of the service' is Catholic, Orthodox and Anglo-Catholic vocabulary.
findings.fix: "Communion should be celebrated every week."

findings.claim: 'The church, not the individual reader, is the final interpreter of Scripture' is a false dichotomy for the Reformed, who hold that neither is: Scripture interprets Scripture and the church's role is ministerial. Honest answers scatter from -1 to +1 on the same convictions.
findings.evidence: WCF 1.9: 'the infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself'; WCF 1.10: the supreme judge 'can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture'; WCF 31.2-3: synods do have real, though fallible, authority to settle controversies. Mathison, The Shape of Sola Scriptura (listed in this axis's read-more) is an entire book against 'the individual reader' as final interpreter, yet a Reformed reader who follows Mathison is pushed toward the 'with tradition' pole by this statement.
findings.fix: "The church's official teaching, not Scripture interpreting Scripture, has the final say on what a passage means." (Catholic/Orthodox +2 per Dei Verbum 10 and 12; Reformed -2 per WCF 1.9-10; the individualist alternative is no longer smuggled in.)

findings.claim: 'A person can genuinely resist God's grace and refuse salvation to the very end' can be honestly affirmed by a Calvinist, because the Reformed teach that the non-elect do resist the Spirit's common operations and refuse to the end; only saving, effectual grace cannot be finally resisted.
findings.evidence: WCF 10.4: others not elected 'may have some common operations of the Spirit, yet they never truly come unto Christ'; Acts 7:51 ('you always resist the Holy Spirit') is a standard Reformed prooftext; Canons of Dort III/IV.12 and Rejection of Errors 8 deny only that God's regenerating grace can be frustrated. A careful Reformed reader will answer Disagree, but a fair share will read the plain words and answer Agree, moving Grace from 0 to 17-33.
findings.fix: "God's saving grace can be finally resisted: someone God is drawing to himself can still refuse to the end."

findings.claim: The 'Scripture alone' side is described as holding that 'tradition can be a valuable guide', which is the biblicist position, not the confessional Protestant one. Reformed and Lutheran churches hold that creeds and confessions carry real, subordinate, ministerial authority and require subscription from office-bearers.
findings.evidence: WCF 31.2: decrees of synods, if consonant with the Word, 'are to be received with reverence and submission; not only for their agreement with the Word, but also for the power whereby they are made'; Belgic 9 receives the Apostles', Nicene and Athanasian creeds; Belgic 7 and WCF 1.10 keep Scripture alone infallible. The summary offers only 'God's appointed means... real authority' or 'valuable guide', so the confessional position is described by neither pole.
findings.fix: Replace the second sentence with: "Those who hold to Scripture alone hold that creeds and confessions carry real but subordinate authority as summaries of Scripture, and insist that only Scripture is infallible: any council may err, and no council or teacher can bind the conscience where Scripture is silent or says otherwise."

findings.claim: Because S13 and S15 reward denying any authority to creeds, the 'Scripture alone' band (80+) is reachable only by biblicists, while the Reformation's actual sola scriptura position scores 50-75 and is labelled 'balanced on authority' or 'Scripture-first'. The axis name contradicts its own read-more list.
findings.evidence: Continental persona (Belgic 9, S13 +2) scores 50 -> 'balanced on authority'; Hodge-style persona scores 42 -> the same. Mathison, The Shape of Sola Scriptura (right-pole read-more) distinguishes sola scriptura (Scripture the only infallible authority, read within the creeds) from 'solo scriptura' (no creed has authority), and argues the Reformers held the former; the quiz gives the pole name 'Scripture alone' to the latter.
findings.fix: bands: ["rooted in tradition", "tradition-friendly", "creedal", "Scripture-first", "Scripture alone"], together with the S15 rewrite, so a confessional Protestant lands at 75 'Scripture-first' and a middle score reads as 'creedal' rather than 'balanced'.

findings.claim: The sacramental pole says 'baptism joins a person to Christ and his church, and so the children of believers are baptized', which makes paedobaptism follow from baptismal regeneration. The Reformed baptize infants because of the covenant, and expressly deny that grace is so tied to baptism that everyone baptized is regenerated.
findings.evidence: WCF 28.1: baptism is 'a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, of his ingrafting into Christ'; WCF 28.5: 'grace and salvation are not so inseparably annexed unto it, as that no person can be regenerated or saved without it, or that all that are baptized are undoubtedly regenerated'; WCF 28.4 and HC 74 ground infant baptism in the children being 'included in the covenant and church of God'; Genesis 17:7 and Acts 2:39 are the standard prooftexts. As written, a Reformed reader must accept a description of 'their' pole in Lutheran and Catholic terms.
findings.fix: "The sacramental view holds that God really gives grace through the sacraments: Christ is truly present in the Supper, whether bodily or by the Spirit to faith, and baptism is God's sign and seal that brings a person into Christ's covenant people, which is why the children of believers are baptized."

findings.claim: The middle band 'centered on the sacraments' is a non sequitur: a score of 41-59 means mixed answers (a real-presence credobaptist, a memorialist paedobaptist), not a person more sacrament-centered than the 'sacramental' band at 0-20.
findings.evidence: A 1689 Reformed Baptist answering S4 +2 (LBCF 30.7 'really and indeed... spiritually receive and feed upon Christ'), S5 +2, S6 -2 scores raw 2 -> 67 'memorial-leaning', and one answering S4 +1 scores 58 -> 'centered on the sacraments', which is the opposite of what the answers say. Both a Reformed and a Baptist reader will notice that 'sacramental' < 'centered on the sacraments' makes no sense as a scale.
findings.fix: bands: ["sacramental", "sacramental-leaning", "mixed on the sacraments", "memorial-leaning", "memorialist"].

findings.claim: The list omits the two texts the Reformed actually reach for: 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 for the Supper and Genesis 17:7 for infant baptism. As it stands the sacramental case is John 6 (Catholic) and the paedobaptist case is Acts 2:39 and Colossians 2 only.
findings.evidence: Calvin, Institutes IV.17.10 builds the whole doctrine of spiritual presence on 1 Cor 10:16 ('the cup of blessing... is it not a participation in the blood of Christ?'); WCF 29.7 and Belgic 35 cite it; WCF 28.4 and HC 74 cite Genesis 17:7 and 1 Corinthians 7:14 for the covenant status of children; every Reformed-Baptist debate turns on Genesis 17.
findings.fix: key_passages: ["John 6:53–58", "1 Corinthians 10:16–17", "1 Corinthians 11:23–29", "Genesis 17:7", "Acts 2:38–39", "Colossians 2:11–12", "Romans 6:3–4", "Matthew 26:26–28"].

findings.claim: The history jumps from Chrysostom (c. 390) to Azusa Street (1906) and then presents Warfield (1918) as the first Protestant cessationist, which reads as if cessationism were a twentieth-century reaction to Pentecostalism. It was confessional 270 years earlier.
findings.evidence: WCF 1.1 (1646): 'those former ways of God's revealing his will unto his people being now ceased'; WCF 1.6: nothing is to be added to Scripture 'whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men'; Calvin, Institutes IV.19.18, on the gift of healing having 'vanished away'. Warfield's book is the classic apologetic, not the origin.
findings.fix: Insert before the Warfield entry: { "when": "1646", "what": "Westminster Confession 1.1 and 1.6: the 'former ways of God's revealing his will' have ceased; no new revelations of the Spirit are to be added to Scripture." }

findings.claim: Representing the cessationist side by 'MacArthur, Strange Fire' pairs our position with its most polemical book; the standard Reformed exegetical case is Gaffin.
findings.evidence: Richard Gaffin, Perspectives on Pentecost (1979), is the text Reformed seminaries assign and the one the 'open but cautious' and continuationist Reformed engage; Strange Fire is a conference polemic that continuationists cite as evidence of cessationist unfairness. The continuationist side gets two irenic scholarly titles (Grudem, Storms); the cessationist side gets one scholar and one polemic.
findings.fix: right: ["Gaffin, Perspectives on Pentecost", "Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles"].

findings.claim: 'Frame, Worship in Spirit and Truth' is filed under the 'Free' pole, but Frame is a Westminster Seminary Reformed theologian whose book is a defense of the regulative principle; he is not an advocate of worship 'led by the Spirit in the moment'.
findings.evidence: Frame, Worship in Spirit and Truth (1996), chapters 3-4 restate and defend the regulative principle from WCF 21.1 (broadened in application, but still 'only what God commands'). Listing him as the Free-pole authority tells a Reformed reader that the quiz thinks the regulative principle is free worship.
findings.fix: right: ["Kauflin, Worship Matters", "Liesch, The New Worship"]; if a third-stream entry is wanted, add "Old, Worship: Reformed According to Scripture" under a note on the regulative principle, or under the middle band.

findings.claim: The middle band 'centered on the kingdom' describes no position; a score of 41-59 is a historic premillennialist or progressive dispensationalist with mixed answers, and both poles claim to be 'centered on the kingdom'.
findings.evidence: Ladd (history entry 4) answers S10 0 or +1, S11 +1, S12 -2 -> raw -2 to -1 -> 33-42, so the quiz's own example of the middle position gets 'covenantal-leaning' or 'centered on the kingdom', neither of which is a thing anyone calls themselves.
findings.fix: bands: ["covenantal", "covenantal-leaning", "mixed on Israel and the church", "dispensational-leaning", "dispensational"].

findings.claim: 'A set liturgy that connects us to the historic church' is ambiguous for the Reformed: a Presbyterian with a fixed order of worship but no prayer book, or a Continental church with set forms for baptism and the Supper but free prayer, cannot tell whether to agree.
findings.evidence: The Westminster Directory (1645) prescribes the order and content of worship while forbidding an imposed liturgy; the URCNA/CRC Church Order requires set liturgical forms for the sacraments. Simulation answers range from -1 to +1 on identical convictions, a 17-point swing.
findings.fix: "Worship should follow a fixed liturgy with set prayers shared with the historic church." The Reformed then answer Disagree with confidence and land where the axis intends.

findings.claim: 'The church is the true Israel, heir to every promise' is the wording covenant theologians are accused of ('replacement theology'), not the wording they use; the Reformed say the promises are fulfilled in Christ and the church inherits them in him, and many still expect a future conversion of ethnic Israel.
findings.evidence: Galatians 3:16 ('the seed... who is Christ'), 2 Corinthians 1:20; WLC 191 prays that 'the Jews [be] called'; Murray on Romans 11:26 and Hodge both expect a future large-scale conversion of Israel while remaining fully covenantal. Most Reformed will still answer Agree, but some will hesitate at 'true Israel' and score 8-17 instead of 0.
findings.fix: "In Christ, the church of Jew and Gentile together inherits every promise God made to Abraham."

findings.claim: The cessationist description ends at 'passed away', with no positive statement, which is the continuationist caricature of cessationism as denying that the Spirit still acts.
findings.evidence: WCF 21.3 and James 5:14-16 prooftexts: Reformed cessationists pray for healing and expect answers; Gaffin and Warfield both distinguish extraordinary gifts from the Spirit's ongoing work through Word, sacrament, prayer and providence.
findings.fix: Append: "...and the New Testament was complete, while the Spirit still works powerfully through Word, sacrament, prayer, and providence."

findings.claim: Closing the Spirit history with '2013: Strange Fire conference restates the cessationist case' makes the most combative event the last word for our side, while the continuationist entries are all movements and renewals.
findings.evidence: The standard scholarly marker for the late-20th-century debate is Grudem (ed.), Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views (1996), where Gaffin (cessationist), Saucy (open but cautious), Storms and Oss set out the cases side by side.
findings.fix: { "when": "1996", "what": "Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? sets the cessationist (Gaffin), open-but-cautious (Saucy), and continuationist (Storms, Oss) cases side by side." }

findings.claim: 'His saving grace cannot finally be refused', with nothing about the will being made willing, lets monergism read as coercion; the Reformed confessions are emphatic that the called come freely.
findings.evidence: WCF 10.1: 'yet so, as they come most freely, being made willing by his grace'; Canons of Dort III/IV.12: grace does not treat men 'as senseless stocks and blocks' but makes the will 'itself active'; III/IV.16: grace does not 'take away the will and its properties'.
findings.fix: "...and his saving grace cannot finally be refused, because it makes the unwilling willing, so that those he calls come freely."

findings.claim: Romans 8:28-30, the 'golden chain', is the most-cited Reformed text after Romans 9 and Ephesians 1 and is absent.
findings.evidence: WCF 3.6 and Canons of Dort I.7 and V.8-9 rest perseverance and effectual calling on Romans 8:29-30; Perkins' A Golden Chaine (1591) takes its title from it.
findings.fix: key_passages: add "Romans 8:28–30".

findings.claim: The right pole gets its primary source (Arminius, Works) but the left gets no confessional primary source, although the history line names the Synod of Dort's five points.
findings.evidence: The Canons of Dort (1618-19) are the actual reply to the Remonstrance and the shortest, most readable monergist primary text; Institutes III is 400 pages.
findings.fix: left: ["Canons of Dort", "Calvin, Institutes III.21–24", "Sproul, Chosen by God"].

findings.claim: Dating the Reformed spiritual presence to 'Calvin's final Institutes' (1559) makes it look like one man's late opinion; the Reformed churches united on it in 1549 and confessed it in 1561-63.
findings.evidence: Consensus Tigurinus (1549), Calvin and Bullinger: Christ truly given in the Supper by the Spirit to faith; Belgic Confession 35 (1561); Heidelberg Catechism 75-79 (1563); WCF 29.7 (1646).
findings.fix: { "when": "1549", "what": "Consensus Tigurinus: Calvin and Bullinger unite the Reformed churches on a real presence given by the Spirit and received by faith; confessed in Belgic 35 and Heidelberg 75–79." }

findings.claim: The covenantal description omits the mechanism ('in Christ') and gives no room for the common Reformed expectation of a future conversion of ethnic Israel, so a Reformed reader who holds it may hesitate on S10.
findings.evidence: Galatians 3:16, 29; WLC 191; Murray, Romans 11:26; Hodge, Systematic Theology III.xx.4; the postmillennial wing (Bahnsen, Gentry, Mathison) also expects the kingdom to fill the earth before the return.
findings.fix: "The covenantal view sees one people of God across both testaments: in Christ, the church of Jew and Gentile together inherits the promises to Abraham; Christ's kingdom is present now and, for many, will yet see Israel's large-scale conversion, with his return bringing the new creation."

findings.claim: Galatians 3:16 and Hebrews 8:6-13 are the covenantal texts the dispensationalist debate actually turns on and are absent, while Daniel 9 and 1 Thessalonians 4 (dispensational) are present.
findings.evidence: Horton and Riddlebarger (the left read-more) both argue from Galatians 3:16 (the seed is Christ) and Hebrews 8 (the new covenant promised to Israel is fulfilled in the church).
findings.fix: key_passages: add "Galatians 3:16" and "Hebrews 8:6–13".

findings.claim: '1600s: Puritans articulate the regulative principle' is a century late and mis-attributed; Calvin and the Scottish Reformation articulated it, and the dated landmark is the Westminster Directory of 1645.
findings.evidence: Calvin, The Necessity of Reforming the Church (1543): God 'disapproves of all modes of worship not expressly sanctioned by his Word'; Scots Confession 20 (1560); Westminster Directory for the Publick Worship of God (1645); WCF 21.1 (1646).
findings.fix: { "when": "1543–1645", "what": "Calvin, then the Westminster Directory, set out the regulative principle: worship is ordered by what Scripture commands, without an imposed prayer book." }

findings.claim: None of the regulative-principle texts appear, so the passage list presents the axis as liturgy versus spontaneity only.
findings.evidence: WCF 21.1 prooftexts: Deuteronomy 12:32, Exodus 20:4-6, Matthew 15:9; Leviticus 10:1-3 (Nadab and Abihu) is the sermon text every Reformed hearer knows on this subject.
findings.fix: key_passages: add "Deuteronomy 12:32" and "Leviticus 10:1–3".

findings.claim: The middle response is labelled 'Unsure', but the honest middle answer for a confessional reader on S13, S16 and S18 is 'partly' or 'it depends', not ignorance; being forced to click 'Unsure' on your own tradition's distinctives is a small indignity, and it nudges people toward a pole instead.
findings.evidence: Simulation: S16 requires 'Unsure' from a Presbyterian who is entirely sure worship should be ordered but not bound to a liturgy.
findings.fix: Relabel the 0 option "Neither / it depends" (HTML answers group, data-v="0").

lens: progressive mainline Protestant (PCUSA, ELCA, Episcopal, UMC progressive wing)

simulation.headline: Sacramental, liturgy-leaning, open to the gifts
simulation.comment: Persona: an informed progressive PCUSA/ELCA-type pastor (Barth- and Luther-literate on election, sacramental, not cessationist but not charismatic, amillennial, creedal, service-book worship with communion weekly-to-monthly). Answers in order: S1 0 (Barthian: cannot affirm 'chosen who' particularism, will not deny 'cannot fail'), S2 +1, S3 +1, S4 +2, S5 -2, S6 +2, S7 0 (healing rites yes, 'tongues as in Acts' no), S8 -1, S9 +1, S10 -2, S11 -2 (supersessionism is formally repudiated by PCUSA 1987, ELCA 1994, UMC 1996, TEC 1988), S12 -2, S13 +1, S14 -1, S15 0, S16 +1, S17 -1, S18 +1. Raw: grace (-1*0)+(1*1)+(-1*1)=0 -> 50; table (-1*2)+(1*-2)+(-1*2)=-6 -> 0; spirit (-1*0)+(1*-1)+(-1*1)=-2 -> round(4/12*100)=33; kingdom (1*-2)+(-1*-2)+(1*-2)=-2 -> 33; tradition (-1*1)+(1*-1)+(-1*0)=-2 -> 33; worship (-1*1)+(1*-1)+(-1*1)=-3 -> 25. Headline: |s-50| = 0,50,17,17,17,25 -> table (band 0 'sacramental'), worship (25, band 1 'liturgy-leaning'), then a three-way tie at 17 broken by index to spirit (33, band 1 'open to the gifts'). Distances from (50,0,33,33,33,25): Anglican (broad) sqrt(100+625+144+169+9+25)=sqrt(1072)=32.7 (87%); Roman Catholic sqrt(25+25+49+324+529+225)=sqrt(1177)=34.3 (86%); Eastern Orthodox sqrt(1762)=42.0 (83%); Lutheran (confessional) sqrt(2847)=53.4 (78%); Wesleyan / Methodist sqrt(3077)=55.5 (77%); Presbyterian / Reformed sqrt(1600+1225+1764+324+144+400)=sqrt(5457)=73.9 (70%); Reformed Baptist 103.9; Anabaptist 104.6; Southern Baptist 122.9; Charismatic 123.5; Pentecostal 132.7; Dispensational Bible church 145.1. VERDICT: for an Episcopalian this is right (Anglican first). For a PCUSA Presbyterian it is a screenshot: 'Presbyterian / Reformed' ranks 6th of 12, behind Eastern Orthodox and Wesleyan, because that entry is coded as a PCA/OPC profile (grace 10, spirit 75 cessationist). ELCA variant (S1 +1, S13 +2, S16 +2, S17 -2 -> scores 42,0,33,33,25,8): Roman Catholic sqrt(796)=28.2 first, Anglican 33.3, Orthodox 35.9, Lutheran (confessional) sqrt(2646)=51.4 fourth, driven by that entry's spirit 70 (37^2=1369 of the 2646). A Lutheran pastor landing on Rome is the headline screenshot. Two causes: (a) S11 is worded as replacement theology, costing 33 points on Kingdom; (b) there is no mainline entry. Fixing S11 alone makes it WORSE: with kingdom 0 the PCUSA persona (50,0,33,0,33,25) is nearest Roman Catholic sqrt(1078)=32.8, then Anglican 36.1. FIX: add 'Mainline Protestant (PCUSA / ELCA / UMC)' at grace 45, table 10, spirit 35, kingdom 10, tradition 30, worship 20. Check with S11 fixed: PCUSA persona -> sqrt(25+100+4+100+9+25)=sqrt(263)=16.2 (93%), beating RC 32.8 and Anglican 36.1; ELCA persona (42,0,33,0,25,8) -> sqrt(9+100+4+100+25+144)=sqrt(382)=19.5, beating RC sqrt(697)=26.4; UMC progressive (grace 92, table 8, spirit 33, kingdom 0, tradition 33, worship 25) -> Wesleyan sqrt(2306)=48.0 vs Mainline sqrt(2351)=48.5, both correct as the top two. The new entry does not steal existing prototypes: the Anglican (broad) prototype is 21.2 from it and the Roman Catholic prototype 26.0, each still at distance 0 from its own entry. Even with the current unfixed S11, the PCUSA persona is sqrt(25+100+4+529+9+25)=sqrt(692)=26.3 from the new entry, which already beats Anglican 32.7.

findings.claim: The only positive statement for the covenantal pole is written as replacement theology, which every mainline body (and Rome) has formally repudiated, so the least dispensational Christians in the world are scored 33 points toward Dispensational for rejecting a slur they are on record against.
findings.evidence: Text: "The church is the true Israel, heir to every promise God made to Abraham." PCUSA, A Theological Understanding of the Relationship between Christians and Jews (1987): the church "has been engrafted into the people of God established by the covenant with Abraham" and God's covenant with the Jewish people has not been abrogated. UMC, Building New Bridges in Hope (1996) rejects supersessionism; ELCA, Declaration to the Jewish Community (1994); TEC Guidelines for Christian-Jewish Relations (1988); Nostra Aetate 4 (1965) and the Vatican's The Gifts and the Calling of God Are Irrevocable (2015). Arithmetic: mainline answers S10 -2, S11 -2, S12 -2 -> raw (-2)+(+2)+(-2) = -2 -> 33 'covenantal-leaning'; with a non-supersessionist wording they answer +2 -> raw -6 -> 0. The axis's own fair_summary already says 'the church, Jew and Gentile together, inherits the promises' - the statement contradicts the summary.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Gentile believers are grafted into the one people of God, so there is one covenant people across both testaments rather than two." (Romans 11:17-24; 'engrafted' is the PCUSA's own word.) Direction stays -1.

findings.claim: Mainline Protestantism (PCUSA, ELCA, UMC, UCC, Disciples, ABC-USA; TEC is covered by Anglican (broad)) has no tradition entry, so a PCUSA member lands on 'Anglican (broad) / Roman Catholic' with 'Presbyterian / Reformed' in 6th place, and an ELCA member lands on 'Roman Catholic' first with 'Lutheran (confessional)' 4th.
findings.evidence: Simulation: PCUSA persona (50,0,33,33,33,25): Anglican 32.7, Roman Catholic 34.3, Eastern Orthodox 42.0, Lutheran (confessional) 53.4, Wesleyan 55.5, Presbyterian / Reformed 73.9. ELCA persona (42,0,33,33,25,8): Roman Catholic 28.2, Anglican 33.3, Orthodox 35.9, Lutheran (confessional) 51.4. The intro promises 'See which church families sit closest to your answers' and the list contains 12 families of which 7 are evangelical/confessional and none is mainline, though mainline Protestants are roughly a tenth of US adults (Pew) and the PCUSA (~1.1M) is larger than the PCA (~0.4M).
findings.fix: Add {"name": "Mainline Protestant (PCUSA / ELCA / UMC)", "position": {"grace": 45, "table": 10, "spirit": 35, "kingdom": 10, "tradition": 30, "worship": 20}}. With S11 reworded, the PCUSA persona is 16.2 from it (93%) vs 32.8 from Roman Catholic; the ELCA persona 19.5 vs 26.4; the Anglican and Roman Catholic prototypes remain 21.2 and 26.0 away from it and at 0 from their own entries.

findings.claim: Lutheran monergists (ELCA and LCMS alike) affirm that grace can be resisted while denying any human contribution to conversion, so this statement scores the tradition that coined the monergism/synergism contrast as halfway to synergist.
findings.evidence: Text: "A person can genuinely resist God's grace and refuse salvation to the very end." Formula of Concord SD II (Free Will): the will is purely passive in conversion; SD XI (Election): the lost are lost because they resist and despise the Word, not because God withheld grace.
