A confessional Lutheran answers S1 +1, S2 +2, S3 +2 -> raw -1+2-2 = -1 -> 42 'balanced on grace', 22 points from the coded 20.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Whether a person comes to faith depends in part on their own free choice to accept God's offer of grace." (Direction +1.) Wesleyans and Orthodox agree, Lutherans and Reformed disagree, which is the actual monergist/synergist line.

findings.claim: Monergism is defined by irresistible grace, which is the Calvinist form only; Lutheran monergism is excluded from the pole it named.
findings.evidence: Text: "his saving grace cannot finally be refused." Formula of Concord SD XI rejects irresistibility while SD II denies any cooperation in conversion; the Reformed/Lutheran difference here is the whole substance of the 1586 Montbeliard colloquy and of the intra-Protestant debate on grace.
findings.fix: "Monergists hold that salvation is God's work from beginning to end: he chooses, calls, and keeps his people, and the sinner contributes nothing to conversion, not even the decision to believe. (Reformed monergists add that saving grace cannot finally be refused; Lutheran monergists hold that it can be, without faith becoming a human work.)" Keep the synergist sentence as is.

findings.claim: Double-barreled: 'chosen who will be saved' (particular election) and 'his choice cannot fail' (perseverance) are separate questions, and a Barthian Reformed reader, which is the default in PCUSA seminaries, affirms the second and denies the first.
findings.evidence: Text: "Before anyone does anything, God has already chosen who will be saved, and his choice cannot fail." Barth, Church Dogmatics II/2 s.33: Jesus Christ is the electing God and the elected man; humanity is elected in him. Such a reader can only answer Unsure, which nulls the axis's central item (my simulation: S1 = 0).
findings.fix: "God's choice of who will be saved does not depend on anything he foresees in them." (Direction -1; unconditional election alone.)

findings.claim: Triple-barreled (tongues, prophecy, healing) plus a restorationist clause ('as they did in Acts') that only Pentecostals affirm, so a mainline Christian who has healing rites in the service book is pushed toward the center.
findings.evidence: Text: "Tongues, prophecy, and healing continue in the church today, as they did in Acts." BCP 1979 Ministration to the Sick (laying on of hands and anointing), ELW Service of Healing, PCUSA Book of Common Worship healing services; none of these bodies is cessationist, but none claims Acts-level restoration and most members are agnostic about tongues.
findings.fix: "The Spirit still gives gifts such as prophecy, healing, and tongues in the church today." (Direction -1.)

findings.claim: 'Covenantal' is Westminster's vocabulary, imposed as the name and band label for every non-dispensationalist: Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans, Methodists, and mainliners do not call their eschatology 'covenantal' and Lutherans explicitly decline covenant-of-works theology.
findings.evidence: left_pole "Covenantal", bands "covenantal", "covenantal-leaning"; history:1 "Westminster Confession sets out the covenant of works and the covenant of grace" is the only content given the pole's name. Six of twelve traditions are coded 15-25 on this axis, so the label is stamped on half the list.
findings.fix: left_pole: "One people of God"; right_pole: "Israel and church distinct". Bands: ["one people of God", "leaning to one people of God", "undecided on Israel and the church", "dispensational-leaning", "dispensational"]. Keep 'Dispensational' as the right-pole name if preferred; it is that side's own word.

findings.claim: The middle bands 'centered on the sacraments' and 'centered on the kingdom' read as maximal positions, not midpoints, and 'centered on the kingdom' is the progressive mainline's own self-description handed to the undecided.
findings.evidence: table bands[2] "centered on the sacraments" is what a Catholic at 5 would say of herself; kingdom bands[2] "centered on the kingdom" is Rauschenbusch's and every mainline mission statement's phrase. A user at 50 on Table who answered Unsure three times is told they are 'centered on the sacraments'.
findings.fix: table bands[2]: "between sacrament and memorial"; kingdom bands[2]: "undecided on Israel and the church". Rule for the system: the midpoint band must name the two poles or say 'undecided', never a positive emphasis.

findings.claim: Denominational names are used as band adjectives, and the midpoint band calls a sola-gratia Lutheran 'balanced on grace'.
findings.evidence: bands[1] "Reformed-leaning", bands[3] "Arminian-leaning", bands[2] "balanced on grace". A Thomist Catholic at 30 is not 'Reformed-leaning'; an Orthodox at 70 is not 'Arminian-leaning'; an ELCA member scores 42 by the instrument (see statement:2) and is told grace is something they are balanced about, when Augsburg Confession IV is their whole identity.
findings.fix: ["firmly monergist", "monergist-leaning", "mixed on grace and free will", "synergist-leaning", "firmly synergist"].

findings.claim: The free-worship description claims sincerity and whole-congregation participation as its distinctives, which implies liturgical worship lacks both; liturgy means 'the work of the people' and congregational participation is precisely its claim.
findings.evidence: Text: "with an emphasis on spontaneity, sincerity, and the participation of the whole congregation." Sacrosanctum Concilium 14 (1963): 'full, conscious, and active participation' is the liturgical movement's slogan; the 1979 BCP and ELW are built around congregational responses, and the Kyrie, Sanctus, and Lord's Prayer are sung by the whole assembly.
findings.fix: "with an emphasis on spontaneity, heartfelt expression, and freedom for any member to contribute as the Spirit prompts."

findings.claim: Five of six history lines are dispensationalism's internal story or Westminster; the 20th-century rethinking of Israel and church that defines the mainline (and Catholic) 'one people of God' view, and that keeps it from being replacement theology, is absent.
findings.evidence: History runs Augustine 413, Westminster 1646, Darby 1830s, Scofield 1909, Ladd 1950s, Blaising/Bock 1990s. Nothing on Nostra Aetate (1965), PCUSA (1987), ELCA (1994), UMC (1996), or Barth CD II/2 on Israel and the church. Combined with S11 the reader is left thinking 'one people of God' means the church replaced Israel.
findings.fix: Insert after the 1950s entry: {"when": "1965-96", "what": "Nostra Aetate and later Presbyterian, Lutheran, and Methodist statements affirm that God's covenant with the Jewish people is unrevoked: one people of God, but not by replacement."}

findings.claim: The liturgical pole's history stops at Cranmer 1549 while the free pole gets Finney and Hillsong; the Liturgical Movement, which is the reason a mainline church today has a weekly Eucharist and the church year, is missing.
findings.evidence: History: Didache, Justin, 1549 BCP, 1600s Puritans, 1830s Finney, 1970s Jesus movement. Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963), BCP 1979 (Eucharist as 'the principal act of Christian worship on the Lord's Day'), Lutheran Book of Worship 1978, PCUSA Book of Common Worship 1993, ELCA 'The Use of the Means of Grace' 1997 commending weekly communion.
findings.fix: Insert after the 1830s entry: {"when": "1963-79", "what": "The Liturgical Movement: Vatican II's Sacrosanctum Concilium, the 1979 Book of Common Prayer, and new Lutheran and Presbyterian service books restore the weekly Eucharist and the church year across the mainline."}

findings.claim: The Grace and Spirit coordinates cannot be reached by a confessional Lutheran answering the quiz honestly, which is why an ELCA member (and probably an LCMS one) lands on Roman Catholic instead.
findings.evidence: Coded grace 20, spirit 70. By the instrument a Lutheran answers S1 +1, S2 +2, S3 +2 (Formula of Concord SD II and XI) -> raw -1 -> 42, not 20. The Book of Concord teaches no cessationism; Luther's 1540 prayer for Melanchthon's healing and the ELW healing rite are the tradition's practice; 70 'cautious about the gifts' is a Warfieldian import. ELCA persona distance 51.4, of which 37^2 = 1369 comes from the spirit gap alone.
findings.fix: grace 40, spirit 55. (Adding the mainline entry is still required; this fix is for LCMS/WELS members.)

findings.claim: The entry is coded as a PCA/OPC profile but carries the unqualified name 'Presbyterian', while the largest Presbyterian body in the US is PCUSA; a PCUSA member is 74 points from it.
findings.evidence: grace 10, table 35, spirit 75, worship 45 describe the confessional micro-denominations (Westminster strict subscription, cessationism, regulative principle). PCUSA: Book of Confessions with Barmen and the Confession of 1967, no cessationism, Book of Common Worship. The list already qualifies 'Lutheran (confessional)' and 'Southern Baptist (typical)', so consistency demands the same here. Simulation: distance 73.9, 6th of 12.
findings.fix: Rename to "Presbyterian / Reformed (confessional)" and add the mainline entry proposed under general.

findings.claim: Table 40 places the United Methodist Church, the largest body under this name, 32 points from where its own doctrinal statements put a member.
findings.evidence: UMC, This Holy Mystery (2004): real presence affirmed, weekly celebration encouraged; By Water and the Spirit (1996): infant baptism normative, baptism God's act, not a sign of a prior decision. A UMC member answers S4 +1, S5 -2, S6 +2 -> raw -5 -> 8. Coded 40 is 'centered on the sacraments', which mislabels them as near the memorial midpoint.
findings.fix: table 25 (a compromise if the entry must also cover Nazarene/Wesleyan Church members who allow believer's baptism); a UMC progressive then lands 31.8 from the entry instead of 41.8.

findings.claim: The quiz silently assumes an evangelical/Reformed map: the Kingdom axis is an intra-evangelical debate on which six of twelve traditions sit within 10 points of each other, the Spirit right pole is Warfield's argument, the read-more lists contain no mainline author, and the one question that actually divides PCUSA from PCA, ELCA from LCMS, TEC from ACNA, UMC from GMC (how Scripture is read) is never asked.
findings.evidence: Read-more: of 24 entries, 5 are Catholic/Orthodox (Schmemann x2, Newman, Florovsky), 3 are primary sources (Calvin, Arminius, Zwingli), and 16 are conservative evangelical or confessional Reformed (Sproul, Mathison x2, Schreiner & Wright, Grudem, Storms, MacArthur, Warfield, Horton, Riddlebarger, Ryrie, Blaising & Bock, Barrett, Frame, Kauflin, Olson); zero mainline. Kingdom coordinates: RC 15, EO 15, Lutheran 15, Anglican 20, Presbyterian 15, Wesleyan 25. Confession of 1967 (9.29): Scripture is 'the words of men, conditioned by the language, thought forms, and literary fashions' of its time; the Tradition axis's right pole assumes 'only Scripture is infallible', so a progressive is on neither pole.
findings.fix: Candid scope call: keep the six axes (the Kingdom axis is live for the intended audience and half the tradition list depends on it), but (1) add the mainline tradition entry now, (2) reword S11 and the Kingdom pole names, (3) add at least one mainline title per read-more column, and (4) for a v2, consider a seventh axis 'Scripture: plain and inerrant <-> critically read witness'; without it the quiz cannot distinguish the two halves of any of the four denominational splits of the last fifteen years, though it is also the axis most likely to be worded unfairly, so it should not ship without this kind of review.

findings.claim: Double-barreled: an Episcopalian affirms the first clause (Article VI: nothing not 'read therein, nor may be proved thereby' may be required) and denies the second (creeds and prayer book bind ordinands), and a PCUSA officer vows to be 'guided by' the confessions.
findings.evidence: Text: "Every doctrine must be proven from Scripture alone; tradition can never bind the conscience." Thirty-Nine Articles VI and XX; PCUSA Book of Order W-4.0404 ordination questions.
findings.fix: "No creed, council, or church teaching can bind a Christian's conscience beyond what Scripture itself teaches." (Direction +1.)

findings.claim: 'Led by the Spirit' is set as the contrast to a set liturgy, implying that a collect or a eucharistic prayer is not Spirit-led; liturgical Christians will not accept that framing as their opponents' fair words.
findings.evidence: Text: "Worship should be free-form and led by the Spirit in the moment." Every eucharistic prayer in the BCP, ELW, and Book of Common Worship contains an epiclesis invoking the Spirit.
findings.fix: "Worship should be unscripted, leaving room for spontaneous leading rather than a fixed order."

findings.claim: Double-barreled: weekly celebration and 'the center of the service' are separate claims, and Word-and-Sacrament churches (Reformed, Lutheran, Methodist) hold that the sermon and the table are jointly central.
findings.evidence: Text: "Communion should be celebrated every week as the center of the service." Calvin wanted weekly communion (Institutes IV.17.43-46) while insisting on the preached Word; a PCUSA member who agrees with weekly celebration must still hesitate at 'the center'.
findings.fix: "Communion should be celebrated every week."

findings.claim: The left pole is described with 'the church's teaching office', a magisterium concept, though most people who score left of center on this axis are Protestants (Lutheran 35, Anglican 30, Presbyterian 45) who have creeds and councils but no teaching office.
findings.evidence: Text: "the creeds, councils, and the church's teaching office are God's appointed means of guarding and interpreting his Word."
findings.fix: "the creeds, councils, and the church's historic teaching (and, for Catholics and Orthodox, its teaching office) are the Spirit-guided means by which his Word has been guarded and interpreted, and so carry real authority."

findings.claim: Both left-column titles are confessional Reformed, though the pole covers Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans, Methodists, and mainliners; the most widely read book on 'kingdom present, new creation coming' is not listed.
findings.evidence: left: "Horton, Introducing Covenant Theology", "Riddlebarger, A Case for Amillennialism".
findings.fix: Replace Horton with "N. T. Wright, Surprised by Hope" (or add it as a third entry).

findings.claim: The liturgical column has no mainline Protestant title; the standard seminary textbook across Methodist, Presbyterian, and Lutheran schools is missing.
findings.evidence: left: "Schmemann, Introduction to Liturgical Theology", "Webber, Ancient-Future Worship" (Webber is an evangelical rediscovering liturgy).
findings.fix: Add "James F. White, Introduction to Christian Worship" or "Gordon Lathrop, Holy Things".

findings.claim: The history ends in the 1740s; the most consequential modern reworking of election, which is how the Reformed mainline actually holds the doctrine, is absent.
findings.evidence: History: Augustine, Orange, Luther 1525, Dort 1610-19, Wesley/Whitefield 1740s. Barth, Church Dogmatics II/2 (1942), reworks election christologically and is the reason a PCUSA reader cannot answer S1 as written.
findings.fix: Append: {"when": "1942", "what": "Barth, Church Dogmatics II/2: Jesus Christ is both the electing God and the elected man, and humanity is chosen in him."}

findings.claim: Headline ties are broken by axis index in the code but not in the documented rule, and with only 13 possible scores per axis ties are common; the index rule privileges Grace, Table, and Spirit over Kingdom, Tradition, and Worship.
findings.evidence: JSON headline rule: 'take the three axes with the largest |score - 50|'; code: sort by (b.d - a.d) || (a.i - b.i). Simulation: a three-way tie at 17 between spirit, kingdom, and tradition put 'open to the gifts' in a Presbyterian pastor's headline rather than 'covenantal-leaning' or 'tradition-friendly'.
findings.fix: Document the tie-break in the JSON, and prefer a tie-break that does not depend on axis order (for example, the axis whose score is farther from the nearest tradition's mean, or simply drop tied axes and use two adjectives).

findings.claim: The shareable card and share text carry 'Closest traditions' with no trace of the page's caveat, so the card a PCUSA pastor posts reads 'Closest traditions - Anglican (broad) - Roman Catholic' as a flat verdict.
findings.evidence: HTML: card text 'Closest traditions · ' + near[0].name + ' · ' + near[1].name; share text 'Closest: ' + ...; the caveat 'Approximate positions of typical adherents, not official teaching' appears only in the on-page note.
findings.fix: On the card and in the share text use 'Nearest on the map:' instead of 'Closest traditions', which reads as a description of the person rather than a distance.

simulation.headline: Firmly monergist, cessationist, covenantal
simulation.comment: Answers as a typical informed 1689 subscriber. Grace: (-1)(+2)+(+1)(-2)+(-1)(+2) = -6 -> round(0/12*100) = 0, 'firmly monergist'. Table: (-1)(+1)+(+1)(+1)+(-1)(-2) = +2 -> round(8/12*100) = 67, 'memorial-leaning' (statement 4 answered Agree per LBC 30.7 'really and indeed... spiritually receive and feed upon Christ'; statement 5 answered Agree with a grimace at 'decision'). Spirit: (-1)(-2)+(+1)(+2)+(-1)(-2) = +6 -> 100, 'cessationist'. Kingdom: (+1)(-2)+(-1)(+1)+(+1)(-2) = -5 -> round(1/12*100) = 8, 'covenantal'. Tradition: (-1)(+1)+(+1)(+2)+(-1)(-1) = +2 -> 67, 'Scripture-first'. Worship: (-1)(-1)+(+1)(-2)+(-1)(-1) = 0 -> 50, 'flexible in worship'. Headline: |s-50| = 50,17,50,42,17,0; top three by distance with index tie-break = grace(0), spirit(100), kingdom(8) -> 'Firmly monergist, cessationist, covenantal' (acceptable to us). Distances (squared sums): Reformed Baptist 100+9+400+484+144+225 = 1362 -> 36.91 (85% match); Presbyterian / Reformed 100+1024+625+49+484+25 = 2307 -> 48.03 (80%); Lutheran 77.31; Southern Baptist 86.84; Anabaptist 92.56; Anglican 93.82; Dispensational 104.65; Wesleyan 105.01; Roman Catholic 123.96; Eastern Orthodox 134.95; Charismatic 136.83; Pentecostal 148.87. So the typical pattern lands correctly, but the margin is thin and fragile: the largest contributors to the RB distance are the RB entry's own coordinates on Kingdom (30 vs my 8: 484) and Worship (65 vs my 50: 225) and Spirit (80 vs 100: 400), not my answers. A confession-literal RB who answers Strongly agree to statement 4 (30.7 says 'really and indeed') and Disagree to statement 5 (because baptism is a sign of union with Christ, LBC 29.1, not of 'a decision') gets Table = (-1)(+2)+(+1)(-1)+(-1)(-2) = -1 -> 42, and then lands Presbyterian / Reformed (36.50) ahead of Reformed Baptist (46.23). That is a real adherent landing on the wrong tradition. With the proposed RB coordinates [10,65,90,15,60,50] and Presbyterian table 20, the main pattern gives RB 17.38 (93%) vs Presbyterian 59.09, and the confession-literal pattern gives RB 28.76 vs Presbyterian 42.04, so both land correctly.

findings.claim: The Table axis (poles 'Sacramental' / 'Memorial') is scored by two baptism-subject statements (5, 6) and one Supper statement (4), so a 1689 Reformed Baptist who confesses Christ's spiritual presence at the Supper scores 67 and is told he is 'memorial-leaning'; the share text prints '🍞 Table · Sacramental ●●●●●●●○○○ Memorial'. We explicitly reject the memorial (Zwinglian) view.
findings.evidence: 1689 LBC 30.7: worthy receivers 'do then also inwardly by faith, really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally, but spiritually receive, and feed upon Christ crucified, and all the benefits of his death: the body and blood of Christ being then... spiritually present to the faith of believers in that ordinance'. Arithmetic: statement 4 Agree (-1), statement 5 Agree (+1), statement 6 Strongly disagree (+2) = +2 -> 67. The axis name is 'Table' but two-thirds of its weight is baptismal subjects, so the score does not measure what the pole names say.
findings.fix: Either (a) make the axis measure means-of-grace only: replace statement 5 with a means-of-grace statement (see statement:5) and keep statement 6 as the single baptism-subjects item; or (b) if the current statements stay, rename the right pole 'Ordinance' and the bands to 'sacramental / sacramental-leaning / mixed on the sacraments / ordinance-leaning / memorialist', so a 67 reads 'ordinance-leaning', which a Reformed Baptist would accept.

findings.claim: The memorial pole is defined as holding that 'both are ordinances obeyed by believers rather than channels of grace', yet Reformed Baptists are scored toward that pole while confessing the ordinances are means of grace. The sacramental side is also misdescribed: 'baptism joins a person to Christ and his church, and so the children of believers are baptized' derives infant baptism from sacramental efficacy, which is not the Reformed paedobaptist ground.
findings.evidence: Baptist Catechism (Keach, 1693), Q. 93 (numbering varies by edition): 'The outward and ordinary means whereby Christ communicateth to us the benefits of redemption are his ordinances, especially the Word, Baptism, the Lord's Supper and Prayer; all which are made effectual to the elect for salvation.' LBC 30.1: the Supper is for 'confirmation of the faith of believers... their spiritual nourishment, and growth in him'. For the other side: WCF 28.1 and 28.4 ground infant baptism in the covenant ('infants of one or both believing parents are to be baptized'), not in 'and so'; Lutherans and Catholics ground it in baptismal regeneration. The 'and so' is false for every paedobaptist body.
findings.fix: Replace the summary with: 'The sacramental view holds that God really gives grace through the sacraments: Christ is truly present in the Supper, and baptism is a means by which God joins a person to Christ and his church; most on this side also baptize the children of believers, whether as covenant members or for regeneration. The memorial view holds that the Supper is chiefly a remembrance of Christ's death and baptism a believer's public confession of faith, so both are ordinances obeyed by believers rather than channels of grace. Many Baptists stand between: believer's baptism only, but a Calvinist view that Christ feeds his people spiritually at the Table.'

findings.claim: The middle band 'centered on the sacraments' (41-59) reads like the sacramental pole, not a midpoint, and 'memorial-leaning' (60-79) is exactly where Calvinistic Baptists land. A Reformed Baptist who scores 58 would be screenshotted as 'centered on the sacraments'.
findings.evidence: Simulation with Strongly agree on statement 4: Table = (-1)(+2)+(+1)(+1)+(-1)(-2) = +1 -> 58 -> 'centered on the sacraments'. With Agree: 67 -> 'memorial-leaning'. Neither label describes LBC 30.7 plus 29.2.
findings.fix: bands: ['sacramental', 'sacramental-leaning', 'mixed on the sacraments', 'ordinance-leaning', 'memorialist']

findings.claim: 'Baptism is an outward sign of a decision to follow Christ that has already been made' is revivalist/decisionist vocabulary. Reformed Baptists teach that baptism signifies union with Christ and his work, not the candidate's decision; a confessional reader who answers Disagree on those grounds, and Strongly agree on statement 4, lands nearest 'Presbyterian / Reformed'.
findings.evidence: LBC 29.1: baptism is 'a sign of his fellowship with him, in his death and resurrection; of his being engrafted into him; of remission of sins; and of giving up into God... to live and walk in newness of life'; 29.2 restricts subjects to those who 'actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ'. Nothing about a 'decision'. Arithmetic: answers 4=+2, 5=-1, 6=-2 give Table = -2-1+2 = -1 -> 42; distances then Presbyterian / Reformed 36.50 vs Reformed Baptist 46.23.
findings.fix: Replace with a means-of-grace statement, direction +1: 'Baptism and the Lord's Supper are acts of obedience and testimony; God does not give grace through them.' A Zwinglian Baptist agrees, a Reformed Baptist disagrees (Baptist Catechism Q. 93), a Presbyterian strongly disagrees. Then recalibrate Table coordinates: Lutheran 10, Anglican 25, Presbyterian 20, Reformed Baptist 50, Wesleyan 40, Southern Baptist 90, Dispensational 90, Pentecostal 85, Charismatic 85, Anabaptist 90, Catholic/Orthodox 5. If the statement must stay about subjects, use: 'Only those who have personally professed faith in Christ should be baptized.'

findings.claim: The Reformed Baptist coordinates [10, 70, 80, 30, 55, 65] place us 'covenantal-leaning' on Kingdom, 'informal in worship', and only just 'cessationist'. A 1689 subscriber answering the actual statements scores Kingdom 8, Worship 50, Spirit 100, and those three coordinates account for 1109 of the 1362 squared distance in the simulation.
findings.evidence: Kingdom: LBC ch. 7 is covenant theology ('This covenant is revealed in the gospel... until the full discovery thereof was completed in the New Testament', 7.3); chs. 31-32 teach one general resurrection and one judgment with no rapture or tribulation scheme, and even historic-premillennial Reformed Baptists (Spurgeon, many 17th-century Particular Baptists) answer statements 10 and 12 Disagree, giving 8-25, not 30. Spirit: LBC 1.1 'those former ways of God's revealing his will unto his people being now ceased'; 1.6 forbids 'new revelation of the Spirit'; 90 not 80. Worship: LBC 22.1 (regulative principle) is ordered, simple, and Word-centered, not 'informal'; Reformed Baptist and Presbyterian services are nearly identical in shape, so 50 alongside the Presbyterian 45. Arithmetic with [10, 65, 90, 15, 60, 50]: squared sum 100+4+100+49+49+0 = 302 -> 17.38 (93% match) against 36.91 now; and the confession-literal pattern (Table 42) also lands Reformed Baptist (28.76) ahead of Presbyterian (42.04, with Presbyterian table at 20).
findings.fix: Set Reformed Baptist to grace 10, table 65 (or 50 if statement 5 is replaced), spirit 90, kingdom 15, tradition 60, worship 50.

findings.claim: Presbyterian table = 35 is too far toward 'Memorial'; a WCF 28-29 adherent answering the three Table statements scores 0-17, and the 35 narrows the Reformed Baptist / Presbyterian separation that the Table axis is supposed to provide.
findings.evidence: WCF 29.7 (real spiritual feeding) -> statement 4 Strongly agree (-2); WCF 28.4 -> statement 5 Strongly disagree (-2), statement 6 Strongly agree (-2): raw -6 -> 0; a softer -1/-2 pattern gives 8-17. Simulated typical Presbyterian lands at Table 0 and is 51.65 from its own entry.
findings.fix: Presbyterian / Reformed table: 20.

findings.claim: 'A person can genuinely resist God's grace and refuse salvation to the very end' is literally true on Reformed premises (the non-elect do exactly that, and all people resist the Spirit), so a careful monergist reading it plainly answers Agree and is pushed 17-25 points toward 'Synergist'. The intended sense (grace that God intends to save with can be finally refused) is not stated, and 'resist grace' is the Remonstrant vocabulary.
findings.evidence: Acts 7:51 ('you always resist the Holy Spirit') is a text the Reformed affirm; Canons of Dort III/IV art. 16 deny that grace 'treats men as senseless stocks and blocks' and the Canons never use the word 'irresistible'. LBC 10.1: the effectually called 'come most freely, being made willing by his grace'. Arithmetic: statement 2 answered Agree instead of Strongly disagree moves Grace from 0 to 25 and the headline from 'Firmly monergist' to 'Reformed-leaning'.
findings.fix: 'Someone God is drawing to himself can still finally refuse, so that no one is saved without their own free consent.' (direction +1)

findings.claim: 'The creeds and councils of the early church carry real authority, not just historical interest' does not distinguish ministerial (subordinate) authority from magisterial authority. Every confessional Protestant, Reformed Baptists included, answers Agree and is pushed toward 'With tradition', whose summary defines that pole as the church's teaching office being 'God's appointed means... and so carry real authority'.
findings.evidence: LBC 1.10: 'all decrees of councils, opinions of ancient writers, doctrines of men, and private spirits, are to be examined' by Scripture; yet the same body binds its officers to a 32-chapter confession that reaffirms Nicene and Chalcedonian doctrine (chs. 2, 8). Real but subordinate authority is our position, and the statement cannot register it. Simulated effect: Agree costs 8 points and lands us 'Scripture-first' rather than 'Scripture alone', which is our formal principle.
findings.fix: 'The early creeds and councils carry an authority of their own, not only as faithful summaries of what Scripture teaches.' (direction -1) Catholics and Orthodox agree; confessional Protestants disagree.

findings.claim: 'The church, not the individual reader, is the final interpreter of Scripture' is a false dichotomy for the Reformed, who deny both options.
findings.evidence: LBC 1.9: 'The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself'; 1.10: the supreme judge is 'the Holy Scripture delivered by the Spirit'. A Reformed Baptist in a confessional church with elders does not think the individual is the final interpreter either, and may answer Unsure.
findings.fix: 'The church's teaching office can settle the meaning of Scripture with an authority the individual reader must accept.' (direction -1)

findings.claim: 'The church is the true Israel, heir to every promise God made to Abraham' uses the phrasing dispensationalists use to caricature us ('replacement theology'), and 'every promise' trips 1689 Federalists, who distinguish the typological national promises fulfilled under the old covenant from the promise fulfilled in Christ.
findings.evidence: Nehemiah Coxe, A Discourse of the Covenants (1681), and the 1689 Federalism reading of Galatians 3:16 ('to your offspring, who is Christ'): Christ is the true Israel and the church is Israel in him. LBC 7.3 has the covenant of grace revealed 'by farther steps' rather than the church simply inheriting the Abrahamic administration.
findings.fix: 'In Christ, the church, Jew and Gentile together, inherits the promises God made to Abraham.' (direction -1)

findings.claim: 'Worship should follow a set liturgy that connects us to the historic church' is loaded: disagreeing implies wanting no connection to the historic church. Regulative-principle churches disagree with the set liturgy and would object to the implication.
findings.evidence: LBC 22.1 limits worship to what is 'prescribed in the Holy Scriptures', and the Puritans rejected the Book of Common Prayer on precisely that ground while claiming continuity with the apostolic church; Reformed Baptist congregations sing psalms and recite the creeds.
findings.fix: 'Worship should follow a fixed written liturgy, such as a prayer book, used week by week.' (direction -1)

findings.claim: 'Communion should be celebrated every week as the center of the service' is double-barreled (frequency and centrality). A growing number of 1689 churches hold a weekly Supper but a Word-centered service, and cannot answer.
findings.evidence: LBC 30 prescribes no frequency; LBC 22.5 lists 'the reading of the Scriptures, preaching, and hearing the Word of God' first among the parts of worship, with the ordinances alongside. The centrality question is the liturgical distinctive; the frequency question is not.
findings.fix: 'The Lord's Table, more than the sermon, should be the center of the weekly service.' (direction -1)

findings.claim: The Liturgical/Free axis has no place for the regulative principle, so a Reformed Baptist lands at 50 and is labeled 'flexible in worship', and the tradition entry at 65 reads 'informal in worship'. Both are the opposite of a regulative-principle service.
findings.evidence: Simulation: statement 16 Disagree (+1), 17 Strongly disagree (-2), 18 Disagree (+1) = 0 -> 50 -> 'flexible in worship'. LBC 22.1: God 'may not be worshipped according to the imagination and devices of men... or any other way not prescribed in the Holy Scriptures'. That is the least flexible position on the axis.
findings.fix: bands: ['liturgical', 'liturgy-leaning', 'between set forms and free', 'informal in worship', 'free in worship']; and set the Reformed Baptist worship coordinate to 50.

findings.claim: The summary describes only prayer-book liturgy and Spirit-led spontaneity. The Puritan/Reformed 'regulative principle' worship that most Presbyterians and Reformed Baptists practice is neither, and readers who land mid-axis get no description of their own view even though the history line for the 1600s names it.
findings.evidence: LBC 22.1 and 22.5; WCF 21.1 and 21.5 identical in substance: a simple, fixed order of Scripture-commanded elements (reading, preaching, prayer, singing, the ordinances) without a prescribed liturgy or spontaneous forms.
findings.fix: Append: 'Between them, churches shaped by the Puritan regulative principle keep a simple, fixed order of the elements Scripture commands (reading, preaching, prayer, singing, baptism and the Supper) without a prayer book and without improvisation.'

findings.claim: The history jumps from Chrysostom (c. 390) to Azusa Street (1906) and Warfield (1918), then Strange Fire (2013), which makes cessationism look like a 20th-century reaction to Pentecostalism. It was the confessional Protestant position for 250 years before Azusa Street.
findings.evidence: WCF 1.1 (1646) and LBC 1.1 (1677/1689): 'those former ways of God's revealing his will unto his people being now ceased'; LBC 1.6: nothing to be added 'whether by new revelation of the Spirit, or traditions of men'. Calvin, Institutes IV.19.18-19, treats the gift of healing as having ceased.
findings.fix: Insert after the c. 390 entry: {when: '1646 / 1689', what: 'Westminster and London Baptist Confessions (1.1): God\'s former ways of revealing his will are "now ceased".'}

findings.claim: The cessationist description omits what cessationists affirm, and so invites the caricature that we deny God heals or works miracles today.
findings.evidence: Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles, distinguishes the charismata of the apostolic age from God's ongoing providential and answered-prayer working; LBC 5 (providence) and James 5:14-16 are preached in every cessationist church.
findings.fix: Append to the cessationist sentence: ', while God still heals and acts in answer to prayer and the Spirit's ordinary work of illumination and sanctification continues.'

findings.claim: 'MacArthur, Strange Fire' is the most polemical title on the cessationist shelf and is the one continuationists will screenshot; a fairer flagship exists, including one by a Reformed Baptist.
findings.evidence: Gaffin, Perspectives on Pentecost (1979) is the standard exegetical case; Waldron, To Be Continued? (2005) is the Reformed Baptist statement.
findings.fix: right: ['Gaffin, Perspectives on Pentecost', 'Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles'] (or Waldron, To Be Continued?)

findings.claim: The Table passages include two paedobaptist reaches (Acts 2:38-39, Colossians 2:11-12) but none of the credobaptist reaches, and omit 1 Corinthians 10:16, the text the Reformed spiritual-presence view rests on. The page promises 'the passages each side reaches for'.
findings.evidence: LBC 30.7 cites 1 Corinthians 10:16 ('a participation in the blood of Christ'). Credobaptist argument: Acts 2:41, Acts 8:36-38, Matthew 28:19-20, 1 Peter 3:21, and Jeremiah 31:31-34 / Hebrews 8:6-12 ('they shall all know me'), the key text of Baptist covenant theology.
findings.fix: key_passages: ['1 Corinthians 10:16-17', '1 Corinthians 11:23-29', 'John 6:53-58', 'Acts 2:38-41', 'Acts 8:36-38', 'Colossians 2:11-12', 'Jeremiah 31:31-34']

findings.claim: The only Baptist marker on the Table timeline is '1525 First believer's baptisms in Zurich; the Anabaptist movement begins', which implies English Particular Baptists descend from the Anabaptists. They arose from Puritan separatism and said so, and their confession puts a Calvinist Supper inside a credobaptist body, which is the whole point this axis mis-scores.
findings.evidence: First London Confession (1644) title page: 'commonly (though falsely) called Anabaptists'; 1689 LBC 29.4 (immersion) with 30.7 (spiritual presence).
findings.fix: Add a sixth entry after 1559: {when: '1644 / 1689', what: 'The Particular Baptists\' London Confessions: believer\'s baptism by immersion, with Christ "spiritually present to the faith of believers" at the Supper.'}

findings.claim: No read-more title represents believer's baptism with a Reformed view of the Supper; the credobaptist shelf is Zwingli plus a baptism monograph, and the spiritual-presence title (Mathison) is filed under the paedobaptist pole.
findings.evidence: Waldron, A Modern Exposition of the 1689 Baptist Confession of Faith (ch. 30); Hercules Collins, An Orthodox Catechism (1680), a Baptist edition of the Heidelberg Catechism with its Supper doctrine intact.
findings.fix: right: ['Schreiner & Wright, Believer\'s Baptism', 'Waldron, A Modern Exposition of the 1689 Baptist Confession'] and keep Zwingli if a third slot exists.

findings.claim: '1646 Westminster Confession sets out the covenant of works and the covenant of grace' is the only covenantal marker, which implies covenant theology is paedobaptist property and helps explain the RB entry sitting at 30.
findings.evidence: Nehemiah Coxe, A Discourse of the Covenants (1681); 1689 LBC ch. 7 and 20 (covenant of grace 'revealed in the gospel').
findings.fix: Change to: {when: '1646 / 1689', what: 'Westminster and London Baptist Confessions set out the covenant of works and the covenant of grace; Particular Baptists give covenant theology a credobaptist form.'}

findings.claim: Both covenantal titles (Horton, Riddlebarger) are Presbyterian; a Reformed Baptist reader is sent only to paedobaptist covenant theology.
findings.evidence: Denault, The Distinctiveness of Baptist Covenant Theology (2013); Renihan, The Mystery of Christ, His Covenant, and His Kingdom (2019).
findings.fix: left: ['Horton, Introducing Covenant Theology', 'Renihan, The Mystery of Christ, His Covenant, and His Kingdom']

findings.claim: 'centered on the kingdom' (41-59) says nothing about where a person stands between covenantal and dispensational readings.
findings.evidence: All five bands should describe a position on the axis; this one describes neither pole and is not a midpoint.
findings.fix: bands[2]: 'mixed on Israel and the church'

findings.claim: 'Christ's kingdom is present now, with his return bringing the new creation' equates the covenantal pole with amillennialism, leaving covenantal historic-premillennialists and postmillennialists (both common among Reformed Baptists) without a home on their own side.
findings.evidence: Spurgeon and many 17th-century Particular Baptists (Knollys, Keach) were premillennial covenant theologians; the history line for Ladd concedes the position exists.
findings.fix: '...and Christ's kingdom is present now, whatever they hold about a future millennium, with his return bringing the new creation.'

findings.claim: The Scripture-alone side of the timeline begins in 1646; the Reformation is absent. Every Protestant reader will notice that Worms is missing from a history of sola scriptura.
findings.evidence: Luther at the Diet of Worms, 1521: conscience 'captive to the Word of God'; the formal principle of the Reformation predates Westminster by 125 years.
findings.fix: Insert before Trent: {when: '1521', what: 'Luther at Worms: unless convinced by Scripture, his conscience is captive to the Word of God.'}

findings.claim: The Scripture-alone description ('tradition can be a valuable guide') reads as solo scriptura; confessional Protestants hold that creeds and confessions carry real, subordinate authority, which is the distinction Mathison's recommended book exists to make.
findings.evidence: LBC 1.10 examines councils by Scripture yet Reformed Baptist churches require confessional subscription of officers; WCF 31.3 (synods' decisions 'to be received with reverence and submission... if consonant to the Word of God').
findings.fix: '...agree that creeds, confessions, and the church's teaching carry a real but subordinate authority, but insist that only Scripture is infallible...'

findings.claim: 'his saving grace cannot finally be refused' without the confessional 'made willing' clause leaves the monergist open to the coercion caricature that the synergist sentence implicitly trades on.
findings.evidence: LBC 10.1: the called 'come most freely, being made willing by his grace'; Dort III/IV art. 16 rejects the 'stocks and blocks' reading.
findings.fix: '...and his saving grace cannot finally be refused, because it makes the unwilling willing so that they come freely.'

findings.claim: Romans 8:28-30, the 'golden chain', is the monergist reach alongside Romans 9 and is absent; statement 3 (faith as gift) has no supporting passage in the list.
findings.evidence: Every Reformed treatment from Calvin, Institutes III.21-24, to Sproul cites Romans 8:29-30; faith as gift is argued from Ephesians 2:8-9 and Philippians 1:29.
findings.fix: Add 'Romans 8:28-30' and 'Ephesians 2:8-9'; drop one of Hebrews 6:4-6 or 2 Peter 3:9 if the list must stay at six.

findings.claim: 'Reformed-leaning' names a tradition rather than a position; confessional Lutherans are monergists and would refuse the label, which weakens the 'both sides fair' promise even though it does not hurt us.
findings.evidence: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration II (Free Will) is monergist on conversion while rejecting Reformed predestinarianism; the Lutheran entry sits at grace 20, i.e., inside the 'Reformed-leaning' band.
findings.fix: bands: ['firmly monergist', 'leaning monergist', 'balanced on grace', 'leaning synergist', 'firmly synergist']

findings.claim: 'Tongues, prophecy, and healing continue in the church today, as they did in Acts' is loaded against moderate continuationists (who deny today's prophecy equals apostolic prophecy) and its 'healing' clause blurs the cessationist affirmation that God still heals.
findings.evidence: Grudem, The Gift of Prophecy, argues New Testament congregational prophecy is not Acts-level revelation; Warfield distinguishes gifts of healing from God's healing in answer to prayer.
findings.fix: 'The gifts of tongues, prophecy, and healing are still given to the church today.' (direction -1)

findings.claim: There is no landing place for Calvinistic Baptists who are continuationist (Sovereign Grace, Piper-style), which is probably why the Reformed Baptist entry is hedged to spirit 80; adding that entry frees the Reformed Baptist coordinate to reflect the 1689 position.
findings.evidence: Simulation with spirit 90 for Reformed Baptist improves the confessional match from 85% to 93%; a Reformed charismatic entry at [15, 75, 15, 25, 65, 75] would catch the users who currently pull the Reformed Baptist entry leftward.
findings.fix: Add {name: 'Reformed charismatic (Sovereign Grace / Newfrontiers)', position: {grace: 15, table: 75, spirit: 15, kingdom: 25, tradition: 65, worship: 75}} and set Reformed Baptist spirit to 90.

lens: Reformed charismatic (John Piper, Wayne Grudem, Sam Storms, Sovereign Grace Churches, Acts 29 continuationists)

simulation.headline: Firmly monergist, continuationist, covenantal
simulation.comment: Answers as a typical Sovereign Grace / Bethlehem / Acts 29 continuationist: S1 +2, S2 -2 (reading 'God's grace' as effectual grace, see finding on statement 2), S3 +2; S4 +1 (Calvin's spiritual presence, Grudem ST ch. 50), S5 +1, S6 -2; S7 +2, S8 -2, S9 +2; S10 -1, S11 +1, S12 -2; S13 +1 (creeds have real but subordinate authority), S14 +2, S15 -1; S16 -1, S17 0 (planned AND Spirit-led, so the double-barrel forces Unsure), S18 -1. Raw sums (direction x answer): Grace (-1)(2)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(2) = -6 -> round(0/12*100) = 0. Table (-1)(1)+(1)(1)+(-1)(-2) = +2 -> round(8/12*100) = 67. Spirit (-1)(2)+(1)(-2)+(-1)(2) = -6 -> 0. Kingdom (1)(-1)+(-1)(1)+(1)(-2) = -4 -> round(2/12*100) = 17. Tradition (-1)(1)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-1) = +2 -> 67. Worship (-1)(-1)+(1)(0)+(-1)(-1) = +2 -> 67. Headline: |score-50| = 50, 17, 50, 33, 17, 17, so grace (band 0 'firmly monergist'), spirit (band 0 'continuationist'), kingdom (17, band 0 'covenantal'): 'Firmly monergist, continuationist, covenantal' -- this label is accurate and a member would happily share it. Distances (sum of squared diffs -> d -> match = round(100 - d/244.95*100)): Reformed Baptist 100+9+6400+169+144+4 = 6826 -> 82.6 -> 66%; Presbyterian / Reformed 100+1024+5625+4+484+484 = 7721 -> 87.9 -> 64%; Charismatic non-denominational 4900+169+25+1849+324+529 = 7796 -> 88.3 -> 64%; Anglican (broad) 8976 -> 94.7; Anabaptist / Mennonite 9201 -> 95.9; Wesleyan / Methodist 10431 -> 102.1; Pentecostal / AoG 10966 -> 104.7; Southern Baptist 11116 -> 105.4; Lutheran 11241 -> 106.0; Roman Catholic 14971 -> 122.4; Dispensational Bible church 16906 -> 130.0; Eastern Orthodox 16986 -> 130.3. What went wrong: the nearest entry differs from me by 80 points on Spirit (the largest gap the axis allows) and the runner-up by 75; the share card tells a Sovereign Grace member 'Closest: Reformed Baptist · Presbyterian / Reformed', two cessationist families, with a 66% ceiling that is the lowest any real movement gets from this list. Second place is a coin flip: Presbyterian beats Charismatic non-denominational by 0.4 of a distance unit, and changing S17 from Unsure to Agree (worship 67 -> 75) reorders to Reformed Baptist 83.2, Charismatic non-denominational 86.6, Presbyterian 90.2. Fix: add 'Reformed charismatic' at {grace 10, table 65, spirit 10, kingdom 20, tradition 60, worship 70}: distance from my scores 100+4+100+9+49+9 = 271 -> 16.5 -> 93%. It does not poach neighbours: the Reformed Baptist coordinate is 71.2 from it (0 from itself), Presbyterian 77.5, Charismatic non-denominational 80.5, Pentecostal 96.8.

findings.claim: The tradition list has no monergist-continuationist entry, so the coordinates encode a Grace-Spirit correlation that does not exist theologically, and a Reformed charismatic cannot land anywhere honest.
findings.evidence: Every monergist entry is cessationist-leaning (Lutheran grace 20 / spirit 70; Presbyterian 10 / 75; Reformed Baptist 10 / 80) and both continuationist entries are synergist (Pentecostal grace 80 / spirit 5; Charismatic non-denominational 70 / 5). The quadrant grace <= 20 and spirit <= 20 is empty. Real, sizable movement lives there: Sovereign Grace Churches (Statement of Faith affirms unconditional election and effectual calling and that all New Testament gifts continue), Newfrontiers, Acts 29 (Reformed soteriology, explicitly not cessationist), Bethlehem Baptist under Piper, Grudem's Systematic Theology (the best-selling evangelical systematic, continuationist), Storms. Dort and Westminster say nothing that ties election to cessation. Simulation: (0, 67, 0, 17, 67, 67) lands on Reformed Baptist at 82.6 (66%) and Presbyterian at 87.9 (64%), both 75-80 points away on Spirit; runner-up is a 0.4-unit tie with Charismatic non-denominational.
findings.fix: Add {"name": "Reformed charismatic", "position": {"grace": 10, "table": 65, "spirit": 10, "kingdom": 20, "tradition": 60, "worship": 70}}. Distance from the simulated member: 271 -> 16.5 -> 93%. Distances from existing coordinates to the new point: Reformed Baptist 71.2, Presbyterian 77.5, Charismatic non-denominational 80.5, Pentecostal 96.8, so no existing family is captured.

findings.claim: 'A person can genuinely resist God's grace and refuse salvation to the very end' does not say which grace, so an informed Calvinist can honestly agree and be mis-scored toward synergism.
findings.evidence: Reformed theology affirms that the non-elect resist the external call to the end: Canons of Dort III/IV art. 9 (those called through the ministry of the word 'refuse to come'), WCF 10.4 (the non-elect 'may be called by the ministry of the Word... yet they never truly come'), Acts 7:51. Only effectual (saving) grace is 'irresistible'. Arithmetic: a five-point Calvinist who answers Agree here scores raw -3 -> 25 -> 'Reformed-leaning' instead of 0 -> 'firmly monergist', and moves 25 points toward Wesleyan/Anglican in the distance table.
findings.fix: Even someone God is drawing to himself can finally refuse him and be lost.

findings.claim: 'God's promises to national Israel will be fulfilled literally in a future earthly kingdom' is double-barreled: Israel/church distinction plus a future earthly kingdom, and historic premillennialists hold the second without the first.
findings.evidence: Piper, Grudem (Systematic Theology ch. 55) and Ladd, whom this axis's own history cites at 1950s, expect an earthly millennial reign of Christ and a future conversion of ethnic Israel (Rom 11:26) while denying a separate national program; they cannot answer without conceding a dispensational distinctive they reject. The Israel/church question is already covered by statement 11.
findings.fix: Old Testament promises to Israel (land, throne, temple) must be fulfilled literally to ethnic Israel, not fulfilled in Christ and the church.

findings.claim: 'Worship should be free-form and led by the Spirit in the moment' yokes two things my tradition splits: we reject 'free-form' and affirm 'led by the Spirit in the moment'.
findings.evidence: Kauflin, Worship Matters (cited by the quiz on this pole) has a chapter 'Planned and Spontaneous' arguing for both; Sovereign Grace and Acts 29 services are carefully planned (call to worship, songs, confession, sermon, Supper) with room for prophetic contributions per 1 Cor 14:26-33. The honest answer is Unsure, which throws away the information.
findings.fix: Worship should leave room for the Spirit to lead in the moment rather than follow a set script.

findings.claim: 'Communion should be celebrated every week as the center of the service' bundles frequency with centrality; Reformed people who follow Calvin on weekly communion but keep the preached Word central cannot answer.
findings.evidence: Calvin, Institutes 4.17.43-46, argues for the Supper 'at least once a week' while the sermon remains central; a growing number of Acts 29 and Reformed Baptist congregations do exactly this. The discriminating question between the poles is what sits at the center, not how often.
findings.fix: The Lord's Supper, not the sermon, should be the center of the Sunday service.

findings.claim: 'Sacramental' vs 'Memorial' folds two independent questions (Christ's presence in the Supper; who is baptized) into one axis, so the Calvinistic credobaptist position held across my tradition has no place and is scored into a meaningless middle.
findings.evidence: 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7: worthy receivers 'spiritually receive, and feed upon Christ crucified'; Grudem, Systematic Theology ch. 50 (spiritual presence); Piper likewise; all credobaptist. Arithmetic: S4 +2, S5 +1, S6 -2 -> raw +1 -> 58 -> 'centered on the sacraments' (nonsense for a Baptist); S4 +1 -> 67 -> 'memorial-leaning' (denies what they affirm about the Supper).
findings.fix: Keep the axis but say so: add to the fair summary 'Between them stand many Reformed Baptists and evangelicals who hold Christ's spiritual presence in the Supper yet baptize only believers', and relabel the middle band (see labels finding).

findings.claim: 'baptism joins a person to Christ and his church, and so the children of believers are baptized' gives the Reformed paedobaptist a Lutheran/Catholic baptismal-regeneration rationale, and 'rather than channels of grace' denies Reformed Baptists a view they confess.
findings.evidence: WCF 28.1 calls baptism 'a sign and seal of the covenant of grace'; 28.5 says grace 'is not so inseparably annexed unto it' that all the baptized are regenerated; Larger Catechism Q166 baptizes infants because they are 'within the covenant'. Heidelberg Q74 likewise. The 'and so' is therefore not their argument. On the other pole, 1689 LBC 30.7 and Grudem ST ch. 50 hold that Christ spiritually nourishes believers at the table. As my tradition's opponents are misdescribed, our people would end up arguing against a straw man.
findings.fix: Sacramental: 'Christ is truly present in the Supper, baptism is a sign and seal of God's covenant promise (for some, the very means of new birth), and so the children of believers are baptized.' Memorial: 'the Supper is a remembrance of Christ's death and baptism a public confession of a faith already held, so both are ordinances for believers; some who hold this still speak of Christ nourishing his people spiritually at the table.'

findings.claim: All three baptism passages listed are paedobaptist proof-texts; the credobaptist case is absent.
findings.evidence: 'Acts 2:38-39' (the promise 'for you and for your children') and 'Colossians 2:11-12' (circumcision/baptism) are the standard infant-baptism texts; Romans 6:3-4 is shared. Schreiner & Wright, Believer's Baptism, which the quiz cites, rests its case on Jeremiah 31:31-34 / Hebrews 8 (all new-covenant members know the Lord), Acts 8:36-38, Galatians 3:26-27 and 1 Peter 3:21. The result page promises 'the passages each side reaches for'.
findings.fix: Add 'Jeremiah 31:31-34' and 'Acts 8:36-38'; drop 'Matthew 26:26-28' if the list must stay at six (it duplicates 1 Corinthians 11).

findings.claim: The band 'Scripture alone' (>= 80) is reachable only by denying the creeds any real authority, so the Reformation slogan is handed to biblicists while confessional Protestants get the un-owned label 'Scripture-first'.
findings.evidence: Confessional answers (S13 Agree, S14 Strongly agree, S15 Disagree) give raw +2 -> 67 -> 'Scripture-first'. Mathison, The Shape of Sola Scriptura (cited by the quiz on this pole), distinguishes sola scriptura (Scripture the only infallible norm, creeds carrying real subordinate authority) from solo scriptura (no creed but the Bible); the quiz labels Mathison's own position 'Scripture-first' and gives 'Scripture alone' to the view his book argues against.
findings.fix: bands: ["rooted in tradition", "tradition-friendly", "mixed on authority", "Scripture alone", "Scripture only"].

findings.claim: The Tradition history is four entries for the tradition pole (Vincent, Trent, Newman, Dei Verbum) against one for Scripture alone (Westminster).
findings.evidence: history array: 434 Vincent, 1546 Trent, 1646 WCF, 1845 Newman, 1965 Dei Verbum. The intro promises 'both sides of every axis get a fair hearing'. The defining Scripture-alone moment is Luther at Worms, 1521, and the 1521 gap is also what makes the 1546 Trent line read as unprovoked.
findings.fix: Insert before the 1646 entry: {"when": "1521", "what": "Luther at Worms refuses to recant unless convinced by Scripture and plain reason: his conscience is captive to the Word of God."}

findings.claim: 'Free worship keeps the form open so that the Spirit can lead in the moment, with an emphasis on spontaneity, sincerity, and the participation of the whole congregation' describes revivalist spontaneity only, contradicts the pole's own read-more and history, and 'sincerity' implies liturgical worship is less sincere.
findings.evidence: The right-pole read-more is Frame, Worship in Spirit and Truth (a defense of the regulative principle) and Kauflin, Worship Matters (planned services, 'Rooted and Relevant'); the history's 1600s line is the Puritan regulative principle. None of these is 'spontaneity'. Sovereign Grace and Bethlehem worship is Word-regulated and planned with room for the Spirit. A Prayer Book Anglican would screenshot 'sincerity'.
findings.fix: Free worship holds that Scripture prescribes the elements of worship (the Word read and preached, prayer, song, the ordinances) but no fixed script, so each service can be shaped freshly, with room for the Spirit to lead in the moment and for the whole congregation to take part.

findings.claim: 'informal in worship' (60-79) is a judgement about manner, not form, and lands in the headline of people whose worship is planned and reverent.
findings.evidence: My simulated member scores 67 here; a Sovereign Grace member whose worship pastor wrote Worship Matters would be sharing a card reading 'informal in worship'. The mirror band on the other side is 'liturgy-leaning', which is descriptive, not evaluative.
findings.fix: bands[3]: "free-leaning in worship".

findings.claim: The Spirit history has no entry for the third wave, the movement that produced every Reformed continuationist the quiz cites, so continuationism reaches the reader as Azusa plus mainline/Catholic renewal, always non-Reformed.
findings.evidence: Wagner coined 'third wave' in 1983 for Wimber's Vineyard and evangelicals embracing the gifts without Pentecostal second-blessing theology; Grudem, The Gift of Prophecy in the New Testament and Today (1988); Piper's 1990-91 sermons on gifts; Sovereign Grace (PDI, 1982) and Newfrontiers; Grudem ed., Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? (1996). The axis's own read-more (Grudem, Storms) belongs to this stream, which the history never mentions.
findings.fix: Insert before the 2013 entry: {"when": "1980s-90s", "what": "The 'third wave' (Wimber's Vineyard; Grudem, Storms, Piper) brings the gifts into Reformed and evangelical churches without Pentecostal second-blessing theology."}

findings.claim: Between the 2nd century and 1906 the history offers only cessationist data (Montanist wariness, Chrysostom), which is the cessationist storyline that the gifts vanished early.
findings.evidence: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.32.4 (c. 180), reports prophecy, healing and exorcism continuing in the churches; Augustine, City of God 22.8 (c. 426), records healings at Hippo and in Retractationes 1.13.7 withdraws his earlier statement that miracles had ceased. Both are the continuationist historical anchors used by Storms and Grudem.
findings.fix: Insert before the 1906 entry: {"when": "c. 426", "what": "Augustine, City of God XXII.8, retracts his earlier view that miracles had ceased and records healings at Hippo."}

findings.claim: The covenantal pole is described as amillennial only ('his return bringing the new creation') and, with history entry 1646 'covenant of works and the covenant of grace', as Westminster covenant theology, which excludes the historic premillennialists and Baptists who make up most of my tradition.
findings.evidence: Piper and Grudem (ST ch. 55) are historic premillennialists after Ladd, whom the history itself lists at 1950s; Bethlehem, Sovereign Grace and Acts 29 are Baptist bodies that do not hold a covenant of works, and progressive covenantalists (Gentry & Wellum) reject covenant theology as a system while holding one people of God. All of them score 15-30 on this axis and are told they are 'covenantal'.
findings.fix: ...the church, Jew and Gentile together, inherits the promises to Abraham, and Christ's kingdom is present now; his return brings the new creation, for some after an earthly reign of Christ. Many Baptists who reject covenant theology as a system still stand on this side.

findings.claim: The share text renders the left pole as an empty bar, so a Reformed charismatic's card shows Grace and Spirit as ten empty circles, which screenshots as 'no grace, no Spirit'.
findings.evidence: shareText: f = round(score/10); circle k is filled only if k < f, so score 0 yields '○○○○○○○○○○'. My card reads '⚖️ Grace · Monergist ○○○○○○○○○○ Synergist' and '🔥 Spirit · Continuationist ○○○○○○○○○○ Cessationist'. The explanatory caption at line 457 is not part of the copied text.
findings.fix: Use one filled marker among eleven slots at position round(score/10): 'Continuationist ●○○○○○○○○○○ Cessationist', 'Monergist ●○○○○○○○○○○ Synergist'.

findings.claim: The three middle-band labels 'balanced on grace', 'centered on the sacraments', 'centered on the kingdom' are evaluative or false: 'balanced' implies the poles are unbalanced, and a 50 on Table is not sacrament-centered (the typical mid-scorer is a Calvinistic credobaptist).
findings.evidence: bands[2] for grace, table, kingdom; contrast 'undecided on the gifts', 'balanced on authority', 'flexible in worship', which are at least descriptive. A five-point Calvinist would object to a scheme that calls the midpoint 'balanced'.
findings.fix: "mixed on grace", "mixed on the sacraments", "mixed on the kingdom".

findings.claim: With twelve sparse points, second place is often decided by fractions of a distance unit, yet the headline, subtitle and share text print both names as if equally meaningful.
findings.evidence: Simulation: Presbyterian 87.87 vs Charismatic non-denominational 88.30; one answer change (S17 Unsure -> Agree) reorders the top three. renderResult writes 'Closest traditions: A, B' and shareText 'Closest: A · B' with no match % in the shared text.
findings.fix: Include the match % in the share line ('Closest: Reformed Baptist 66% · Presbyterian / Reformed 64%'), and show only one name when the second is within 2 distance units of the third.

findings.claim: 'a decision to follow Christ that has already been made' is revivalist vocabulary; Reformed Baptists baptize on profession of faith, not a 'decision'.
findings.evidence: Piper's long-standing aversion to decisionism; 1689 LBC 29.2 baptizes 'those who do actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ'. The direction still scores correctly, but the wording makes them wince.
findings.fix: Baptism is for those who already profess faith in Christ, as a sign of that faith.

findings.claim: 'as they did in Acts' is Pentecostal restorationist phrasing; Reformed continuationists ground continuation in 1 Corinthians 1:7 and 13:10 (until Christ returns), and Grudem distinguishes congregational prophecy from apostolic-era authority.
findings.evidence: Grudem, The Gift of Prophecy in the New Testament and Today, chs. 1-3; Storms, Practicing the Power, ch. 1. A careful Reformed charismatic hesitates at 'as they did in Acts' and answers Agree rather than Strongly agree for a reason that has nothing to do with cessation.
findings.fix: Tongues, prophecy, and healing are still given by the Spirit to the church today.

findings.claim: 'carry real authority, not just historical interest' offers no room for the Protestant answer (real but subordinate authority), so every confessional Protestant is pulled one notch toward the 'teaching office' pole for affirming Nicaea.
findings.evidence: WCF 31.4: councils 'may err' and are 'not to be made the rule of faith, or practice; but to be used as a help in both'. Sovereign Grace and Acts 29 both affirm the ecumenical creeds. The discriminating question is whether creeds bind in their own right.
findings.fix: The creeds and councils of the early church carry binding authority in their own right, not only insofar as they summarize Scripture.

findings.claim: 'The church, not the individual reader, is the final interpreter of Scripture' is a false dilemma written in Rome's vocabulary for the Protestant position ('private interpretation').
findings.evidence: WCF 1.9-10: the infallible rule of interpretation is Scripture itself and the supreme judge is 'the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture'; neither church nor individual. A Reformed reader disagrees but only by rejecting a caricature of his own view.
findings.fix: When Scripture and the church's settled teaching seem to conflict, the church's teaching should prevail.

findings.claim: 'a set liturgy that connects us to the historic church' bakes the argument into the statement; non-liturgical Reformed churches claim the historic connection too.
findings.evidence: Kauflin, Worship Matters, 'Rooted and Relevant'; Sovereign Grace and Bethlehem sing Watts, Newton and Wesley and recite the creeds. A member disagrees with the first clause while affirming the second.
findings.fix: Worship should follow a set liturgy shared with the wider church.

findings.claim: 'The church is the true Israel, heir to every promise God made to Abraham' uses supersessionist vocabulary the covenantal side increasingly avoids, and 'every promise' makes historic premillennialists who expect a future for ethnic Israel hesitate.
findings.evidence: Piper and Grudem hold Romans 11:26 as a future conversion of ethnic Israel; covenant theologians prefer 'the church is the expansion of Israel' to 'replaces'. Galatians 3:29 supplies neutral wording.
findings.fix: Believers in Christ, Jew and Gentile alike, are Abraham's offspring and heirs of the promises made to him.

findings.claim: 'his saving grace cannot finally be refused' leaves standing the caricature that irresistible grace coerces, which the Canons explicitly reject.
findings.evidence: Canons of Dort III/IV art. 16: regenerating grace does not treat people 'as if they were blocks and stones' but makes the unwilling willing (cf. Ps 110:3; WCF 10.1 'yet so as they come most freely').
findings.fix: ...and his saving grace, far from forcing anyone, makes the unwilling willing so that they come freely and cannot finally be lost.

findings.claim: Romans 8:28-30, the passage Reformed preachers reach for first, is absent.
findings.evidence: The 'golden chain' (foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified) is the text behind Piper's and Sproul's popular treatments and Dort I.7; the list has Romans 9, Ephesians 1 and John 6 but not it.
findings.fix: Add 'Romans 8:28-30'.

findings.claim: 'notes that the sign gifts had ceased' puts a 20th-century cessationist category into Chrysostom's mouth.
findings.evidence: Homily 29 on 1 Corinthians says the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12 'used to occur but now no longer take place'; he has no 'sign gifts' class. Grudem and Storms argue the New Testament has no such category, so the phrase is contested vocabulary in a line meant to be neutral.
findings.fix: Chrysostom, preaching on 1 Corinthians 12, remarks that such gifts no longer occur in his day.

findings.claim: The cessationist summary's 'and the New Testament was complete' attributes the canon-cessation argument that the strongest cessationist scholars decline.
findings.evidence: Gaffin, Perspectives on Pentecost, and Gaffin in Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? take 1 Corinthians 13:10 as the parousia and rest cessation on the apostolic foundation (Eph 2:20), not on the canon; Waldron, To Be Continued?, likewise. Continuationists win too easily against the canon argument, so it is unfair to the other side.
findings.fix: ...those sign gifts authenticated the apostles and their message, and passed away with them once the church's foundation was laid (Ephesians 2:20).

findings.claim: 1 Thessalonians 5:19-21, the signature Reformed-charismatic text, is missing.
findings.evidence: 'Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything' is the text behind statement 9's 'weighed carefully' wording, Piper's sermons on the gifts and Storms's Practicing the Power; the list has Joel and Acts 2 but not it.
findings.fix: Add '1 Thessalonians 5:19-21'.

findings.claim: Both covenantal read-more titles are Presbyterian/URC amillennial, leaving the historic premillennialism the history features (Ladd) and the Baptist wing unrepresented.
findings.evidence: 'Horton, Introducing Covenant Theology', 'Riddlebarger, A Case for Amillennialism'. Storms, Kingdom Come (amillennial, from a Reformed charismatic) or Ladd, The Gospel of the Kingdom would serve the same pole more broadly.
findings.fix: Replace Riddlebarger with 'Storms, Kingdom Come' or add 'Ladd, The Gospel of the Kingdom'.

findings.claim: 'Reformed Baptist' with spirit 80 describes the 1689 confessional Baptist, but the label is also used loosely for Piper, Grudem and Sovereign Grace, who are 75-80 points away on that axis.
findings.evidence: 1689 LBC 1.1 ('those former ways of God's revealing his will unto his people being now ceased') justifies the 80; the loose usage is common enough that a continuationist Baptist told 'Closest: Reformed Baptist' will assume the quiz means him and wonder why the match is 66%.
findings.fix: Rename to "Reformed Baptist (1689)", in the style of "Lutheran (confessional)", once a "Reformed charismatic" entry exists.

simulation.headline: Memorialist, Scripture alone, firmly synergist
simulation.comment: Profile simulated: the modal SBC member, a non-Calvinist ('Traditionalist') who holds eternal security, memorial ordinances, open-but-cautious cessationism, pew-level pretrib premillennialism, sola Scriptura, and a planned but non-liturgical service. Raw sums (direction x answer): Grace (-1)(-1)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-1)=4 -> round(10/12*100)=83; Table (-1)(-2)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-2)=6 -> 100; Spirit 1+1+1=3 -> 75; Kingdom 1+1+1=3 -> 75; Tradition 1+2+2=5 -> round(91.67)=92; Worship 1+0+1=2 -> round(66.67)=67. Headline: |s-50| = 33,50,25,25,42,17 -> Table(100 'memorialist'), Tradition(92 'Scripture alone'), Grace(83 'firmly synergist'). Squared distances to every tradition: Southern Baptist 38^2+15^2+0+5^2+7^2+3^2=1752 -> 41.86 (match 83%); Dispensational Bible church 43^2+10^2+15^2+20^2+2^2+8^2=2642 -> 51.40 (79%); Anabaptist 3247 -> 56.98; Pentecostal 5712 -> 75.58; Charismatic 6272 -> 79.20; Reformed Baptist 9652 -> 98.24; Wesleyan 9947 -> 99.73; Presbyterian 15847 -> 125.88; Anglican 17452 -> 132.11; Lutheran 20277 -> 142.40; Roman Catholic 24607 -> 156.87; Eastern Orthodox 25962 -> 161.13. So this profile lands correctly, but note that 1444 of the 1752 squared distance comes from the Grace axis alone, because the SBC coordinate (45) is an average of two populations that no actual member occupies. TWO VARIANTS THAT MATTER: (a) Historic premillennial Traditionalist (Ladd-type, the dominant view among SBC seminary faculty; BF&M X is deliberately silent on the millennium): S10=+1, S11=-1, S12=-2 -> Kingdom raw 0 -> 50. Scores [83,100,75,50,92,67]. Anabaptist/Mennonite: 8^2+15^2+20^2+20^2+22^2+7^2=1622 -> 40.27; Southern Baptist: 38^2+15^2+0+20^2+7^2+3^2=2127 -> 46.12. A real Southern Baptist lands on 'Anabaptist / Mennonite' first. That is a blocker. With the proposed non-Calvinist SBC entry at grace 75 the same answers give 8^2+15^2+0+20^2+7^2+3^2=747 -> 27.33, comfortably first. (b) Calvinist Southern Baptist (about 30% of SBC pastors per Lifeway 2012): S1=+2, S2=-2, S3=+2 -> Grace 0; scores [0,100,75,75,92,67]. Southern Baptist 45^2+15^2+0+5^2+7^2+3^2=2333 -> 48.30; Dispensational Bible church 2393 -> 48.92; Reformed Baptist 4423 -> 66.51. Lands on SBC by 0.6 points of distance, i.e. by luck. With a split entry 'Southern Baptist (Calvinist)' at [15,85,75,55,85,70]: 15^2+15^2+0+20^2+7^2+3^2=908 -> 30.13, clearly first, and the two SBC entries do not crowd each other out (the non-Calvinist entry is 77 away from this profile and the Calvinist entry is 73 away from the Traditionalist profile).

findings.claim: The Grace coordinate 45 ('balanced on grace') describes no Southern Baptist: the convention is split between Calvinists (Grace ~0-15) and non-Calvinist Traditionalists (Grace ~75-85), and the average of the two populations makes a real historic-premillennial Southern Baptist land on 'Anabaptist / Mennonite' first.
findings.evidence: Lifeway Research 2012: about 30% of SBC pastors describe their congregation as Calvinist; the 2012 'Statement of the Traditional Southern Baptist Understanding of God's Plan of Salvation' (Hankins et al.) was written precisely because the other ~70% reject Calvinism. Arithmetic: a Traditionalist who is historic premillennial (S10 +1, S11 -1, S12 -2, Kingdom 50; the view of much SBC seminary leadership, BF&M X being silent on the millennium) scores [83,100,75,50,92,67]; distance to Anabaptist = sqrt(64+225+400+400+484+49) = 40.3, to Southern Baptist = sqrt(1444+225+0+400+49+9) = 46.1. Even the pretrib profile in the simulation loses 1444 of its 1752 squared distance to the Grace axis alone, capping the match at 83% for a textbook member. The label '(typical)' also stands out: the parallel qualifiers are '(confessional)' and '(broad)', which name a subgroup, while '(typical)' grades the person and implies the SBC has no confessional standard (it has the BF&M 2000).
findings.fix: Replace the single entry with two: 'Southern Baptist (non-Calvinist)' = {grace 75, table 85, spirit 75, kingdom 70, tradition 85, worship 70} and 'Southern Baptist (Calvinist)' = {grace 15, table 85, spirit 75, kingdom 55, tradition 85, worship 70}. Check: historic-premil Traditionalist -> non-Calvinist entry sqrt(64+225+0+400+49+9)=27.3 vs Anabaptist 40.3; Calvinist profile [0,100,75,75,92,67] -> Calvinist entry sqrt(225+225+0+400+49+9)=30.1 vs Dispensational 48.9 vs Reformed Baptist 66.5. If only one entry is kept, put grace at 70 and rename it 'Southern Baptist (BF&M 2000)'.

findings.claim: The right-hand band adjectives 'Arminian-leaning' and 'firmly synergist' will be applied to the majority of the largest Protestant body in the United States, which has spent a decade insisting in print that it is neither Arminian nor synergist.
findings.evidence: The 2012 Traditional Statement's preamble distinguishes traditional Southern Baptist soteriology from both Calvinism and Arminianism; its Article 4 denies that 'the response of faith is in any way a meritorious work that earns salvation' and Article 9 affirms the security of the believer, which classical Wesleyan Arminianism denies. 'Synergist' is the word Calvinist polemics use for this group, not a word it uses for itself. In the simulation a Traditionalist scores 83 and receives 'firmly synergist' as the third word of the headline card that the quiz invites them to share; a pastor at 75 gets 'Arminian-leaning'. That card will be screenshotted with the caption 'this quiz calls Southern Baptists Arminians'.
findings.fix: bands: ['firmly monergist', 'Reformed-leaning', 'balanced on grace', 'free-will-leaning', 'firmly free-will']. Both Traditionalists (Traditional Statement Art. 2 affirms 'free will') and Wesleyans use 'free will' of themselves, and Catholics accept it.

findings.claim: A foreknowledge-election Baptist can honestly agree with every word of 'Before anyone does anything, God has already chosen who will be saved, and his choice cannot fail', so the statement fails to separate conditional from unconditional election and pushes non-Calvinists toward the monergist pole.
findings.evidence: Traditional Statement Art. 6: election is 'God's eternal, gracious, and certain plan in Christ to have a people who are His by repentance and faith'. Romans 8:29 ('those whom he foreknew he also predestined') is the Traditionalist proof text: the choice is made in eternity ('before anyone does anything'), it is certain ('cannot fail'), and it is conditioned on foreseen faith. Nothing in the statement excludes that reading. Only open theists and pure corporate-election holders are actually filtered out.
findings.fix: Make S1 carry the effectual-calling question, leaving unconditional election to a repaired S3: 'When God sets out to save a particular person, that person will certainly come to faith.' (direction -1)

findings.claim: 'Refuse salvation to the very end' reads to a Baptist as the perseverance question (can a believer fall away?) rather than the resistibility question (can an unbeliever refuse?), and a Traditionalist who holds both resistible grace and eternal security has no honest answer.
findings.evidence: BF&M 2000 Art. V: 'All true believers endure to the end. Those whom God has accepted in Christ ... will never fall away from the state of grace, but shall persevere to the end.' Traditional Statement Art. 9 affirms the same. Such a person agrees that grace can be refused but hears 'to the very end' as 'a saved person can end lost' and hedges to Unsure, pulling the score toward center and hiding the position they actually hold.
findings.fix: 'A person who hears the gospel can genuinely resist God's grace and refuse to be saved; God does not override that refusal.' (direction +1)

findings.claim: 'Saving faith is itself a gift God gives to those he has chosen, not the reason he chose them' is double-barreled: a non-Calvinist Baptist agrees with the first clause in the loose sense preached from Ephesians 2:8 every week and disagrees with the second, which is the only clause that actually discriminates.
findings.evidence: Traditional Statement Art. 4 says grace takes 'all of the initiative' and unites the believer to Christ 'through the Holy Spirit by faith' (faith as grace-enabled gift) while Art. 6 denies that God 'predestined certain people for salvation' apart from their faith (faith as the ground of election). The two clauses pull a Traditionalist in opposite directions.
findings.fix: 'God's choice of who will be saved was not based on anything, including faith, that he foresaw in them.' (direction -1)

findings.claim: 'Real authority' does not distinguish ministerial authority under Scripture (which Reformation and Baptist theologians affirm) from magisterial authority in its own right (which they deny), so the better-informed a sola Scriptura respondent is, the more the statement pushes them toward the 'with tradition' pole.
findings.evidence: BF&M 2000 preamble: 'confessions are only guides in interpretation, having no authority over the conscience', yet SBC theologians (Mohler, Timothy George, the 2024 convention debate over adding the Nicene Creed to the BF&M) treat Nicene orthodoxy as normative for the church. A seminary professor answers Agree, a pew member answers Disagree, and both hold identical views on Scripture's supremacy. The statement is measuring education, not conviction.
findings.fix: 'The early creeds and councils bind what the church must believe in their own right, not only because they agree with Scripture.' (direction -1)

findings.claim: 'The church, not the individual reader, is the final interpreter of Scripture' offers a false binary, and the only way a Baptist can register sola Scriptura is to appear to affirm that 'the individual reader' is the final interpreter, which is the standard caricature ('just me and my Bible') used against Baptists.
findings.evidence: BF&M 2000 Art. I: 'The criterion by which the Bible is to be interpreted is Jesus Christ'; the preamble pairs 'soul competency and the priesthood of believers' with 'our accountability to each other under the Word of God'; Art. VI locates discernment in the gathered congregation. Baptists name neither the isolated individual nor a teaching office as final interpreter; Scripture interprets Scripture under the Spirit in the congregation. The statement lets a Catholic or Orthodox respondent answer in their own vocabulary but makes the Protestant answer in a caricature.
findings.fix: 'A living teaching office (bishops, councils, or a magisterium) has the final say on what Scripture means.' (direction -1)

findings.claim: 'Worship should be free-form and led by the Spirit in the moment' defines the Free pole in Pentecostal vocabulary, so the single most common Protestant service in America, the planned but non-liturgical Baptist order (hymns, prayer, offering, sermon, invitation), has no honest answer and is pulled to the center.
findings.evidence: James F. White, Protestant Worship: Traditions in Transition (1989), classifies Baptist worship as the 'Frontier' tradition: deliberately ordered around preaching, revival-shaped, and non-liturgical, but never 'free-form'. A typical SBC member answers Unsure (as in the simulation) or Disagree, which is why the SBC coordinate has to sit at 70 rather than 85 on an axis where Baptists are the paradigm 'free church'.
