findings.fix: 'Worship need not follow any fixed liturgy; each congregation is free to order its own service as it judges best.' (direction +1). Then raise the Southern Baptist worship coordinate to 80.

findings.claim: The monergist summary bundles perseverance ('he chooses, calls, and keeps his people') as if it were distinctive of monergism, while the synergist summary says nothing about security, so the largest non-Calvinist group in American Protestantism, Baptists who hold resistible grace and eternal security together, fits neither description.
findings.evidence: BF&M 2000 Art. V (perseverance) sits in the same confession that says election 'is consistent with the free agency of man'. Traditional Statement Art. 4 (grace can be resisted) and Art. 9 (the believer's security) are held simultaneously. A Traditionalist reading the current text sees their own view split across the two paragraphs.
findings.fix: Append to the synergist half: 'Many synergists, including most Baptists, nonetheless hold that those who truly believe are kept by God to the end.'

findings.claim: Hebrews 6:4-6 is an apostasy text; listing it as a synergist passage tells the reader that the right pole means 'you can lose your salvation', which non-Calvinist Baptists explicitly deny, and the list omits the texts they actually reach for.
findings.evidence: BF&M 2000 Art. V: believers 'will never fall away from the state of grace'; Traditional Statement Art. 9. No Southern Baptist Traditionalist argues from Hebrews 6:4-6; they argue from Romans 8:29-30 (foreknowledge), John 3:16, 1 Peter 1:2, Acts 7:51 ('you always resist the Holy Spirit'), and Matthew 23:37 ('you were not willing'). 1 Timothy 2:3-4 and 2 Peter 3:9 are the right kind of text; Hebrews 6 is the wrong one.
findings.fix: Replace 'Hebrews 6:4-6' with 'Romans 8:29-30' and add 'Acts 7:51'.

findings.claim: 'Synergist' as a pole name is accepted by academic Arminians (Olson) but rejected by the non-Calvinist Baptists who will make up a large share of respondents; it appears at the end of every axis bar, in the share text, and on the result card.
findings.evidence: The Traditional Statement (2012) avoids the word entirely and Art. 4 denies that faith 'earns' anything, which is what 'synergism' means in the popular Calvinist usage most respondents have heard. The pole pair 'Monergist / Synergist' is also one side's taxonomy of the debate.
findings.fix: Pole names both sides use of themselves: left 'Effectual grace', right 'Resistible grace' (Dort II/IV vs. Remonstrance Art. 4; Traditional Statement Art. 4 denies grace 'cannot be resisted').

findings.claim: The right-hand reading list sends a non-Calvinist Southern Baptist to Arminius and Olson, neither of whom they would recognize as their tradition, when the SBC has its own standard literature.
findings.evidence: Allen & Lemke (eds.), Whosoever Will: A Biblical-Theological Critique of Five-Point Calvinism (B&H 2010) is the SBC non-Calvinist text; Schreiner & Ware (eds.), Still Sovereign (Baker 2000) is the SBC Calvinist one. The history array likewise has no entry after 1740, though the 2012 Traditional Statement is the most recent widely read document on this axis.
findings.fix: right: add 'Allen & Lemke, Whosoever Will'; left: add 'Schreiner & Ware, Still Sovereign'. History: add {when: '2012', what: 'The Traditional Statement marks the Calvinist/non-Calvinist divide inside the Southern Baptist Convention.'}

findings.claim: The midpoint band 'centered on the sacraments' describes the center of a sacramental-versus-memorial axis in the left pole's own vocabulary, so a Baptist who lands at 50 is told they are 'centered on the sacraments'.
findings.evidence: BF&M 2000 Art. VII calls baptism and the Supper 'ordinances' and 'symbolic act[s] of obedience'; a Baptist at 50 is exactly the person who is not centered on sacraments. The headline builder will print this phrase capitalized as the first word of the label.
findings.fix: bands[2]: 'between sacrament and symbol'.

findings.claim: There is no believer's-baptism text in the list: four passages are sacramental proof texts, two are shared, and Acts 2:38-39 ('the promise is for you and your children') is the paedobaptist text, so a Baptist sees only the other side's Bible.
findings.evidence: The passages Baptists actually reach for: Acts 8:36-38 (the eunuch: belief, then 'went down into the water'), Matthew 28:19-20 (make disciples, then baptize), Acts 2:41 ('those who received his word were baptized'), Luke 22:19 / 1 Corinthians 11:24-26 ('in remembrance of me', 'proclaim the Lord's death until he comes'). Schreiner & Wright, Believer's Baptism (already in read-more) builds on exactly these.
findings.fix: Add 'Acts 8:36-38' and 'Matthew 28:19-20'; keep Acts 2:38-39 since both sides use it.

findings.claim: The memorial summary reduces the Supper to 'a remembrance' and says the ordinances are 'rather than channels of grace', which is thinner than the Baptist confessional statement and excludes Reformed Baptists (also Southern Baptists) who hold a spiritual feeding; and the sacramental half's 'and so the children of believers are baptized' is a non sequitur for Reformed paedobaptists.
findings.evidence: BF&M 2000 Art. VII: members 'memorialize the death of the Redeemer and anticipate His second coming'; 1 Corinthians 11:26 'proclaim'. Second London Confession 30.7: worthy receivers 'spiritually receive and feed upon Christ crucified'. On the other side, Westminster Confession 28.4 grounds infant baptism in covenant membership ('infants of one or both believing parents'), not in baptism joining the child to Christ.
findings.fix: Memorial half: 'The memorial view holds that the Supper is a remembrance and proclamation of Christ's death until he comes, and baptism a public confession of a faith already held, so both are ordinances obeyed by believers rather than means by which grace is conferred.' Sacramental half: '...baptism joins a person to Christ and his church, and the children of believers are baptized as members of the covenant people.'

findings.claim: The only origin given for believer's baptism is the Anabaptists (1525); English Baptists are not Anabaptists and Southern Baptists are sensitive to being filed under them, yet the tradition that supplies most of the right pole's adherents has no line at all.
findings.evidence: John Smyth's congregation in Amsterdam (1609) and the Particular Baptists' First London Confession (1644), which first specified immersion, are the Baptist line of descent; the 1644 immersion clause is the source of BF&M VII's 'immersion of a believer in water'.
findings.fix: Add after the 1525 entry: {when: '1609 / 1644', what: 'English Baptists: John Smyth's congregation baptizes believers; the First London Confession specifies immersion.'}

findings.claim: The axis conflates two questions, Israel-and-church and rapture-timing, and names the left pole after paedobaptist covenant theology, so the two positions most common among informed Southern Baptists, historic premillennialism and progressive covenantalism, fall off the axis entirely.
findings.evidence: BF&M 2000 Art. X deliberately says only that Christ 'will return personally and visibly in glory'. A historic premillennialist (Ladd; SEBTS president Danny Akin; the SBC's Broadus tradition) answers S10 +1, S11 -1, S12 -2 -> raw 0 -> 50, i.e. 'centered on the kingdom', a label that means nothing for a convinced premillennialist. Progressive covenantalism (Gentry & Wellum, Southern Seminary) rejects both the Westminster covenant of works/grace scheme and dispensationalism. The left pole's history line (1646 Westminster) and read-more (Horton) make 'covenantal' mean specifically the framework Baptists reject.
findings.fix: Either (a) rename the poles 'One people of God' / 'Israel and church distinct' and drop the rapture statement (S12) for a second Israel/church statement, or (b) at minimum add historic premillennialism to the covenantal summary, add Gentry & Wellum to read-more, and rename bands[2] as proposed under axis:kingdom:bands.

findings.claim: The covenantal summary describes amillennialism only ('Christ's kingdom is present now, with his return bringing the new creation'), so a historic premillennialist who holds one people of God is told the left pole excludes a future millennium and the right pole excludes his ecclesiology.
findings.evidence: The history array itself (1950s, Ladd) says historic premillennialism holds 'a future millennium, one people of God', but neither summary paragraph contains that combination. It is the most common eschatology among SBC seminary faculty and is the view of Blomberg & Chung (eds.), A Case for Historic Premillennialism (2009).
findings.fix: '...and Christ's kingdom is present now, with his return bringing the new creation (some, the historic premillennialists, expect a millennial reign first, but still with one people of God).'

findings.claim: 'Centered on the kingdom' is the band a historic-premillennial Southern Baptist receives (score 50), and it describes no eschatological position; every Christian is 'centered on the kingdom'.
findings.evidence: S10 +1, S11 -1, S12 -2 -> raw 0 -> 50 for a Ladd-type premillennialist; the phrase would be the first word of that person's headline.
findings.fix: bands[2]: 'between covenant and dispensation'.

findings.claim: The 1646 Westminster line makes the left pole explicitly paedobaptist covenant theology and nothing on the timeline records the Baptist middle way that arose in the SBC's own seminary.
findings.evidence: Gentry & Wellum, Kingdom through Covenant (Crossway 2012; 2nd ed. 2018) and Wellum & Parker (eds.), Progressive Covenantalism (B&H 2016), both from Southern Seminary, are the standard statement of a position that is neither Westminster covenantalism nor dispensationalism.
findings.fix: Add {when: '2012', what: 'Gentry and Wellum, Kingdom through Covenant: progressive covenantalism, a Baptist alternative to both Westminster covenant theology and dispensationalism.'}

findings.claim: A Baptist who scores toward the left pole is sent to Horton and Riddlebarger, both Presbyterian amillennialists whose covenant theology grounds infant baptism, with no Baptist or premillennial option on that side.
findings.evidence: Horton, Introducing Covenant Theology, argues for paedobaptism from the covenant of grace; a Southern Baptist reading it as 'their' side's book will object. Gentry & Wellum, Kingdom through Covenant, and Blomberg & Chung, A Case for Historic Premillennialism, are the books a Baptist on this side actually reads.
findings.fix: left: ['Horton, Introducing Covenant Theology', 'Gentry & Wellum, Kingdom through Covenant', 'Blomberg & Chung, A Case for Historic Premillennialism']

findings.claim: 'Free worship keeps the form open so that the Spirit can lead in the moment, with an emphasis on spontaneity' describes Pentecostal worship, not the free-church principle; Baptists are the paradigm 'free church' and their services are planned, sermon-centered, and not spontaneous.
findings.evidence: The Baptist principle is that Scripture prescribes no fixed liturgy and each autonomous congregation (BF&M 2000 Art. VI) orders its own worship, historically under the regulative principle (Second London Confession ch. 22); White's 'Frontier' tradition is ordered and preaching-centered. As written, the summary tells a First Baptist congregation with a choir, orchestra, and printed order of service that their side of the axis is about spontaneity.
findings.fix: 'Free worship holds that Scripture prescribes no fixed liturgy, so each congregation orders its own service as it judges best, usually around the preaching of the Word; in some churches this leaves room for spontaneity and congregational participation in the moment.'

findings.claim: 'Informal in worship' is the band a typical Southern Baptist receives (60-79), and it is simply false of the traditional Baptist service; non-liturgical is not informal.
findings.evidence: The simulation lands at 67 -> 'informal in worship'. First Baptist Dallas, Bellevue, and thousands of SBC churches hold ordered services with robed choirs and printed bulletins. The word will read as a put-down on a shared card.
findings.fix: bands: ['liturgical', 'liturgy-leaning', 'flexible in worship', 'non-liturgical', 'free in worship']

findings.claim: 'Communion should be celebrated every week as the center of the service' is double-barreled (frequency and centrality), and weekly frequency is not a liturgical marker: memorialist, non-liturgical churches keep a weekly Supper.
findings.evidence: Churches of Christ and Plymouth Brethren observe the Supper weekly as a memorial with no liturgy; a growing number of SBC churches (Capitol Hill Baptist and other 9Marks-influenced congregations) do likewise while keeping the sermon central. A Baptist in such a church who agrees on frequency but not centrality has no answer.
findings.fix: 'The service should be built around the Lord's Supper rather than around the sermon.' (direction -1)

findings.claim: 'A decision to follow Christ' is revivalist decisionism vocabulary that many SBC pastors have publicly repudiated, and the statement omits the one word Baptists consider confessional about baptism, immersion.
findings.evidence: BF&M 2000 Art. VII: 'Christian baptism is the immersion of a believer in water ... symbolizing the believer's faith in a crucified, buried, and risen Saviour.' The 2012 SBC resolution on the 'sinner's prayer' was occasioned by an intra-SBC argument against decision-based evangelism; Reformed Baptists in the convention will wince at 'decision'.
findings.fix: 'Baptism is for those who already believe: a public confession of a faith already present, not the means by which faith is given.' (direction +1)

findings.claim: Listing 'tongues, prophecy, and healing' together forces a Southern Baptist who prays for the sick and expects God to heal, but denies tongues and prophecy, to answer for all three at once.
findings.evidence: James 5:14-15 anointing and prayer is ordinary SBC practice; the IMB's 2005 ban on private prayer language and its 2015 reversal show the SBC's internal variance is specifically about tongues. 'As they did in Acts' helps but does not remove the third barrel.
findings.fix: 'The gifts of tongues and prophecy continue in the church today, as they did in Acts.' (direction -1)

findings.claim: 'The miraculous sign gifts' adopts the cessationist classification of tongues, prophecy, and healing as 'sign gifts', which continuationists dispute; it is the other side's vocabulary and a fair-minded cessationist should not want the quiz to lean on it.
findings.evidence: The 'sign gift' category is Warfield's and MacArthur's framework (both in read-more). Grudem and Storms (read-more, left) argue the gifts were for edification, not merely attestation.
findings.fix: 'The miraculous gifts of tongues, prophecy, and healing ended with the apostles or the completion of the New Testament.' (direction +1)

findings.claim: 'Truly present in a way that goes beyond a symbol' makes symbol and presence contraries, so a Baptist who affirms that Christ is truly present with his gathered church at the Supper (Matthew 18:20) while holding the bread remains a symbol is torn.
findings.evidence: BF&M 2000 Art. VII: 'a symbolic act of obedience'; Baptist treatments such as Hammett, Forty Questions About Baptism and the Lord's Supper, argue for a spiritual presence within a memorial view. The discriminating question is whether Christ is given in or through the elements.
findings.fix: 'In the Lord's Supper Christ is given to believers in or through the bread and cup, not only remembered.' (direction -1); this still catches Calvin's view and Lutheran/Catholic views on the sacramental side.

findings.claim: The headline system produces 'Memorialist, Scripture alone, firmly synergist' for a typical Southern Baptist, and three of the six midpoint bands ('centered on the sacraments', 'centered on the kingdom', 'undecided on the gifts') are either one pole's vocabulary or not a position at all.
findings.evidence: Simulation: Table 100, Tradition 92, Grace 83 -> those three adjectives. The SBC's 'open but cautious' stance on the gifts is a position, not indecision; 'centered on the sacraments' at a memorial/sacramental midpoint is the left pole's word; 'centered on the kingdom' is content-free. The share bar also prints the pole name 'Synergist' at the end of every Grace bar.
findings.fix: Adopt the band replacements proposed per axis (grace, table, kingdom, worship) and rename spirit bands[2] 'open but cautious on the gifts'; rename the Grace poles 'Effectual grace / Resistible grace' so the share bar and card carry names both sides accept.

findings.claim: Reformed Baptists (many of them inside the SBC) are given tradition 55, 'balanced on authority', although the 1689 confession is as sola Scriptura as Westminster; and 'Reformed Baptist' versus 'Southern Baptist' mixes a soteriological label with a denominational one, since the two overlap heavily.
findings.evidence: Second London Confession 1.10: 'The supreme judge ... can be no other but the Holy Scripture.' A 1689 Baptist answers S13 +1 (creeds have real authority), S14 +2, S15 -2 -> raw 3 -> 75. Founders Ministries, the main Reformed Baptist network, is an SBC organization.
findings.fix: Set tradition to 70. If the SBC entry is split as proposed, consider renaming this entry 'Baptist (1689 / Reformed)' so the categories read as parallel.

findings.claim: The shared line 'Closest: Southern Baptist (typical) · ...' carries the '(typical)' qualifier into the one place it will be seen without context, and the result card and share text omit the on-page caveat that positions are 'approximate positions of typical adherents, not official teaching'.
findings.evidence: shareText() prints near[0].name verbatim; renderCard() prints 'Closest traditions · ' + names with no caveat, while the result page note only appears in the 'Closest traditions' panel.
findings.fix: Rename the entry as proposed and add a short caveat line to the card ('Traditions are approximate positions, not official teaching').

findings.claim: There is no axis for church polity, which after believer's baptism is the defining Baptist distinctive; the Table axis carries the whole weight of Baptist identity, and a congregational Baptist and a presbyterian or episcopal Christian who happen to agree on the ordinances are indistinguishable.
findings.evidence: BF&M 2000 Art. VI: 'A New Testament church ... is an autonomous local congregation of baptized believers ... operates under the Lordship of Christ through democratic processes'; preamble: Baptists 'deny the right of any secular or religious authority to impose a confession of faith upon a church'. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist positions all differ on this and it is invisible in the six axes.
findings.fix: If a seventh axis is feasible: 'Church: Connectional ↔ Congregational', with statements such as 'Each local congregation governs itself under Christ; no bishop, presbytery, or convention can bind it' (+1), 'Bishops or presbyteries rightly hold authority over local congregations' (-1), 'Church membership should be limited to those who have personally professed faith' (+1). If not, say in the intro that polity is deliberately out of scope.

findings.claim: The tradition list has no historically Black Baptist entry, although the National Baptist Convention USA is the second-largest Baptist body in the country and its members will take this quiz; they share the SBC's ordinances and Scripture-alone stance but are markedly more open on the gifts and freer in worship, so they will be scattered between 'Southern Baptist' and 'Pentecostal'.
findings.evidence: NBC USA's Articles of Faith descend from the same 1925 Baptist confessional family as the BF&M; Black Baptist worship is neither cessationist-leaning nor 'planned Frontier' in the SBC sense.
findings.fix: Add 'National Baptist (historically Black Baptist)' at approximately {grace 70, table 85, spirit 50, kingdom 65, tradition 85, worship 80}.

findings.claim: The passage list cannot deliver what the page promises. The section intro says these are "the passages each side reaches for", but key_passages is a flat, unlabeled chip list (theology-compass.html lines 997-999), whereas read_more is split by pole (lines 1002-1003). Nothing tells a reader that Ephesians 2:20 is a cessationist text and Acts 2:17-18 a continuationist one, that 1 Corinthians 13:8-12 is read both ways, or that John 6 is claimed by both the sacramental and the Zwinglian side.
findings.evidence: Line 449: "A fair summary of both poles, a short dated history, and the passages each side reaches for." Line 998: a.passages.map renders each string as a bare chip with a "Read in Scripture Web" CTA and no pole or gloss. Compare the more-pole span used for books. The brief asks that 1 Corinthians 13:8-12 be included "read both ways"; the data structure has no way to say so.
findings.fix: Restructure key_passages per axis as {"left": [...], "right": [...], "both": [...]} and render three labeled rows like read_more (left pole name, right pole name, "Read both ways"). If chips must stay flat, add a 6-10 word gloss to each, e.g. "1 Corinthians 13:8-12 - 'when the perfect comes': the canon, or Christ's return", "Ephesians 2:20 - apostles and prophets as the church's foundation", "Acts 2:17-18 - 'in the last days... your sons and daughters shall prophesy'".

findings.claim: The single most-cited predestination text in the whole debate, Romans 8:28-30, is absent, and it is the one passage both poles build on: the Reformed 'golden chain' (foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified) and the Arminian 'those whom he foreknew' that grounds the summary's own clause "election follows God's foreknowledge of faith". The synergist pole also lacks its resistible-grace text, Acts 7:51, which is what statement 2 ("can genuinely resist God's grace") is drawn from.
findings.evidence: Calvin, Institutes III.21-24 and Canons of Dort I.6-7 and I.17 argue from Romans 8:29-30 with Ephesians 1; the Remonstrant Articles (1610) art. 1 and Arminius, Works (Declaration of Sentiments, on predestination) rest election-on-foreknowledge on Romans 8:29 and 1 Peter 1:2; Olson, Arminian Theology (in read_more), Myth 6 on resistible grace, argues from Acts 7:51 and Matthew 23:37. The fair_summary asserts the foreknowledge view but the list gives the reader no verse for it.
findings.fix: Add "Romans 8:28–30" (read both ways) and "Acts 7:51" (synergist). Resulting list: "Romans 9", "Romans 8:28–30", "Ephesians 1:3–14", "John 6:37–44", "1 Timothy 2:3–4", "2 Peter 3:9", "Acts 7:51", "Hebrews 6:4–6".

findings.claim: "Ephesians 1:3–11" is not a conventional unit. Verses 3-14 are one sentence in Greek and are paragraphed as a unit in NA28/UBS5 and every major English version; stopping at v.11 cuts the sentence mid-clause (v.12 'so that we... might be to the praise of his glory'). The predestination verses are 4-5 and 11, so either the whole berakah or the specific verses should be cited.
findings.evidence: NA28 paragraphing Eph 1:3-14; ESV/NIV/NRSV headings 'Spiritual Blessings in Christ' 1:3-14. The stop at v.11 looks chosen to end on 'predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will', which a synergist reader will notice.
findings.fix: Replace "Ephesians 1:3–11" with "Ephesians 1:3–14" (or, if brevity matters, "Ephesians 1:4–6, 11").

findings.claim: The monergist half of the summary defines monergism as Reformed monergism only: "he chooses, calls, and keeps his people, and his saving grace cannot finally be refused." Confessional Lutherans are monergists (Luther's Bondage of the Will headlines history[2]) yet reject irresistible grace and teach that the justified can fall away. A Lutheran reads this summary and finds their own position described as the other side, and Hebrews 6:4-6 in the list is a text they, as monergists, reach for.
findings.evidence: Augsburg Confession XII condemns those "who deny that those once justified can lose the Holy Ghost"; Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration II (Free Will) and XI (Election) teach that conversion is wholly God's work while affirming that a person can resist the Holy Spirit and that the regenerate can fall (Lutheran dogmatics: gratia resistibilis). The tradition coordinate for "Lutheran (confessional)" at grace=20 already presupposes they answer statement 2 'Agree'.
findings.fix: Replace the first sentence with: "Monergists hold that salvation is God's work from beginning to end: he chooses, calls, and gives faith, and no one contributes anything to their own conversion. Most monergists (the Reformed) add that his saving grace cannot finally be refused and that he keeps his people to the end."

findings.claim: "John 6:53–58" is cropped to the sacramental half of the Bread of Life discourse and omits v.63, "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all", which is the memorialist's verse in the same passage and the very verse the Marburg Colloquy (history[3]) was fought over. As listed, John 6 reads as a one-sided proof text.
findings.evidence: Zwingli, On the Lord's Supper (1526, in read_more) and Commentary on True and False Religion (1525) build the memorial reading on John 6:63; at Marburg (1529) Zwingli pressed 6:63 against Luther's 'hoc est corpus meum'. Baptist and Zwinglian commentators also deny that John 6 concerns the Supper at all, a point the reader cannot see when the chip stops at v.58.
findings.fix: Replace "John 6:53–58" with "John 6:51–63" and, if glosses are added, mark it read both ways ('my flesh is true food' v.55 / 'the flesh is no help at all' v.63).

findings.claim: Two loci classici are missing. For the sacramental pole: 1 Corinthians 10:16-17, the koinonia text ('a participation in the blood of Christ... in the body of Christ'), which is Calvin's central Supper passage and a catechism proof text for both Reformed and Catholic teaching. For the memorial/credobaptist pole there is no baptism text that is distinctively theirs; every baptism entry (Acts 2:38-39, Colossians 2:11-12, Romans 6:3-4) is one paedobaptists cite at least as readily. The believer's-baptism argument from the order 'make disciples... baptizing them' (Matthew 28:19-20) and from 'the pledge of a good conscience' (1 Peter 3:21) is absent.
findings.evidence: Heidelberg Catechism Q.77 and CCC 1396 quote 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 in full as the Supper's meaning; Calvin, Institutes IV.17 (history[4]) argues the real spiritual presence from it. Second London Baptist Confession 29.2 and Schreiner & Wright, Believer's Baptism (in read_more), ch. 1-2, argue from Matthew 28:19-20, Acts 8:12, 36-38 and 1 Peter 3:21.
findings.fix: Add "1 Corinthians 10:16–17" (sacramental), "Matthew 28:19–20" (memorial/credobaptist) and "1 Peter 3:21" (read both ways). Resulting list: "John 6:51–63", "1 Corinthians 10:16–17", "1 Corinthians 11:23–29", "Matthew 26:26–28", "Acts 2:38–39", "Matthew 28:19–20", "Colossians 2:11–12", "Romans 6:3–4", "1 Peter 3:21".

findings.claim: "Joel 2:28–29" and "Acts 2:17–18" are the same text (Peter quotes Joel verbatim), so the continuationist column is padded with a duplicate while the cessationist flagship, 2 Corinthians 12:12 ('the signs of a true apostle'), is missing entirely. The continuationist pole in turn lacks 1 Thessalonians 5:19-21, the 'do not despise prophecies, but test everything' text that statement 9 ("weighed carefully, but it can genuinely come from the Spirit") and the summary's "sought and tested" are paraphrasing, and James 5:14-16, the text continuationists reach for on healing, which statement 7 names.
findings.evidence: Acts 2:17-21 = LXX Joel 3:1-5 (English 2:28-32). Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles (in read_more), ch. 1, rests cessation on miracles as the credential of apostles from 2 Corinthians 12:12 and Hebrews 2:3-4; MacArthur, Strange Fire, uses the same verse. Grudem, The Gift of Prophecy (in read_more), grounds weighed, fallible congregational prophecy on 1 Corinthians 14:29 and 1 Thessalonians 5:20-21; Storms, Practicing the Power, on James 5:14-16.
findings.fix: Replace "Joel 2:28–29" with "2 Corinthians 12:12"; add "1 Thessalonians 5:19–21" and "James 5:14–16". Resulting list: "1 Corinthians 12–14", "1 Corinthians 13:8–12", "Acts 2:17–18", "1 Thessalonians 5:19–21", "James 5:14–16", "Ephesians 2:20", "Hebrews 2:3–4", "2 Corinthians 12:12".

findings.claim: "passed away once the apostolic foundation was laid and the New Testament was complete" makes the canon reading of 1 Corinthians 13:10 ('the perfect' = completed Scripture) part of the cessationist position as such. Statement 8 correctly says "or"; the summary says "and". The leading academic cessationists explicitly reject the canon reading and hold the foundation argument alone.
findings.evidence: Gaffin, Perspectives on Pentecost (1979), pp. 109-112, reads to teleion as the parousia and disowns the canon interpretation; Warfield never argued from 1 Corinthians 13:10. Popular cessationism (some Strange Fire speakers) does use the canon reading, so it should be marked as a subset, not the definition.
findings.fix: Replace with: "...and passed away once the apostolic foundation was laid; some add that this coincided with the completion of the New Testament."

findings.claim: The dispensational pole is represented only by eschatological timetable texts (Daniel 9:24-27, 1 Thessalonians 4:13-17) and has none of the Abrahamic covenant passages on which dispensationalism actually rests: the unconditional, 'everlasting' land promise of Genesis 12:1-3; 15:18-21; 17:7-8 is what statement 10 ("promises to national Israel will be fulfilled literally") means. The covenantal pole lacks its new-covenant text, Hebrews 8:6-13 (quoting Jeremiah 31:31-34), where a covenant made 'with the house of Israel' is applied to the church, and Galatians 6:16, 'the Israel of God', the phrase behind statement 11's "the church is the true Israel".
findings.evidence: Ryrie, Dispensationalism (in read_more), ch. 8, and Walvoord, The Millennial Kingdom, ch. 12-13, ground the Israel-church distinction on the unconditional Abrahamic covenant of Genesis 12, 15, 17; Scofield's notes on Genesis 12:1 and 15:18 do the same. Horton, Introducing Covenant Theology (in read_more), ch. 3-4, and Riddlebarger, A Case for Amillennialism, ch. 4, argue one people of God from Jeremiah 31/Hebrews 8 and Galatians 6:16.
findings.fix: Add "Genesis 17:7–8" (dispensational; or "Genesis 12:1–3") and "Hebrews 8:6–13" (covenantal); if space allows, also "Galatians 6:16". Resulting list: "Genesis 17:7–8", "Romans 11", "Galatians 3:26–29", "Hebrews 8:6–13", "Ephesians 2:11–22", "Daniel 9:24–27", "Revelation 20:1–6", "1 Thessalonians 4:13–18", "Matthew 24".

findings.claim: "1 Thessalonians 4:13–17" stops one verse short of the unit; v.18, 'Therefore encourage one another with these words', closes the paragraph in every standard edition, and the pastoral purpose clause is part of what both pretribulational and posttribulational readers argue from.
findings.evidence: NA28 paragraphing 1 Thess 4:13-18; ESV/NIV/NRSV heading 'The Coming of the Lord' 4:13-18; Ryrie, Blaising & Bock and Ladd all cite 4:13-18.
findings.fix: Replace "1 Thessalonians 4:13–17" with "1 Thessalonians 4:13–18".

findings.claim: Statement 13 is about the authority of councils, yet the one council in Scripture, the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15 with its formula 'it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us' (15:28), is absent; it is the passage every Catholic and Orthodox writer reaches for first on conciliar authority. The Scripture-alone pole is likewise missing its sharpest text, Galatians 1:8-9, the apostolic anathema on any authority, 'even an angel from heaven', that preaches a different gospel, which is the classic Protestant ground for refusing to let church authority bind the conscience beyond Scripture.
findings.evidence: Florovsky, 'The Authority of the Ancient Councils and the Tradition of the Fathers', in Bible, Church, Tradition (in read_more), takes Acts 15 as the type of every council; Dei Verbum 10 and CCC 880-892 build the teaching office on the apostolic college of Acts 15 and Matthew 16:18-19. Westminster Confession 1.6 (history[2]) cites Galatians 1:8-9 with 2 Timothy 3:15-17 as its proof texts for the sufficiency of Scripture.
findings.fix: Add "Acts 15:22–29" (with tradition) and "Galatians 1:8–9" (Scripture alone). Optionally add "2 Peter 1:20–21" as a read-both-ways text for statement 15. Resulting list: "2 Thessalonians 2:15", "1 Timothy 3:15", "Acts 15:22–29", "John 16:13", "2 Timothy 3:16–17", "Acts 17:11", "Matthew 15:3–9", "Galatians 1:8–9".

findings.claim: Statement 18 asserts weekly communion, but the only New Testament text for weekly frequency, Acts 20:7 ('on the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread'), is not listed. The free pole has no Spirit-led text beyond John 4:23-24; Ephesians 5:18-20 ('be filled with the Spirit... singing and making melody... with your heart') is what free-worship writers actually cite. Matthew 6:7-13 is a natural read-both-ways addition: v.7 against 'empty phrases' for the free pole, v.9 'Pray then like this' as the Lord's own set form for the liturgical pole.
findings.evidence: Calvin, Institutes IV.17.43-46, argues weekly communion from Acts 2:42 and 20:7; the Restoration Movement built its weekly Supper on Acts 20:7. Frame, Worship in Spirit and Truth (in read_more), ch. 1-2, works from John 4:24 and Ephesians 5:18-20; Anglican and Orthodox apologists for set prayer cite Matthew 6:9 and Luke 11:2 ('When you pray, say...').
findings.fix: Add "Acts 20:7", "Ephesians 5:18–20" and "Matthew 6:7–13". Resulting list: "Acts 2:42", "Acts 20:7", "Hebrews 12:28", "Matthew 6:7–13", "1 Corinthians 14:26–40", "Colossians 3:16", "John 4:23–24", "Ephesians 5:18–20", "Psalm 150".

findings.claim: "Unsure" is scored as 0, the exact midpoint, so "I don't know" is indistinguishable from "I hold a deliberate middle position"; a respondent who answers Unsure to all eighteen items receives a confident result.
findings.evidence: computeScores: raw[s.a] += s.d * (ans[i] || 0). Eighteen Unsures -> scores [50,50,50,50,50,50] -> headline "A theological centrist" -> Closest traditions "Wesleyan / Methodist 83% match", "Anabaptist / Mennonite 78%". All-Agree and all-Disagree respondents also get "A theological centrist" (scores 42/58 on every axis). Standard practice (Krosnick & Presser, Handbook of Survey Research ch. 9) is to separate the scale midpoint from a no-opinion option and exclude the latter from the score.
findings.fix: Rename option 3 "Neither agree nor disagree" (scored 0) and add a sixth, unscored "Skip / don't know". Axis score = 50 + 25 x mean(direction x response) over answered items. Require at least 2 of 3 (3 of 4) answered; otherwise show the axis as "not enough answers" and exclude it from the headline and from the tradition distance (distance over the k scored axes, scaled by sqrt(6/k)). Show "A theological centrist" only when at least four axes are scored and all are centered; if fewer, say "No clear lean yet".

findings.claim: No axis distinguishes Roman Catholic from Eastern Orthodox, so which one a Catholic or Orthodox respondent "lands" on is decided by rounding on the Grace items.
findings.evidence: Distance between the two coordinate sets is 13.2, less than two answer steps on one axis (one step = 100/12 = 8.3 points). A Catholic who answers devoutly Catholic on five axes and leans free-will on Grace (S1 Unsure, S2 Strongly agree, S3 Disagree) scores [75,0,25,8,0,0] -> "Eastern Orthodox 93%", "Roman Catholic 88%". A Thomist Catholic scores [42,0,25,8,0,0] -> "Roman Catholic 89%", "Eastern Orthodox 89%" (identical percentages). Same structure for Pentecostal / Assemblies of God vs Charismatic non-denominational (18.7 apart, second slot always the twin).
findings.fix: For v1 either merge each pair into one family ("Catholic or Orthodox", "Pentecostal / charismatic") or add unscored tie-break items used only in nearest-tradition: "The bishop of Rome holds a God-given authority over the whole church." (Catholic yes, Orthodox no; Lumen Gentium 22 vs. Orthodox rejection of universal jurisdiction) and "Speaking in tongues is the initial physical evidence of baptism in the Holy Spirit." (Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths, art. 8; most non-denominational charismatics say no).

findings.claim: "The creeds and councils of the early church carry real authority, not just historical interest" is affirmed by every confessional Protestant, so agreeing pushes sola scriptura Christians toward "With tradition" and lands Lutherans and Anglicans in "balanced on authority" or below.
findings.evidence: Formula of Concord, Epitome, Rule and Norm 3 and Solid Declaration: "we pledge ourselves" to the three ecumenical creeds; Thirty-Nine Articles VIII: the three creeds "ought thoroughly to be received and believed"; WCF 31.3: decrees of councils are "to be received with reverence and submission... also for the power whereby they are made." Worked case, confessional Lutheran (S13 Strongly agree, S14 Unsure or Agree, S15 Disagree): raw -2 or 0 -> 33 or 50; axis row reads "58% toward With tradition" or "50% centered". A Presbyterian answering per WCF lands 58, "58% toward Scripture alone": two sola scriptura confessions on opposite sides of center. The discriminator between the poles as the fair_summary defines them is infallibility/binding force, not "real authority".
findings.fix: Replace with: "Some church teaching is binding on Christians even where it cannot be proved from Scripture." (15 words, direction -1). Catholics and Orthodox agree (Trent Sess. 4: unwritten traditions; Dei Verbum 9); Protestants disagree (Art. VI: "whatsoever is not read therein, nor may be proved thereby, is not to be required of any man").

findings.claim: The Grace band adjectives "Reformed-leaning" and "Arminian-leaning" are tradition names, so Lutherans, Thomist Catholics, and Orthodox are labelled with a rival tradition on a quiz that promises tradition-neutrality.
findings.evidence: A confessional Lutheran scores 33-42 on Grace (worked case above) and is told "Reformed-leaning" in the headline; Lutherans define themselves against the Reformed precisely on predestination (Formula of Concord XI rejects the Reformed reading). All-Strongly-agree acquiescent answers also produce the headline "Reformed-leaning, sacramental-leaning, open to the gifts". Eastern Orthodox (coordinate 65) would be "Arminian-leaning" though Orthodox synergism predates Arminius by a millennium. Every other axis uses position words, not tradition names.
findings.fix: bands: ["firmly monergist", "monergist-leaning", "balanced on grace", "synergist-leaning", "firmly synergist"].

findings.claim: "Before anyone does anything, God has already chosen who will be saved, and his choice cannot fail" is double-barreled (election + certainty) and is affirmed by many synergists, so it does not discriminate monergism.
findings.evidence: Arminius, Declaration of Sentiments, fourth decree: God decreed "to save and damn certain particular persons" founded on foreknowledge, from eternity, so a foreknowledge-Arminian can agree that God "has already chosen" and that his choice "cannot fail". Aquinas, ST I q.23 a.5 (predestination not on foreseen merits) and Formula of Concord SD XI (unconditional election with resistible grace) both agree while sitting at Grace 55 and 20 respectively.
findings.fix: Replace with: "When God sets out to save a particular person, that person will certainly come to faith." (16 words, direction -1). Calvinists agree; Lutherans (universal grace, 1 Tim 2:4), Arminians, and Orthodox disagree.

findings.claim: "A person can genuinely resist God's grace and refuse salvation to the very end" is true on Calvinist premises for the non-elect, so a Calvinist can agree and be pushed toward Synergist; the sign is right but the item does not separate the poles.
findings.evidence: WCF 10.4: the non-elect "never truly come unto Christ" though called by the ministry of the Word; Canons of Dort III/IV art. 9: the unconverted are lost through their own resistance. The only grace a Calvinist holds cannot be finally resisted is the effectual call to the elect, which the sentence never names.
findings.fix: Replace with: "A person whom God is drawing to salvation can still finally refuse him and be lost." (16 words, direction +1).

findings.claim: "Saving faith is itself a gift God gives to those he has chosen, not the reason he chose them" is double-barreled: the first clause is affirmed by every synergist tradition, so synergists are torn between Agree and Disagree.
findings.evidence: Trent Sess. 6 ch. 8 and canon 3: faith is the beginning of salvation and impossible without prevenient grace; Arminius, Declaration of Sentiments: faith is "a gift of God"; Wesley on prevenient grace. Only "not the reason he chose them" discriminates.
findings.fix: Replace with: "God's choice of who will be saved was not based on foreseeing who would believe." (15 words, direction -1).

findings.claim: "Christ is truly present in a way that goes beyond a symbol" is affirmed by Reformed Baptists and many Baptists (Christ present spiritually with the gathered church), so memorialists on the Supper are pulled toward Sacramental.
findings.evidence: Second London Baptist Confession (1689) 30.7: worthy receivers "really and indeed... spiritually receive, and feed upon Christ crucified." Reformed Baptist coordinate is table 70 yet a 1689 subscriber answers Agree here (worked case scores 75; with Strongly agree, 67). The item must locate the presence in the elements, which is what actually divides the poles.
findings.fix: Replace with: "In the Lord's Supper Christ is received through the bread and wine themselves, not only remembered." (16 words, direction -1).

findings.claim: "Baptism is an outward sign of a decision to follow Christ that has already been made" uses the paedobaptist definition of a sacrament ("outward sign") and decision-theology vocabulary, so paedobaptists agree for converts and Reformed Baptists balk at "decision".
findings.evidence: BCP Catechism: a sacrament is "an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace"; WSC 92 "sensible sign". A Presbyterian baptizing an adult convert agrees with the sentence as written. The discriminating idea is whether God gives anything through baptism, which the item never states.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Baptism is a public testimony to a faith already held, not a means by which God gives grace." (18 words, direction +1).

findings.claim: "Tongues, prophecy, and healing continue in the church today, as they did in Acts" is triple-barreled and the tag "as they did in Acts" makes moderate continuationists hesitate while cessationists affirm that God still heals.
findings.evidence: Grudem, The Gift of Prophecy in the New Testament and Today, distinguishes fallible congregational prophecy from apostolic prophecy; MacArthur, Strange Fire, affirms that God heals today while denying a gift of healing. Both groups are pushed toward the centre by wording rather than belief.
findings.fix: Replace with one gift per item: "The Spirit still gives the gift of tongues to some Christians today." (12 words, direction -1); leave prophecy to statement 9.

findings.claim: "The miraculous sign gifts ended with the apostles or the completion of the New Testament" uses the cessationist category "sign gifts", which continuationist authors explicitly reject, so the statement embeds one side's conclusion.
findings.evidence: The term comes from Warfield and later dispensational cessationism; Grudem, Systematic Theology ch. 52, and Deere, Surprised by the Power of the Spirit, argue Paul has no such category. A continuationist cannot answer the item without conceding the premise. Standard item-writing guidance (DeVellis, Scale Development) bars vocabulary that presupposes the answer.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The gifts of tongues, prophecy, and healing belonged to the apostolic age and have ceased." (15 words, direction +1).

findings.claim: "A modern-day prophecy should be weighed carefully, but it can genuinely come from the Spirit" leads with a concession everyone accepts, and "prophecy" is undefined, so cessationists who allow Spirit-given impressions or Spirit-illumined preaching can agree.
findings.evidence: Concessive openers raise agreement rates regardless of the second clause (acquiescence literature; Krosnick & Presser). Cessationist writers routinely affirm that the Spirit prompts and guides believers today while denying prophecy; the item lets them answer Agree.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The Spirit still gives some Christians specific prophetic words for the church today." (13 words, direction -1).

findings.claim: "fulfilled literally" is dispensationalist self-description; covenantal readers claim they also read literally according to genre, and Reformed readers who expect a future calling of the Jews half-agree with "promises to national Israel will be fulfilled".
findings.evidence: Ryrie, Dispensationalism, makes "consistent literal interpretation" the sine qua non; Westminster Larger Catechism Q.191 prays that "the Jews [be] called". The direction (+1) is correct.
findings.fix: Replace with: "God will yet give the nation of Israel its promised land and kingdom on this earth." (16 words, direction +1).

findings.claim: "The church is the true Israel, heir to every promise God made to Abraham" is supersessionist phrasing that many covenantal Christians, including Catholics (kingdom coordinate 15), refuse, so they are pushed toward Dispensational.
findings.evidence: Nostra Aetate 4 and CCC 839-840 affirm the Jewish people's irrevocable election (Rom 11:29); many covenantal theologians say Christ, not the church, is the true Israel. A Catholic answering S10 Strongly disagree, S11 Disagree, S12 Strongly disagree scores 25 instead of 8. "True Israel" is also the phrase dispensationalists cite as "replacement theology", so it reads as partisan on both sides.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The promises God made to Abraham and Israel are inherited by the church, Jew and Gentile together in Christ." (19 words, direction -1).

findings.claim: "Believers will be caught up to meet Christ before a seven-year tribulation" measures the pretribulational rapture, a sub-position, so one third of the Kingdom axis is spent on a question that post-tribulational and pre-wrath dispensationalists answer against their own pole.
findings.evidence: Gundry, The Church and the Tribulation (post-trib, dispensational); Rosenthal, The Pre-Wrath Rapture of the Church; "seven-year tribulation" is itself dispensational vocabulary (Dan 9:27 reading). Worked case: a post-trib dispensationalist (S10 +2, S11 -2, S12 -2) scores 67, "dispensational-leaning", not "dispensational". Everyone else floors the item, so it adds no information about covenantal respondents.
findings.fix: Replace with the core construct: "Israel and the church are two distinct peoples with distinct roles in God's plan." (14 words, direction +1). Keep the rapture item for an extended version.

findings.claim: "Every doctrine must be proven from Scripture alone; tradition can never bind the conscience" is double-barreled and overstates the Protestant standard, so material-sufficiency Catholics and Orthodox can agree with the first clause while rejecting the second.
findings.evidence: WCF 1.6 limits the claim to what is "expressly set down... or by good and necessary consequence"; Art. VI to "things necessary to salvation". Congar and much post-conciliar Catholic theology hold the material sufficiency of Scripture, so clause one does not separate the poles.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Only Scripture is infallible; every creed, council, and teacher can err and must be tested by it." (17 words, direction +1). WCF 31.4 ("all synods or councils... may err") vs. Catholic/Orthodox infallibility of ecumenical councils.

findings.claim: "The church, not the individual reader, is the final interpreter of Scripture" poses a false dichotomy that confessional Protestants also affirm, compounding statement 13's pull of sola scriptura respondents toward "With tradition".
findings.evidence: Mathison, The Shape of Sola Scriptura (listed in this axis's own read_more, right side) argues exactly that the church, not the individual, interprets within the rule of faith, against "solo scriptura". WCF 1.10 makes "the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture" the supreme judge, which is neither of the two options offered.
findings.fix: Replace with: "A church council or teaching office can settle the meaning of Scripture with final, unappealable authority." (16 words, direction -1). Dei Verbum 10 (authentic interpretation entrusted to the Magisterium) vs. WCF 31.4.

findings.claim: "Worship should follow a set liturgy that connects us to the historic church" attaches a rationale to the claim, so regulative-principle churches with a fixed order but no prayer book answer Unsure.
findings.evidence: Westminster Directory for Public Worship (1645) prescribes a fixed order while rejecting set forms; such respondents agree with "set" and disagree with "liturgy that connects us to the historic church".
findings.fix: Replace with: "Sunday worship should follow a fixed, historic order of service, not one planned fresh each week." (16 words, direction -1).

findings.claim: "Worship should be free-form and led by the Spirit in the moment" measures spontaneity, not non-liturgical worship, and its "led by the Spirit" clause makes disagreement feel like denying the Spirit; typical planned non-liturgical churches disagree and are pushed toward Liturgical.
findings.evidence: Worked case: a Southern Baptist with a planned, non-liturgical service answers S16 Disagree, S17 Disagree, S18 Disagree -> raw +1 -> 58, "58% toward Free", against a Southern Baptist coordinate of 70. Liturgical charismatics (e.g., Anglican renewal parishes) agree with "led by the Spirit" and disagree with "free-form".
findings.fix: Replace with: "Each congregation should shape its own order of service rather than follow a prescribed liturgy." (15 words, direction +1). If spontaneity is wanted, make it a separate item.

findings.claim: "Communion should be celebrated every week as the center of the service" cross-loads on the Table axis and is practised by memorialist non-liturgical groups while many liturgical churches do not, so it mis-sorts both.
findings.evidence: Churches of Christ and Plymouth Brethren keep a weekly memorial Supper with no liturgy; Methodists historically communed monthly or quarterly, most Presbyterian churches monthly, and many Anglican evangelical parishes make Morning Prayer the main service. Worked case: a Brethren member (S16 Strongly disagree, S17 Agree, S18 Strongly agree) scores 58, "flexible in worship", though their open meeting is the archetype of free worship.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The church year (Advent, Lent, Easter, Pentecost) should shape what a congregation does each Sunday." (15 words, direction -1).

findings.claim: Keying is unbalanced on every axis (two items toward one pole, one toward the other; five axes lean left-keyed, Kingdom right-keyed), so acquiescence produces a systematic profile, and three items give only 13 score levels with a single answer step of 8.3 points crossing a band boundary in 4 of 12 transitions.
findings.evidence: All 18 direction signs are correct given the pole definitions (agreement with 1,3,4,6,7,9,11,13,15,16,18 pushes left; with 2,5,8,10,12,14,17 pushes right). All-Strongly-agree -> [33,33,33,67,33,33] -> "Reformed-leaning, sacramental-leaning, open to the gifts"; all-Agree -> [42,42,42,58,42,42]. One flip Strongly agree -> Strongly disagree moves an axis 33 points (two bands). Three heterogeneous items per axis will not reach conventional reliability (alpha .70).
findings.fix: v1: four items per axis (24 items, ~4 minutes), keyed 2/2, using the rewrites above plus one opposite-keyed addition per axis; six per axis if per-axis reliability is to be reported. Candidates (direction in brackets): Grace: [+1] "Someone truly born again can later fall away and be finally lost."; [+1] "God gives everyone enough grace to believe; the difference lies in how each person responds."; [-1] "Whether a person believes is ultimately decided by God, not by the person." Table: [+1] "Baptism should be given only to those old enough to profess faith for themselves."; [+1] "The bread and wine remain ordinary bread and wine; the Supper's value is in remembering."; [-1] "In baptism God himself acts: he washes, seals, or joins the person to Christ." Spirit: [+1] "With the Bible complete, the church no longer needs prophecy to hear from God."; [+1] "Tongues today are learned or emotional speech, not the gift described in the New Testament."; [-1] "Every Christian should eagerly seek the gifts of the Spirit, including the more dramatic ones." Kingdom: [-1] "There will be no future period in which God deals with Israel separately from the church."; [-1] "The Old Testament land promises find their fulfilment in Christ and the new creation."; [+1] "Ethnic Israel still has a distinct future role in God's plan that the church has not taken over." Tradition: [+1] "A Christian with an open Bible may rightly reject a teaching that every council has affirmed."; [+1] "Practices not found in Scripture, however ancient, may be dropped by any church."; [-1] "What the apostles handed down by word of mouth carries the same authority as what they wrote." Worship: [+1] "Spontaneous prayer in one's own words suits public worship better than prayers read from a book."; [+1] "A church should adapt its service style to the people it serves rather than keep historic forms."; [-1] "The congregation should say or sing set responses, creeds, and prayers together each week."

findings.claim: The permalink code quantizes scores to multiples of 4, so a shared link can show a different band and headline from the one the taker saw; the band edge at 59/60 sits 1.7 points from a reachable score.
findings.evidence: encode: Math.round(score/4), decode: q*4. Raw +1 -> 58 ("centered", band 2) -> code 15 -> decoded 60 -> band 3 ("memorial-leaning", "Scripture-first", etc.). Raw 0 -> 50 ("50% centered") -> decoded 52 -> "52% toward [right pole]". Also 42->44, 17->16, 25->24, 33->32, 67->68, 75->76, 83->84. The thresholds themselves are sound: in raw terms bands are [-6..-4], [-3,-2], [-1..1], [2,3], [4..6], and the same cutpoints (mean of direction x response at +/-0.36 and +/-1.2) stay sensible for 4 to 6 items.
findings.fix: Encode the exact raw sums: n = sum over axes of (raw_i + 6) x 13^i (max 13^6 - 1 = 4,826,808, five base-36 characters), decode back to the identical score; or encode the eighteen answers (5^18, nine base-36 characters). Document the bands in raw/mean terms: centered = |mean| <= 0.36, leaning = 0.36 < |mean| < 1.2, firm = |mean| >= 1.2.

findings.claim: The headline takes the three largest deviations even when only one or two axes deviate, so "no position" adjectives appear as if they were positions, and ties are broken by axis index so Grace, Table, and Spirit are over-represented.
findings.evidence: [8,50,50,50,50,58] -> "Firmly monergist, flexible in worship, centered on the sacraments". [33,67,50,50,50,50] -> "Reformed-leaning, memorial-leaning, undecided on the gifts". Tie rule (b.d - a.d) || (a.i - b.i): with 13 discrete values, |d| in {8,17,25,33,42,50} ties constantly; [50,50,50,67,50,33] -> "Dispensational-leaning, liturgy-leaning, balanced on grace".
findings.fix: Candidates = axes with band != 2, sorted by |score - 50| descending, ties broken by the number of Strongly answers on that axis, then by index; take at most three. Zero candidates -> "A theological centrist"; one or two -> those adjectives followed by "centered elsewhere" (e.g. "Firmly monergist, centered elsewhere").

findings.claim: The nearest-tradition percentage is distance over a 245-point diagonal nobody spans, so all matches cluster at 75-95%, first and second places can show identical percentages, the second slot is usually a fixed twin, and a single-answer change on one unreliable axis decides the ranking.
findings.evidence: MAXD = sqrt(6 x 100^2) = 244.9. Person at the exact Roman Catholic coordinates: 100% Catholic, 95% Orthodox; Thomist Catholic: 89% / 89%; all-Unsure: 83% Wesleyan. Closest tradition pairs: Roman Catholic-Eastern Orthodox 13.2, Pentecostal-Charismatic 18.7, Southern Baptist-Dispensational 30.8. Largest inter-tradition distance is 171.5 (Dispensational Bible church vs Eastern Orthodox), so even the farthest possible real profile reads about 30%. Axis tradition spreads are 70-85 points, so equal weighting is defensible for v1; the problem is reliability (one step = 8.3 points, one flip = 33), not weighting.
findings.fix: match = max(0, round(100 - 100 x d / 170)) with 170 = largest distance between listed traditions; show the primary result as "N of 6 axes within one band of this tradition"; if the two nearest are under 20 apart, present them as one family and use the unscored tie-break items (see general finding) to pick the name; never display equal percentages for different ranks without the distance-ordered rank being visible.

findings.claim: The result copy "Match is 100 minus your distance across all six axes" describes a formula the page does not use; a reader who checks the arithmetic will find it false.
findings.evidence: Code: match = round(100 - d / MAXD * 100). Worked Lutheran case: d = 25.8, displayed match 89%, whereas "100 minus your distance" gives 74.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Match is 100 minus your distance from that tradition, taken as a share of the longest possible distance across all six axes." (or, after the formula change above: "...as a share of the distance between the two farthest-apart traditions").

findings.claim: The 41-59 adjectives "centered on the sacraments" and "centered on the kingdom" read as substantive theological positions (sacrament-centred, kingdom-centred), not as "in the middle of this axis", and can appear in the headline.
findings.evidence: headline() joins band adjectives directly: a memorialist-leaning respondent at Table 58 can be headlined "centered on the sacraments"; Table 42 rows show "58% toward Sacramental" next to "centered on the sacraments". Other axes use unambiguous middle labels ("balanced on grace", "balanced on authority", "flexible in worship").
findings.fix: table bands[2]: "between sacramental and memorial"; kingdom bands[2]: "between covenantal and dispensational".

findings.claim: The per-axis lean text "N% toward <pole>" contradicts the band adjective shown beside it: a score of 42, banded "balanced on grace", is printed as "58% toward Monergist", and 50 prints as "50% · centered".
findings.evidence: lean(): s < 50 ? (100 - s) + '% toward ' + left : s + '% toward ' + right; s === 50 -> '50% · centered'. Raw -1 (one net Agree) becomes a "58%" majority-sounding lean in the Axis-by-axis rows and the history accordion headers.
findings.fix: lean() -> |score - 50| + " points toward " + pole + " · " + band adjective (e.g. "8 points toward Monergist · balanced on grace"); at 50: "at the center"; at 0/100: "at the Monergist pole".

findings.claim: "undecided on the gifts" labels a deliberate mediating position as indecision; the 41-59 band on this axis is a recognised, named view.
findings.evidence: Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views (Zondervan, ed. Grudem) names the mediating position "open but cautious" (Saucy). A respondent who affirms prophecy but denies tongues answers decisively yet lands in this band. "open to the gifts" (band 1) and "cautious about the gifts" (band 3) also reuse the same two words at different strengths.
findings.fix: bands: ["continuationist", "continuationist-leaning", "open but cautious", "cessationist-leaning", "cessationist"].

findings.claim: The pole definitions make infant baptism definitional of the sacramental view ("and so the children of believers are baptized") and believer's baptism definitional of the memorial view, so credobaptist sacramentalists and paedobaptist memorialists have no place on the axis.
findings.evidence: Churches of Christ / Restoration Movement (roughly 1.5 million in the US) baptize believers only and hold baptism is "for the remission of sins" (Acts 2:38) while keeping a weekly memorial Supper; Reformed Baptists confess spiritual feeding on Christ (1689 LBCF 30.7) with believer's baptism. Two of the three Table items (5, 6) are about baptism's subjects, one about the Supper, so the axis is two constructs (efficacy, subjects) scored as one.
findings.fix: Define the poles by efficacy only and demote subjects to an indicator: "...baptism joins a person to Christ and his church (most such churches therefore also baptize believers' infants)." and "...so both are ordinances of obedience rather than channels of grace (most such churches baptize only those who profess faith)." Keep S6 as one item among four, not as the pole's definition.

findings.claim: tradition: 35 places confessional Lutherans in the "tradition-friendly" band, contradicting the Formula of Concord, and the value only "fits" because statements 13 and 15 currently push Lutherans to 42-58.
findings.evidence: Formula of Concord, Epitome, Rule and Norm 1: "the only rule and norm according to which all doctrines and teachers alike must be appraised and judged are the prophetic and apostolic writings of the Old and New Testament alone." Same problem for Anglican (broad) 30 (Art. VI) and Presbyterian / Reformed 45 (WCF 1.6, 1.10), both banded at or below "balanced on authority" on a Scripture-alone axis while Southern Baptist sits at 85.
findings.fix: After the statement 13/14/15 rewrites: Lutheran (confessional) 65, Anglican (broad) 60, Presbyterian / Reformed 70; leave Roman Catholic 10 and Eastern Orthodox 5. Re-check with the worked cases (a confessional Lutheran answering the rewritten items scores 75-83).

findings.claim: "Chrysostom... notes that the sign gifts had ceased" puts a modern cessationist term of art in a fourth-century mouth.
findings.evidence: Chrysostom, Homily 29 on 1 Corinthians, says the passage is obscure "by their cessation, being such as then used to occur but now no longer take place"; he speaks of the charismata, not of "sign gifts", a category continuationists reject (see statement 8).
findings.fix: "Chrysostom, preaching on 1 Corinthians, notes that the gifts Paul describes there no longer occur."

lens: Wesleyan / Methodist (Wesley's sermons, Articles of Religion, Global Methodist / UMC evangelical wing)

simulation.headline: Firmly synergist, sacramental, covenantal
simulation.comment: Answers (statement: answer -> direction*answer). Grace: S1 -2 -> +2 (Wesley, 'Free Grace', rejects unconditional election); S2 +2 -> +2 (resistible grace); S3 -1 -> +1 (I affirm faith is God's gift but deny 'to those he has chosen', so I can only Disagree). raw +5, score round(11/12*100)=92, band 'firmly synergist'. Table: S4 +2 -> -2 (Art. XVIII, spiritual real presence); S5 -1 -> -1 (Art. XVII: 'not only a sign of profession'); S6 +2 -> -2 (Art. XVII: infant baptism 'to be retained'). raw -5, score round(1/12*100)=8, 'sacramental'. Spirit: S7 +1 -> -1; S8 -1 -> -1; S9 +1 -> -1 (Wesley to Middleton 1749; 'The More Excellent Way'). raw -3, score 25, 'open to the gifts'. Kingdom: S10 -1 -> -1; S11 +1 -> -1; S12 -2 -> -2. raw -4, score round(2/12*100)=17, 'covenantal'. Tradition: S13 +1 -> -1; S14 +1 -> +1 (Art. V); S15 -1 -> +1. raw +1, score round(7/12*100)=58, 'balanced on authority'. Worship: S16 +1 -> -1; S17 -1 -> -1; S18 +1 -> -1 ('Duty of Constant Communion'). raw -3, score 25, 'liturgy-leaning'. Headline: |score-50| = 42, 42, 25, 33, 8, 25; top three = grace (idx 0, tie broken by index), table, kingdom -> 'Firmly synergist, sacramental, covenantal'. Distances (squared sums): Wesleyan/Methodist (80,40,45,25,45,40): 144+1024+400+64+169+225 = 2026 -> 45.0 (82% match). Eastern Orthodox: 729+9+100+4+2809+400 = 4051 -> 63.6. Roman Catholic: 1369+9+225+4+2304+225 = 4136 -> 64.3. Anglican (broad): 2704+289+400+9+784+25 = 4211 -> 64.9. Lutheran 88.4, Anabaptist 93.0, Presbyterian 102.6, Charismatic 113.5, Pentecostal 121.6, Reformed Baptist 124.0, SBC 127.3, Dispensational 152.5. Lands correctly, but note (a) the 45-point gap to my own tradition is almost entirely the table coordinate (32 of it) plus spirit and worship: the entry is set at 40/45/40 where Wesley and the Articles put us near 10-25/35/25; with the proposed coordinates (85,25,35,25,45,35) the distance falls to 27.8 (89%), and a 'pew' Methodist (answers -2,2,0,1,0,2,0,-1,1,-1,1,-1,1,1,0,1,-1,0 -> 83,25,33,25,50,33) goes from 21.3 to 6.1; (b) second-nearest is Eastern Orthodox rather than Anglican, which an informed Methodist would find odd since Methodism is an Anglican offshoot, driven by Anglican (broad) being set at grace 40; (c) a Methodist who answers S3 'Agree' because faith is God's gift drops to grace 75 and the headline changes to 'Sacramental, covenantal, Arminian-leaning' (see statement:3).

findings.claim: A person who answers 'Unsure' to all eighteen statements is told their closest tradition is 'Wesleyan / Methodist' at 83% match (second: Anabaptist / Mennonite). The Wesleyan entry sits nearest the six-dimensional center, so it becomes the default label for people with no convictions, which caricatures Methodism as the tradition that believes nothing in particular.
findings.evidence: All-Unsure scores are (50,50,50,50,50,50). Distance to Wesleyan / Methodist (80,40,45,25,45,40): 900+100+25+625+25+100 = 1775, sqrt = 42.1, match = round(100 - 42.1/244.9*100) = 83%. Anabaptist: 625+1225+25+400+400+100 = 2775, sqrt 52.7. Anglican (broad): 2950, sqrt 54.3. The headline correctly says 'A theological centrist' but the result subtitle, the card, and the share text still say 'Closest traditions: Wesleyan / Methodist, Anabaptist / Mennonite'.
findings.fix: Two changes together: (1) when the headline rule fires (all six axes within 10 of 50), replace the 'Closest traditions' list with 'Your answers sit too close to the center to name a nearest tradition' and omit the 'Closest:' line from the share text and card; (2) move the Wesleyan entry off the median to (grace 85, table 25, spirit 35, kingdom 25, tradition 45, worship 35), which makes its all-Unsure distance 54.3 (no longer first). Also consider normalizing match % by a realistic maximum (e.g. 150) rather than sqrt(6)*100 = 244.9, which currently turns a 42-point miss into '83% match'.

findings.claim: table: 40 places Methodists in the 'sacramental-leaning' band, only ten points from the midpoint toward memorialism. Methodist doctrinal standards are firmly sacramental: infant baptism, baptismal regeneration language, and a real spiritual presence. spirit: 45 and worship: 40 are also slightly too high for a tradition whose founder was a soft continuationist and a weekly communicant.
findings.evidence: Articles of Religion (Methodist), Art. XVI: sacraments are 'certain signs of grace, and God's good will toward us, by the which he doth work invisibly in us'; Art. XVII: baptism is 'a sign of regeneration or the new birth. The Baptism of young children is to be retained in the Church'; Art. XVIII: 'the body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten in the Supper, only after an heavenly and spiritual manner.' Wesley, 'A Treatise on Baptism' (1756); 'The Duty of Constant Communion' (Sermon 101). UMC 'By Water and the Spirit' (1996) and 'This Holy Mystery' (2004, recommends weekly communion); the Global Methodist Book of Doctrines and Discipline retains the Articles verbatim. Wesley to Conyers Middleton (1749) and Sermon 89 'The More Excellent Way': the gifts ceased because 'the love of many waxed cold', not by design. A member answering S4 +2, S5 -1, S6 +2 scores table 8; even a 'pew' Methodist (+1, 0, +2) scores 25. Score 40 requires agreeing that baptism is 'a sign of a decision already made', which is the credobaptist view the Articles reject. Arithmetic: informed-member distance to the entry falls from 45.0 to 27.8, pew-member from 21.3 to 6.1, with the proposed coordinates.
findings.fix: Set Wesleyan / Methodist to {grace: 85, table: 25, spirit: 35, kingdom: 25, tradition: 45, worship: 35}. If the entry is meant to also cover the Wesleyan-Holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan Church, Free Methodist, Salvation Army), whose Manuals use memorial language and allow dedication instead of infant baptism, split it: 'Methodist (UMC / Global Methodist)' at the coordinates above and 'Wesleyan-Holiness (Nazarene / Wesleyan)' at about {grace: 85, table: 60, spirit: 35, kingdom: 35, tradition: 65, worship: 60}. The list already splits Baptists three ways, so this is proportionate.

findings.claim: 'Saving faith is itself a gift God gives to those he has chosen, not the reason he chose them' is double-barreled. Wesleyans affirm the first clause (faith is God's gift, given through prevenient grace) and deny the second (election rests on foreseen faith). A Methodist who answers the clause they hear first is pushed 17 points toward monergism and loses the 'firmly synergist' headline.
findings.evidence: Wesley, 'Salvation by Faith' (Sermon 1): faith 'is the gift of God'; Art. IX 'Of the Justification of Man'; Wesley, 'Predestination Calmly Considered' (1752): election 'according to the foreknowledge of God' (1 Pet 1:2). With the other grace answers fixed at -2 and +2, S3 = -1 gives grace 92 ('firmly synergist'); S3 = +1 gives grace 75 and headline 'Sacramental, covenantal, Arminian-leaning'. A statement that a real adherent can honestly answer either way on a 17-point swing is not measuring what it claims.
findings.fix: Replace with a single-barreled monergism-of-conversion statement that Wesleyans, Catholics and Orthodox will disagree with and Reformed and Lutherans will agree with: 'God alone creates saving faith in a person; the sinner contributes nothing to conversion, not even the decision to believe.' (direction -1). Move the election content into statement 1 (see statement:1).

findings.claim: The top synergist band is 'firmly synergist', while the band below it is 'Arminian-leaning'. Methodists happily accept 'Arminian' (Wesley named his magazine after it) but do not call themselves 'synergists'; in Reformed polemics 'synergism' is the standard pejorative for semi-Pelagianism, so a fully committed Wesleyan gets the one label on the axis their critics use and their own theologians avoid.
findings.evidence: Wesley, 'The Question, What Is an Arminian? Answered by a Lover of Free Grace' (1770); The Arminian Magazine (founded 1778). Randy Maddox, 'Responsible Grace' (1994), coins that phrase precisely to avoid 'synergism'; Kenneth Collins, 'The Theology of John Wesley' (2007), argues the new birth and entire sanctification are God's work alone and resists the unqualified 'synergist' label. Roger Olson ('Arminian Theology: Myths and Realities') is the one major voice who embraces 'evangelical synergism', and he always qualifies it. The band system is symmetric ('firmly monergist' / 'Reformed-leaning' vs 'Arminian-leaning' / 'firmly synergist'), so the asymmetry is in the acceptability of the words, not the structure.
findings.fix: bands: ['firmly monergist', 'Reformed-leaning', 'balanced on grace', 'Arminian-leaning', 'firmly Arminian']. Keep 'Monergist / Synergist' as the pole names (the Orthodox use 'synergy' as their own word, and their coordinate 65 already lands on 'Arminian-leaning', so nothing gets worse for them), and add one clause to the fair summary naming both vocabularies: 'called Arminian or Wesleyan among Protestants and synergy in the Christian East'.

findings.claim: 'Monergists hold that ... his saving grace cannot finally be refused' defines monergism as irresistible grace. That excludes confessional Lutherans, whom the quiz itself places at grace 20 ('firmly monergist'): they confess that conversion is entirely God's work and that grace can be resisted. A fair summary of the other pole should not describe it in a way one of its own major traditions rejects.
findings.evidence: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration II (Free Will): conversion is 'solely' the work of the Holy Spirit, yet man 'can resist' the Spirit; SD XI (Election): election is not based on foreseen faith, and the lost are lost through their own resistance. Statement 2 ('A person can genuinely resist God's grace') is one a Lutheran answers Agree, which the quiz scores as synergist; the summary then tells them monergists deny what their confession affirms.
findings.fix: Monergists hold that salvation is God's work from beginning to end: he chooses his people without regard to anything he foresaw in them, and he alone works faith in them, so that the sinner contributes nothing to conversion, not even the decision to believe.

findings.claim: The middle bands 'centered on the sacraments' (table 41-59) and 'centered on the kingdom' (kingdom 41-59) read as strong positive claims, not as 'in between'. A Baptist at 50 is told his life is 'centered on the sacraments'; a Methodist at 50 on kingdom is told he is 'centered on the kingdom', which sounds like an eschatological position rather than indecision between covenantal and dispensational.
findings.evidence: Every other axis uses a genuinely neutral middle label ('balanced on grace', 'undecided on the gifts', 'balanced on authority', 'flexible in worship'). 'Centered on X' is the pun on 'center' failing: in ordinary English it means 'X is central to me'. The headline joins these adjectives with commas, so 'Firmly synergist, centered on the sacraments, open to the gifts' will be read literally and screenshotted.
findings.fix: table bands[2]: 'mixed on the sacraments'; kingdom bands[2]: 'mixed on Israel and the church' (or 'between covenantal and dispensational').

findings.claim: 'Before anyone does anything, God has already chosen who will be saved, and his choice cannot fail' can be read temporally. A careful Wesleyan holds that God did choose before the foundation of the world (Eph 1:4), according to foreknowledge of faith, and that this choice cannot fail, so the statement does not cleanly isolate unconditional election.
findings.evidence: Wesley, 'Predestination Calmly Considered' §§ 17-20 and Explanatory Notes on Rom 8:29 and 1 Pet 1:2: God elects those he foreknows will believe; the elect are certainly saved. The phrase 'before anyone does anything' is meant to signal 'not because of anything they do' but says only 'earlier than'.
findings.fix: God chose who will be saved without regard to anything he foresaw in them, and his choice cannot fail. (direction -1, unchanged)

findings.claim: 'each person must freely respond and can decline' is the language Wesleyans are most often accused with ('free will'). Wesley insisted the will is freed by prevenient grace, not free by nature, and the summary never uses the one term every Methodist reader would look for.
findings.evidence: Wesley, 'On Working Out Our Own Salvation' (Sermon 85): 'preventing grace ... the first wish to please God'; 'Some Remarks on Mr. Hill's Review': 'natural free-will ... I do not assert'. The Confession of Faith (EUB) Art. VIII: 'prevenient grace'.
findings.fix: Synergists hold that God's grace always comes first (Wesleyans call it prevenient grace) and frees the will to believe, but that each person, so enabled, must respond and can decline, so that election follows God's foreknowledge of faith or rests on his choice of a people in Christ.

findings.claim: 'Baptism is an outward sign of a decision to follow Christ that has already been made' conflates 'sign of profession' (which Methodists partly accept, for adult converts) with 'sign of a prior decision' (credobaptism). Because the axis already has a dedicated infant-baptism statement (S6), this second baptism statement adds noise rather than information, and a Methodist thinking of adult baptisms who answers Agree is pushed from table 8 to 25.
findings.evidence: Art. XVII: 'Baptism is not only a sign of profession and mark of difference ... but it is also a sign of regeneration.' UMC 'By Water and the Spirit': baptism is 'God's gift', not primarily the candidate's act. Arithmetic: S5 -1 -> raw -5 -> 8; S5 +1 -> raw -3 -> 25.
findings.fix: Replace with a means-of-grace statement that tests the Supper and baptism together and uses vocabulary both poles recognize: 'Baptism and the Lord's Supper are means through which God actually gives grace, not only acts of obedience and remembrance.' (direction -1)

findings.claim: 'Tongues, prophecy, and healing continue in the church today, as they did in Acts' is double-barreled: continuation (a Methodist says yes) and same manner and frequency as Acts (most Methodists say Unsure). The tail clause pushes non-charismatic continuationists toward the cessationist pole.
findings.evidence: Wesley to Middleton (1749) and Sermon 89 argue the gifts were never withdrawn by God, while not claiming Acts-level frequency. The statement's own pair, S8, is single-barreled.
findings.fix: Tongues, prophecy, and healing are still given to the church today. (direction -1)

findings.claim: 'Communion should be celebrated every week as the center of the service' is double-barreled for Methodists, who follow Wesley on weekly (constant) communion but hold Word and Table together as the center, with the sermon at least co-central. A Methodist who agrees with weekly but not 'the center' answers Unsure and loses a liturgical point.
findings.evidence: Wesley, 'The Duty of Constant Communion': 'as often as he can'; UMC 'This Holy Mystery' recommends weekly celebration and describes the service as 'Word and Table'; the Basic Pattern of Worship in the UMC Book of Worship is Entrance, Word, Table, Sending.
findings.fix: Communion should be celebrated every week, not monthly or a few times a year. (direction -1)

findings.claim: 'The church is the true Israel, heir to every promise God made to Abraham' with 'every' leaves no room for the widespread non-dispensational hope for a future turning of ethnic Israel (Romans 11), which Wesley held. Many amillennial and historic-premillennial readers hedge to Unsure on a statement they broadly agree with.
findings.evidence: Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Rom 11:26: 'all Israel shall be saved ... the Jews' as a nation, in a future ingathering. The fair summary itself says the church 'inherits the promises', without 'every'.
findings.fix: The promises God made to Abraham are fulfilled in Christ and belong to the church, Jew and Gentile together. (direction -1)

findings.claim: 'Worship should be free-form and led by the Spirit in the moment' implies that liturgical worship is not led by the Spirit. A Methodist who prays the Great Thanksgiving believes the Spirit leads through the set form; the statement makes disagreeing feel like denying the Spirit.
findings.evidence: The fair summary for the liturgical pole describes 'words tested over centuries' as the congregation praying 'with the historic church', which any liturgical Christian would say is itself Spirit-led. The liturgical statement (S16) contains no matching jab at the free side.
findings.fix: Worship should be free-form, open to what happens in the moment rather than following a fixed order. (direction +1)
