findings.claim: '1740s: Wesley and Whitefield divide the evangelical revival over predestination' is a decade late and omits the document a Methodist would name.
findings.evidence: Wesley preached and published 'Free Grace' in 1739 (Bristol, April 1739); Whitefield's 'A Letter to the Rev. Mr. John Wesley in Answer to His Sermon Entitled Free Grace' is dated 24 December 1740 and was published in 1741.
findings.fix: 1739–41: Wesley's sermon 'Free Grace' and Whitefield's reply divide the evangelical revival over predestination.

findings.claim: The right-pole read-more ('Arminius, Works', 'Olson, Arminian Theology') gives a Methodist reader a Dutch Reformed source and a modern Baptist-Arminian one but not Wesley, whose short treatise is the text Methodists actually hand people.
findings.evidence: Wesley, 'Predestination Calmly Considered' (1752) is the standard Methodist statement on election and is freely available; 'Arminius, Works' (three volumes) is not a realistic read-more for a lay reader.
findings.fix: right: ['Wesley, Predestination Calmly Considered', 'Olson, Arminian Theology'] (keep Arminius as a third if space allows).

findings.claim: The synergist passages (1 Tim 2:3-4, 2 Pet 3:9, Heb 6:4-6) omit the prevenient-grace texts Wesleyans reach for first.
findings.evidence: Wesley's sermons and the Confession of Faith Art. VIII ground prevenient grace in Titus 2:11 ('the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men'), John 1:9 ('the true Light, which lighteth every man'), and John 12:32 ('I will draw all men unto me').
findings.fix: Add 'Titus 2:11' and 'John 1:9' (or 'John 12:32') so the list runs Romans 9, Ephesians 1:3–11, John 6:37–44, 1 Timothy 2:3–4, Titus 2:11, John 1:9, Hebrews 6:4–6.

findings.claim: The sacramental side's most-cited Protestant real-presence text is missing: 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 is the passage behind Art. XVIII's 'partaking', Calvin's IV.17, and Charles Wesley's Hymns on the Lord's Supper.
findings.evidence: Art. XVIII quotes 1 Cor 10:16 ('the bread which we break is a partaking of the body of Christ'); Charles Wesley, Hymns on the Lord's Supper (1745), Hymn 57 and passim.
findings.fix: Add '1 Corinthians 10:16–17'.

findings.claim: The history jumps from Chrysostom (c. 390) to Azusa Street (1906), so Pentecostalism appears from nowhere. Its immediate parent was the Wesleyan-holiness movement, and Wesley himself is the earliest major Protestant voice against cessationism.
findings.evidence: Wesley to Conyers Middleton (Jan 1749) and Sermon 89 'The More Excellent Way' (1787): the gifts declined because Christians 'were turned heathens again', not by divine withdrawal. John Fletcher's 'dispensation of the Spirit', Phoebe Palmer, and the National Camp Meeting Association (1867) taught a post-conversion 'baptism with the Holy Spirit'; Parham and Seymour were holiness preachers. Standard account: Vinson Synan, 'The Holiness-Pentecostal Tradition'.
findings.fix: Insert before the 1906 entry: '1749–1867: Wesley denies the gifts were withdrawn by God; the holiness movement's 'baptism with the Holy Spirit' prepares the ground for Pentecostalism.'

findings.claim: '1830s: Charles Finney's revivalist new measures reshape Protestant services' presents Finney as the origin of revivalist worship. The camp meeting and the mourner's bench were Methodist practices a generation earlier, and Finney's 'anxious bench' was borrowed from them. The axis also has no entry for Wesley's 1784 Sunday Service, which is the liturgical side's Methodist root.
findings.evidence: Cane Ridge revival (1801) and the Methodist camp meetings organized from 1802 (Francis Asbury's journals); the mourner's bench is documented in Methodist revivals by the 1800s-1810s; Finney's 'Lectures on Revivals of Religion' (1835) defends the anxious seat as an existing measure. Wesley, 'The Sunday Service of the Methodists in North America' (1784), an abridged Book of Common Prayer.
findings.fix: Insert before Finney: '1801–: Cane Ridge and the Methodist camp meetings bring revival worship and the mourner's bench to the American frontier.' Optionally add '1784: Wesley sends the American Methodists an abridged Prayer Book, the Sunday Service.'

findings.claim: Nothing in the eighteen statements touches perseverance, yet Hebrews 6:4-6 is listed as a key grace passage. For lay Methodists, 'can a true believer fall away' is the single most common way they distinguish themselves from Baptists ('once saved, always saved'), and the quiz cannot see it. Entire sanctification and assurance are likewise invisible, so the only thing that makes the Wesleyan entry Wesleyan is grace plus infant baptism.
findings.evidence: Wesley, 'Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints' (1751) and 'A Call to Backsliders' (Sermon 86) deny unconditional perseverance; the Confession of Faith Art. XI ('Of Sanctification and Christian Perfection'). Statement 2 tests pre-conversion resistance, not post-conversion apostasy. Arithmetic if S2 were replaced by 'Someone who has truly been born again cannot finally fall away and be lost' (direction -1): Wesleyan -2 -> +2, SBC-typical +2 -> -2 (grace 50 vs coordinate 45), Reformed +2 -> -2, so the axis keeps its spread while separating Methodists from Baptists on the point they themselves name.
findings.fix: If a seventh statement is too many, replace statement 2 with the perseverance statement above; if the six-axis frame is fixed, at least drop Hebrews 6:4–6 from the passages or add the statement it belongs to.
